sources.title: Save Data in a Local Database Using Room

questions.text: What is useful about returning Flow from a Room query?

answers.text: It streams rows one at a time as the underlying cursor is read.
It keeps the query result synchronised with the remote server.
It runs the query on the main thread without blocking it.
It lets collectors receive updated query results as data changes.

questions.explanation: An observable Room query re-runs and re-emits whenever the tables it reads are modified, so the UI can observe local data and stay current without polling. Each emission is a complete query result rather than a stream of individual rows, and Room knows nothing about remote data.

sources.title: Save Data in a Local Database Using Room

questions.text: A DAO method deletes the rows for a user and inserts a fresh set in two separate statements. Why should it be annotated @Transaction?

answers.text: It moves the method off the main thread, which Room otherwise forbids.
It makes Room generate a single SQL statement from the two operations.
Without it, an observer can see the table after the delete and before the insert.
It ensures the delete and the insert run in the order the method declares.

questions.explanation: Each statement in an unannotated DAO method commits on its own, so a reader between them sees the intermediate state: for an observable query that means an emission with an empty list, and a crash at that moment leaves the rows deleted and not replaced. @Transaction wraps the whole method so the pair is atomic and observers only ever see the before or the after. It does not merge statements, change threading, or affect statement order, which already follows the code.

questions.text: In an offline-first app, why is a local data source commonly treated as the source of truth?

answers.text: Because the local copy is newer than the server whenever the two differ.
Because the app stays usable and consistent when the network is unavailable.
Because reading from disk removes the need to handle network errors.
Because the server is treated as a cache in front of the local database.

questions.explanation: Reads are served from local storage, so the UI has data immediately and behaves the same whether or not the network is reachable, while synchronisation updates that local store in the background. The remote source is still authoritative for data the device did not create; the local database is the source the UI reads from, not a claim that local data is always fresher.

questions.text: Which advantage does DataStore have over SharedPreferences for reading a stored user setting?

answers.text: It encrypts the stored values so they cannot be read from device storage.
It writes synchronously so the value is durable before the call returns.
It stores arbitrary object graphs without a serializer being supplied.
It exposes reads as a Flow instead of a blocking call on the caller's thread.

questions.explanation: SharedPreferences reads go through a synchronous API that can block the calling thread, and its apply() reports no result. DataStore exposes data as a Flow and performs writes in a suspending call that surfaces failures, which is what makes it safe to use from coroutine code. It is not an encryption layer, and typed storage still requires a serializer that the caller provides.

questions.text: A Room database version is incremented and the app ships without a matching Migration. What happens on a device holding the older database?

answers.text: Room opens the database and adds the new columns from the entity definitions.
Room throws at open time, because no migration covers every version step.
Room silently recreates the database, discarding the stored rows.
Room keeps the old schema and reports the mismatch on the first query.

questions.explanation: Room compares the stored version with the compiled schema when the database opens and fails immediately if it cannot find a migration between them. Nothing is inferred from the entities, because Room cannot know how existing rows should be transformed. Destructive recreation is a behaviour the developer has to opt into explicitly, precisely because it loses data.

questions.text: A Room entity uses @Relation to load a list of children with its parent. What does @Relation itself provide?

answers.text: A database-level foreign key constraint enforcing referential integrity.
A cascading delete that removes the children with their parent row.
A single SQL join that returns parent and children in one statement.
A convenience query that fetches the children and attaches them in memory.

questions.explanation: @Relation tells Room to run an additional query for the related rows and assemble the object graph, which is why the annotated field must be a collection on a plain data class rather than on the entity itself. Constraints and cascading behaviour come from @ForeignKey, which is a separate and independent declaration, and the fetch is not one join.

questions.text: A Room entity stores a value of a type SQLite does not support. What does adding a @TypeConverter accomplish?

answers.text: It teaches Room how to translate the type to and from a supported column type.
It makes Room store the value as a serialized blob without further configuration.
It registers the type so Room can query its fields inside a WHERE clause.
It generates an additional table so the value is stored in normalized form.

questions.explanation: A type converter is a pair of functions mapping an unsupported type onto one SQLite understands, so the column holds a primitive or text value and Room reconstructs the object on read. The stored form is whatever the converter produces rather than an automatic blob. Because the value lands in a single column, its internals are not addressable in SQL, which is why a field that must be filtered on belongs in its own column or table.

questions.text: An offline-first repository caches a remote list locally. Which policy question most determines whether the UI can show stale data?

answers.text: Whether the cached rows are stored in Room or in an in-memory structure.
Whether the cache records when the data was fetched so freshness can be judged.
Whether the remote call runs on Dispatchers.IO rather than Dispatchers.Default.
Whether the local query returns a Flow rather than a one-shot suspend call.

questions.explanation: Deciding whether cached data may still be shown requires knowing how old it is, so the cache has to persist a fetch timestamp or equivalent marker against which a staleness rule can be applied. Where the rows live, which dispatcher performs the network call, and whether reads are observable all matter for other reasons, but none of them tells the app whether what it holds is still good enough to display.

questions.text: A frequently filtered column gets an index. What is the main cost of that index?

answers.text: Reads of unindexed columns in the same table become measurably slower.
The table can no longer be modified inside a single transaction.
Every write touching the column maintains the index too, so writes cost more.
Queries must name the index explicitly for the planner to consider it.

questions.explanation: An index is a second structure the database keeps in step with the table, so every insert, update, or delete touching the indexed column has to update it too, and the file grows. That is the trade the read speedup is bought with, and it is why indexes are added for queries that actually run rather than by default. The planner selects indexes on its own, and transactions are unaffected.

questions.text: Why does HTTP idempotency matter when designing retry behavior?

answers.text: It means the server returns an identical response body on every call.
It means the request can be retried without any backoff delay.
It indicates whether retrying a request may repeat unintended side effects.
It means the request is certain to succeed on a later attempt.

questions.explanation: An idempotent request produces the same server-side effect whether it is made once or several times, which is what makes automatic retry safe. It says nothing about the response body, which may legitimately differ between calls, and nothing about whether a retry will succeed or how it should be paced. Non-idempotent operations such as many POSTs need an idempotency key to be retried safely.

questions.text: Why should Android network clients configure timeouts?

answers.text: To limit the total number of retries for a failed call.
To bound waiting time for network operations that may stall.
To cap the size of a response body the client will buffer.
To stop idle pooled connections from being reused later.

questions.explanation: Connect, read, and write timeouts bound how long the client waits at each stage, so a stalled server or a half-open connection fails in bounded time instead of holding resources and leaving the user waiting. Retry counts, response size limits, and connection-pool behaviour are configured separately.

questions.text: What is a common use of an OkHttp interceptor?

answers.text: Adding headers and observing or modifying requests and responses.
Defining the endpoint paths and HTTP methods for a service.
Converting response bodies into Kotlin data classes.
Configuring the connection and read timeouts for the client.

questions.explanation: An interceptor sits in the call chain and can inspect, rewrite, short-circuit, or retry a request and its response, which suits cross-cutting concerns such as authentication headers and logging. Declaring endpoints is Retrofit's role, body conversion belongs to a converter factory, and timeouts are set on the OkHttpClient builder.

questions.text: What is the benefit of declaring Retrofit service functions as suspend functions?

answers.text: They retry the request automatically whenever the call fails.
They allow a service interface to be used without a base URL.
They remove the need for a converter factory on the client.
They integrate asynchronous calls with coroutine suspension.

questions.explanation: Declaring a service function as suspend lets Retrofit deliver the result through coroutine suspension, so the call fits structured concurrency: it can be cancelled with its scope and composed with other suspending work without callbacks. Body conversion, base URL configuration, and retry behaviour are unchanged and still configured on the client.

questions.text: What is a key difference between kotlinx.serialization and reflection-heavy JSON libraries?

answers.text: It resolves serializers by reflecting over properties at runtime.
It uses compiler-assisted serializers and supports Kotlin Multiplatform.
It serializes any class without requiring an annotation or plugin.
It requires each model to implement a serializer interface by hand.

questions.explanation: The kotlinx.serialization compiler plugin generates a serializer for each @Serializable class at compile time. Because nothing depends on runtime reflection, it works on Kotlin/Native and Kotlin/JS as well as the JVM, and missing serializers are reported when compiling rather than when the model is first parsed.

questions.text: An API returns 401 when an access token expires and the client should refresh it once and retry. Which OkHttp mechanism is designed for that?

answers.text: An application interceptor, which inspects the response and reissues the call itself.
A network interceptor, which rewrites the request before it reaches the connection.
A call factory, which supplies a fresh request whenever a call is enqueued.
An Authenticator, which OkHttp invokes after it receives an unauthorized response.

questions.explanation: Authenticator is the hook OkHttp calls specifically when a response carries an authorization challenge, and returning a new request makes the client replay the call; OkHttp also tracks the attempts so a persistently failing refresh stops rather than looping. Retrying from an interceptor is possible but the interceptor has to manage concurrency and its own retry limit, which is exactly the bookkeeping Authenticator already handles.

questions.text: A response carries Cache-Control: max-age=0, must-revalidate together with an ETag. What does the client do on the next request?

answers.text: It serves the stored response directly, because an ETag marks it as reusable.
It asks the server whether the stored response is still valid before reusing it.
It skips the cache entirely and downloads the full body again.
It reuses the stored response until the ETag value changes on the client.

questions.explanation: max-age=0 makes the stored response stale immediately, and must-revalidate forbids serving it without checking. The client therefore sends a conditional request carrying the ETag, and the server answers 304 when nothing changed, so the body is not re-downloaded even though a round trip happens. That is the difference from no-store, which prevents caching altogether.

questions.text: A backend adds a field to a JSON response that the Kotlin model does not declare. With kotlinx.serialization defaults, what happens when the client parses it?

answers.text: The unknown key is ignored, because the parser skips fields with no property.
Parsing fails, because the default configuration rejects unknown keys.
The unknown key is stored so it can be re-emitted when the model is serialized.
Parsing succeeds and the value is bound to the closest matching property name.

questions.explanation: A default Json instance is strict and throws when it meets a key with no matching property, which surfaces a schema mismatch loudly but breaks a client the moment the server adds a field. Setting ignoreUnknownKeys = true is the deliberate opt-in that makes additive server changes safe. Nothing is retained for round-tripping, and no fuzzy name matching happens; only @SerialName controls the mapping.

questions.text: A feed is paged with an offset while new items are being inserted at the top. Which problem does keyset pagination solve here?

answers.text: It removes the need for the client to hold previously loaded pages in memory.
It lets the server return every page in a single round trip.
It stops items shifting between pages, which causes duplicates or gaps.
It guarantees that pages arrive in the order the client requested them.

questions.explanation: An offset names a position in a result set that changes as rows are inserted, so a row can move across the page boundary and be fetched twice or missed entirely. A keyset request instead says where to continue from by value, which stays meaningful under concurrent writes. It is a consistency fix rather than a transport or memory optimisation, and both styles still return one page per request.

questions.text: A Retrofit suspend call is wrapped in try/catch that handles IOException. Which failure does that catch NOT cover?

answers.text: A connection that is reset part way through reading the response body.
A DNS lookup that fails because the device has no network route.
A server that replies 500 with a well-formed error body.
A socket that exceeds the client's configured read timeout.

questions.explanation: IOException covers transport failures: the request never completed, so there is no HTTP response to inspect. A 500 is a completed exchange, so the call returns normally and the status has to be examined, either through a Response wrapper or by letting Retrofit throw HttpException. Treating every failure as an IOException is what leads to server errors being reported to users as connectivity problems.

questions.text: An app pins its API server's certificate. What is the principal operational risk?

answers.text: Traffic is no longer encrypted once the pin is validated by the client.
Installed clients break when the server rotates to an unpinned certificate.
The system trust store is bypassed, so expired certificates are accepted.
Pinning applies to every host, so unrelated requests fail validation.

questions.explanation: Pinning narrows trust to a specific key or certificate, so it defends against a compromised or coerced certificate authority. The cost is coupling shipped clients to the server's certificate lifecycle: rotating without shipping the new pin first leaves installed apps unable to connect, which no server-side fix can undo. Pinning adds a check on top of normal validation rather than replacing it, and it is configured per host.

questions.text: A deferrable sync should survive process death and run only when network connectivity is available. Which API is the best fit?

answers.text: A background thread held by an application-scoped singleton.
A coroutine launched in the ViewModel's scope.
WorkManager with a required-network constraint.
A LaunchedEffect that starts when the screen appears.

questions.explanation: WorkManager persists its work queue, so enqueued work survives process death and reboot, and constraints let the system defer it until connectivity is available. Every other option is tied to something shorter-lived: a ViewModel scope ends with the screen, a LaunchedEffect ends when the composable leaves composition, and a thread in a singleton dies with the process.

questions.text: When is a foreground service generally appropriate?

answers.text: For user-noticeable ongoing work that must always show a notification.
For deferrable sync that should run when the device is charging.
For work that must finish after the user swipes the app away.
For periodic polling that should continue while the screen is off.

questions.explanation: A foreground service is for work the user is actively aware of and expects to continue, such as playback or navigation, and it must show an ongoing notification. Deferrable or periodic background work belongs to WorkManager, which the system can schedule under battery and connectivity constraints instead of keeping a service alive.

questions.text: A user action starts an upload that should begin immediately but must survive the app being closed. What does an expedited WorkRequest offer?

answers.text: A guaranteed immediate start, because expedited work bypasses system scheduling.
A promise to run before any other work the app has enqueued.
A request to run as soon as possible, subject to a quota the system enforces.
An exemption from Doze, so the work runs even while the device is idle.

questions.explanation: Expedited work tells the system that this is user-initiated and important, so it is scheduled ahead of ordinary deferrable work instead of waiting for a convenient window. It remains a request rather than a guarantee: each app has a quota derived from its standby bucket, and once that is exhausted expedited requests are treated as regular work, which is why setExpedited takes a policy describing what to do in that case.

questions.text: For apps targeting Android 14 (API 34) or higher, why do foreground service types matter?

answers.text: They select which notification channel the ongoing service posts to.
They declare the foreground work category and related requirements.
They exempt the service from background execution limits.
They set the priority the scheduler gives to the service.

questions.explanation: The declared type states what category of user-visible work the service performs, and recent Android versions require it along with the matching permissions and runtime prerequisites for that category. It is a declaration of purpose that the platform enforces, not an exemption from restrictions or a scheduling hint.

questions.text: An app schedules deferrable work with an API that expresses no constraints, and the work frequently runs late or not at all. Which platform behaviour explains that?

answers.text: Background restrictions apply only to apps that target an older SDK level.
The OS enforces a per-app CPU quota and suspends work that exceeds it.
Background scheduling behaves identically across manufacturers, so the delay must come from the app.
The system defers background execution under Doze, standby buckets, and start limits.

questions.explanation: Android constrains background execution through Doze, app standby buckets, and background-start restrictions, so work scheduled with an API that expresses no constraints can be deferred indefinitely or refused. Choosing an API that states deferrability and its conditions lets the system run the work at a moment it will actually succeed. The limits are not confined to older target SDKs, they are not a CPU quota, and manufacturers add further restrictions of their own.

questions.text: A sync is enqueued as unique work each time the app foregrounds, and a previous run may still be pending. Which policy keeps the pending run instead of replacing it?

answers.text: REPLACE, because it reconciles the request with the one already queued.
APPEND, because it defers the new request until the queue drains.
CANCEL_AND_REENQUEUE, because it restarts the work with the newer request.
KEEP, because it discards the new request when work is already scheduled.

questions.explanation: Unique work needs a policy for the collision, and KEEP is the one that treats an already-scheduled run as sufficient and drops the incoming request, which is what a periodic refresh usually wants. REPLACE cancels the existing work in favour of the new request, so a run that was about to execute is discarded, and APPEND queues the new request to run after the existing one rather than instead of it.

questions.text: A Worker's network call fails with a timeout. What should doWork() return so WorkManager retries it under the configured backoff?

answers.text: Result.failure(), which marks the attempt unsuccessful so it is scheduled again.
Result.success() with output data describing the error for the next run.
It should throw the exception, so WorkManager records it and reschedules.
Result.retry(), which asks WorkManager to run the work again later.

questions.explanation: Result.retry() is the explicit request to run the work again, and WorkManager applies the request's backoff policy and delay before the next attempt. Result.failure() is terminal and stops the chain, which is right for an error no retry can fix, such as invalid input. An uncaught exception is treated as a failure rather than a retry request, so a transient error thrown out of doWork() is lost.

questions.text: A reminder feature wants to fire at a precise user-chosen time on modern Android. What does using an exact alarm require?

answers.text: A permission the app must hold, since exact alarms are restricted use cases.
A foreground service running while the alarm is pending so it is not deferred.
A WorkManager request with an initial delay, which grants exact scheduling.
A wake lock held from scheduling until the alarm is delivered to the receiver.

questions.explanation: Exact alarms bypass the batching the system uses to save power, so recent platform versions gate them behind a permission and expect a user-facing justification such as an alarm clock or calendar reminder. Deferrable work should use an inexact alarm or WorkManager instead, neither of which promises a precise moment. Nothing needs to be kept running in the meantime, since AlarmManager delivers the alarm itself.

questions.text: Which characteristics point towards WorkManager rather than a coroutine in a ViewModel scope? Select all that apply.

answers.text: The work must survive the user leaving the screen and the process being killed.
The work should run only when the device has an unmetered connection.
The work must update UI state that the current screen renders immediately.
The work should be retried with backoff if it fails while the app is closed.
The work must finish before the current screen draws its next frame.

questions.explanation: WorkManager exists for deferrable work that has to be guaranteed: it persists its queue so a run survives process death and reboot, it expresses constraints such as network type or charging, and it applies a backoff policy across attempts. Work whose only consumer is the visible screen has none of those needs, and driving it from WorkManager adds latency and indirection when a scope that dies with the screen is the correct owner.

questions.text: Why do Android notification channels matter?

answers.text: They determine which activity opens when a notification is tapped.
They group related notifications into a single expandable summary.
They give users category-level control over notification behavior.
They set an importance the app can raise later without the user.

questions.explanation: Channels are the unit of user control: the user can mute, change importance, or alter behaviour per category rather than for the app as a whole. Once a channel is created the app cannot raise its importance again, only the user can. Bundling related notifications is done with groups, and the tap target comes from the PendingIntent.

questions.text: On Android 12 and higher, tapping a notification whose PendingIntent starts a BroadcastReceiver that then starts an Activity does nothing. Why?

answers.text: Starting an Activity from a component the notification tap launched is blocked.
A PendingIntent may only wrap an Activity intent from Android 12 onward.
The receiver needs POST_NOTIFICATIONS before it may launch an Activity.
Broadcast receivers may no longer be targeted by a PendingIntent at all.

questions.explanation: Routing a notification tap through a service or receiver that then starts the Activity, a notification trampoline, delayed the screen appearing and made the launch hard to attribute, so from Android 12 the system blocks that Activity start and logs it. The notification's PendingIntent should target the destination Activity directly, building the back stack with TaskStackBuilder or a deep link where one is needed. Receivers and services remain valid PendingIntent targets for work that does not open UI.

questions.text: For Android 13 and higher, what must most apps do before posting non-exempt notifications?

answers.text: Declare POST_NOTIFICATIONS in the manifest, which grants it.
Request the POST_NOTIFICATIONS runtime permission from the user.
Create a notification channel, which implies the permission.
Raise the app's targetSdkVersion to re-enable notifications.

questions.explanation: From Android 13, POST_NOTIFICATIONS is a runtime permission: it must be declared in the manifest and then requested from the user, who can decline. Declaring it alone is not enough, and creating a channel does not grant it. Posting without the grant silently fails for non-exempt notifications.

questions.text: What is a practical difference between FCM notification messages and data messages?

answers.text: Data messages go to app code; the SDK can display notification messages.
Data messages are displayed by the system when the app is backgrounded.
Notification messages are delivered to onMessageReceived in every app state.
Data messages are given higher delivery priority than notification messages.

questions.explanation: A data message carries a key-value payload that is handed to the app to act on, so the app decides whether anything is shown. A notification message can be rendered by the SDK without app code when the app is in the background, and only reaches onMessageReceived while the app is in the foreground. Priority is set per message rather than implied by the type.

questions.text: An app's FCM messages arrive promptly during the day but are delayed for hours while the device sits idle overnight. What most likely explains it?

answers.text: The messages exceed the payload limit and are queued until the app opens.
Notification-type messages are always deferred while the screen is off.
The registration token expired, so messages waited for the app to refresh it.
They are sent at normal priority, which Doze batches until a maintenance window.

questions.explanation: Doze batches deferrable work while a device is stationary and unused, and normal-priority FCM messages are part of what it batches, so they arrive at the next maintenance window rather than on receipt. A high-priority message is what asks the system to wake the device immediately, and it is meant for content the user is waiting on, such as an incoming chat message, which is why using it for everything risks the app's priority being downgraded. A payload that is too large is rejected rather than delayed, and an expired token fails delivery outright.

questions.text: Tapping a notification opens a detail screen deep inside the app. What must be arranged so Back behaves as if the user navigated there?

answers.text: The activity must be declared with a launch mode that clears the existing task.
The notification must set an ongoing flag so the task is retained until dismissed.
The PendingIntent must carry a synthesized back stack for the destination.
The detail screen must finish itself so Back returns to the launcher.

questions.explanation: Launching a deep destination directly leaves nothing beneath it, so Back exits the app rather than moving up the hierarchy. Building the parent chain into the PendingIntent, for example with TaskStackBuilder or a navigation deep link that constructs the stack, gives the user the destinations they would have passed through. Launch modes control task identity rather than synthesizing history.

sources.title: Start an Activity from a Notification

questions.text: An FCM message containing only a notification payload arrives while the app is in the background. What happens?

answers.text: The system tray displays it, and onMessageReceived is not called.
onMessageReceived runs first so the app can decide whether to display it.
The message is queued until the app returns to the foreground.
The message is dropped, since notification payloads need a foreground app.

questions.explanation: With a notification-only payload the SDK renders the message itself when the app is not in the foreground, and app code does not run, which is why display customisation and analytics cannot rely on that callback. In the foreground the same message is delivered to onMessageReceived instead. Including a data payload is what guarantees app code sees the message in both states.

sources.title: Receive Messages in an Android App

questions.text: Which statements about notification channels and importance are correct? Select all that apply.

answers.text: The app can raise a channel's importance later by recreating the channel.
Importance set at creation determines the channel's initial interruption level.
The user can change a channel's importance after the channel exists.
Deleting and recreating a channel restores the app's original settings.

questions.explanation: The app proposes an importance when it creates a channel, and from then on the setting belongs to the user, who may raise or lower it. The app cannot take it back: recreating the channel with the same id does not reset what the user chose, and deleting a channel does not give a clean slate either, since the system remembers settings for a channel id to prevent exactly that reset. Genuinely different behaviour needs a genuinely different channel.

questions.text: Why should Android test strategy include more than only end-to-end UI tests?

answers.text: Because UI tests cannot assert on state held inside a ViewModel.
Because focused lower-level tests run faster and isolate failures precisely.
Because unit tests also catch integration problems between separate modules.
Because end-to-end tests can run only on physical devices.

questions.explanation: A test suite made only of end-to-end tests is slow and reports failures far from their cause, so a regression means bisecting a long path. Smaller tests around units and boundaries run in seconds and point at the responsible code. They do not replace integration coverage, which is why a mix is recommended rather than only one level.

questions.text: What is a common reason to use a fake implementation in a unit test?

answers.text: To record which methods were called and assert on that afterwards.
To run the real implementation with logging added around it.
To replace a dependency with deterministic behavior under test.
To skip the dependency entirely by returning null from it.

questions.explanation: A fake is a working implementation with simplified behaviour, such as an in-memory repository, so the class under test exercises a realistic contract deterministically. Recording calls and asserting on them describes a mock or spy, which verifies interactions instead of behaviour and couples the test to how the code is written.

questions.text: Why are ViewModels often good candidates for local unit tests?

answers.text: Their state transitions can often be tested without rendering UI.
They expose state as plain fields that tests can read synchronously.
They run on the main thread, so tests need no dispatcher control.
They hold no state between events, so each test starts from clean state.

questions.explanation: A ViewModel maps inputs to observable state without touching the view hierarchy, so with fake dependencies its transitions can be asserted in a fast local test. That still requires handling asynchrony: state is usually exposed as a Flow and coroutines need a test dispatcher, so reading a value synchronously is not generally possible.

questions.text: What is the purpose of runTest in coroutine tests?

answers.text: To run every test on a real background thread pool.
To catch exceptions thrown by child coroutines and ignore them.
To make delay() suspend for its real wall-clock duration in tests.
To test suspending code with a controlled coroutine test environment.

questions.explanation: runTest provides a scope backed by a test scheduler that skips delays using virtual time, so a coroutine that waits ten seconds completes immediately while ordering is preserved. It also waits for child coroutines and surfaces their failures rather than swallowing them.

questions.text: A test must assert the sequence of states a ViewModel's StateFlow emits. Which approach captures them without hanging?

answers.text: Call toList() on the StateFlow and assert on the returned list.
Collect from a coroutine the test cancels, or use a Flow-testing library.
Read .value after each action, asserting the current state each time.
Convert the StateFlow to a cold flow with asFlow() so collection terminates.

questions.explanation: A StateFlow never completes, so a terminal operator that waits for completion hangs until the test times out. The reliable shapes are to launch the collection in a coroutine the test controls and cancel it after asserting, or to use a library such as Turbine that bounds the collection and hands over one item at a time. Reading the current value only samples state and misses intermediate emissions, which StateFlow may conflate away in any case, and no conversion makes a hot state holder terminate.

questions.text: Why do Compose UI tests often query by semantics rather than implementation details?

answers.text: Because semantics are generated from the layout node hierarchy.
Because semantics expose meaningful UI information to tests and accessibility.
Because semantics let a test read a composable's remembered state.
Because Compose provides no stable identifier for a composable function.

questions.explanation: The semantics tree describes what the UI means and what can be done with it, and it is the same tree accessibility services consume. Querying it keeps tests aligned with observable behaviour, so refactoring layout structure does not break them. Semantics describe meaning rather than layout, and they do not expose internal remembered state.

questions.text: A test exercises code that calls Android framework classes but must run in the JVM test task. What does Robolectric provide?

answers.text: A mock of every framework class, returning defaults unless the test stubs them.
A bridge that forwards framework calls from the JVM to a connected device.
An implementation of the framework on the JVM, so no device or emulator is needed.
A compiler plugin that strips framework calls out of the code under test.

questions.explanation: Framework classes in the JVM's android.jar throw by default, which is why a plain local test cannot touch them. Robolectric supplies a working implementation of much of the framework on the JVM, so tests needing resources, a Looper, or a real lifecycle run in the local test task in seconds. It is a middle ground rather than a replacement: it approximates a real device, so behaviour depending on a specific OS version, on hardware, or on the real window system still belongs in an instrumented test.

questions.text: A suspending function under test calls delay(10_000). Inside runTest, how long does the test take?

answers.text: Ten seconds, because delay suspends for its real duration in any scope.
Effectively no time, because the scheduler advances virtual time past the delay.
Ten seconds, unless the test explicitly replaces the dispatcher with a fake clock.
Effectively no time, because runTest removes delay calls before executing.

questions.explanation: runTest installs a TestCoroutineScheduler that models time rather than waiting on it: when every coroutine is idle and only waiting on a delay, the scheduler jumps the clock forward. The delay still happens in ordering terms, so code that depends on the sequence behaves correctly, but the wall-clock cost disappears. Nothing is stripped from the code, which is why a busy loop that never suspends still hangs the test.

questions.text: A test calls toList() on a ViewModel's StateFlow to assert the emitted states. What goes wrong?

answers.text: The collection never finishes, because a StateFlow does not complete on its own.
Only the initial value is returned, because StateFlow emits once per collector.
The call throws, because a StateFlow cannot be collected outside a composable.
The states arrive out of order, because StateFlow conflates its emissions.

questions.explanation: toList() is a terminal operator that waits for the flow to complete, and a StateFlow is hot and endless, so the test hangs until it times out. The fix is to bound the collection: take a known number of values, collect in a background coroutine that is cancelled by the test, or use a library built for the purpose. StateFlow does conflate, which is a separate reason a test may not observe every intermediate value.

questions.text: A DAO test builds its database with inMemoryDatabaseBuilder. What does that mainly provide?

answers.text: A database that skips Room's schema validation so migrations need not exist.
A fake implementation of the DAO, so no SQL is actually executed.
A real database discarded at process end, so each test starts from a clean state.
A database that runs queries synchronously, so suspend functions can be called directly.

questions.explanation: An in-memory database is a genuine SQLite instance with the real schema and real query execution, so the DAO's SQL is actually verified; it simply lives in memory and disappears afterwards, which keeps tests isolated and fast without deleting files. It is not a fake, and it does not change threading: suspending DAO functions still need a coroutine, typically through runTest.

questions.text: Which pieces of work belong in a local JVM test rather than an instrumented test? Select all that apply.

answers.text: Asserting a ViewModel's state transitions with fake repositories.
Verifying that a Room migration produces the expected schema on a device.
Confirming that a runtime permission dialog appears and can be accepted.
Checking a mapper that converts a network model into a domain model.

questions.explanation: Local tests run on the JVM and suit logic that does not need the Android runtime: state holders with substituted dependencies, mappers, and pure domain rules all qualify and run in milliseconds. Anything depending on real framework behaviour belongs on a device or emulator, including system permission UI. Room migrations sit in between and are commonly instrumented, since they exercise a real SQLite implementation and its schema handling.

questions.text: A ViewModel obtains its repository through a global singleton object. Why does that make it awkward to test?

answers.text: The test cannot supply a different implementation without mutating shared state.
The ViewModel can no longer be constructed outside the Android runtime.
The singleton makes the ViewModel's coroutines run on the main dispatcher.
The repository is initialized lazily, so its first call always fails in tests.

questions.explanation: When a class reaches out for its collaborators, the only way to substitute one is to change the global the class reads, which leaks between tests and forces careful ordering and teardown. Taking the repository as a constructor parameter lets each test pass its own fake and keeps the cases independent. The class usually remains constructible on the JVM either way, so it is the substitution mechanism rather than the runtime that is the problem.

questions.text: Which practices most directly reduce flakiness in a suite that intermittently fails? Select all that apply.

answers.text: Replacing real waits with a controllable scheduler or clock.
Retrying each failed test automatically before reporting a failure.
Ensuring no state is shared between tests through singletons or files.
Running the whole suite on a single thread to remove all concurrency.

questions.explanation: Flakiness usually comes from timing that varies between runs and from state that survives from one test to the next, so removing real waits and giving each test its own fixtures addresses the causes directly. Automatic retries hide the symptom and let a genuine intermittent bug reach production. Forcing everything onto one thread removes real concurrency from the code under test, which changes what is being verified rather than stabilising it.

questions.text: What is a common cause of an ANR in an Android app?

answers.text: Allocating many short-lived objects during scrolling.
Running a database query on Dispatchers.IO.
Blocking the main thread with long-running work.
Holding a wake lock while the screen is off.

questions.explanation: An ANR is raised when the main thread fails to handle input or a lifecycle event within the system's time limit, so the usual cause is long synchronous work such as disk or network access on that thread. Moving the work to another dispatcher is the fix, not the cause. Heavy allocation can cause jank through collection pauses without producing an ANR.

questions.text: A user returns to an app whose process is still running and whose Activity is still in memory. Which startup type is that, and what dominates its cost?

answers.text: A hot start, dominated by bringing the existing Activity forward and drawing it.
A cold start, dominated by process creation and Application.onCreate().
A warm start, dominated by recreating the Activity and restoring its saved state.
A hot start, dominated by re-running Application.onCreate() for the resumed process.

questions.explanation: The three startup types describe how much work the system can skip. A cold start creates the process and the Application object before any Activity exists. A warm start reuses the process but recreates the Activity, often restoring saved state. A hot start finds both the process and the Activity in memory and needs only to bring it forward and draw, which is why it is the cheapest and why work added to Application.onCreate() shows up in cold starts rather than here.

questions.text: How can retaining an Activity reference in a singleton cause a memory leak?

answers.text: The singleton can keep the Activity reachable after its lifecycle should end.
The Activity is copied into the singleton, doubling its memory use.
The garbage collector cannot reclaim objects that override finalize().
The singleton keeps a weak reference that the collector ignores.

questions.explanation: A singleton lives as long as the process, so a strong reference from it keeps the destroyed Activity and its entire view hierarchy reachable and therefore uncollectable. Nothing is copied; the leak is that one reference. A weak reference would be the fix, since the collector is free to reclaim through it.

questions.text: A team wants a Baseline Profile that reflects the app's real startup path. How is such a profile normally produced?

answers.text: By listing the app's entry-point classes in a file checked into the repository.
By enabling a Gradle flag that derives the profile from the dependency graph.
By collecting the profile from production devices through the Play Console.
By running an instrumented journey that records the classes and methods it exercises.

questions.explanation: A Baseline Profile is the list of classes and methods worth compiling ahead of install, and it is generated by driving the app through the journey it should cover, typically startup and the first screens, with a Macrobenchmark test that records what actually ran. That is why the profile tracks real behaviour rather than a guess, and why it needs regenerating when those paths change. Play does aggregate profiles from the field, but that complements a shipped baseline rather than being how one is authored.

questions.text: What is a reasonable way to reduce unnecessary recomposition work in Compose?

answers.text: Hoist every piece of state to the top-level composable.
Wrap each composable call in remember to cache its output.
Read state as high in the tree as possible so that reads are shared.
Use stable models and scope state changes to where they are needed.

questions.explanation: Compose skips a composable when it can prove its inputs are unchanged, so stable types plus state read close to where it is used keeps invalidation small. Reading state high in the tree has the opposite effect: everything below is invalidated together. remember caches a value across recomposition rather than caching emitted UI.

questions.text: Why should expensive initialization be treated carefully during app startup?

answers.text: Because work in Application.onCreate() runs on a background thread.
Because synchronous startup work can delay first draw and user interaction.
Because the system kills apps whose cold start exceeds a fixed budget.
Because content providers are initialized after the first frame is drawn.

questions.explanation: Application.onCreate() and content-provider initialization both run on the main thread before the first activity draws, so every synchronous library initialized there is added directly to cold-start time. Deferring non-critical work or initializing it lazily keeps the first frame early; the system does not enforce a hard startup budget.

questions.text: A repository launches work in GlobalScope when a screen requests a refresh. What is the main consequence?

answers.text: The work runs at a lower priority, so results arrive after the screen is gone.
The work is duplicated, because each caller creates its own global scope.
The work blocks the main thread until the coroutine reaches a suspension point.
The work outlives the screen and keeps its captured references reachable.

questions.explanation: GlobalScope is tied to the process, so nothing cancels the coroutine when the screen goes away: it keeps running and keeps whatever it captured alive, which wastes work and can retain a destroyed Activity or ViewModel. Giving the work a scope that ends with its owner, such as viewModelScope, makes cancellation automatic. GlobalScope changes neither dispatcher nor priority, so the coroutine is not slower, just unowned.

questions.text: What does shipping a Baseline Profile with an app improve?

answers.text: It shrinks the APK by removing classes that the profile marks as unused.
It moves class loading onto a background thread during application startup.
It caches network responses needed by the first screen ahead of time.
It reduces interpretation and just-in-time work on the first runs after install.

questions.explanation: A Baseline Profile lists the classes and methods on critical paths so they can be compiled ahead of time when the app is installed, rather than being interpreted and progressively JIT-compiled during early runs. The gain shows up in startup and first-use jank. Removing unused code is R8's job, and the profile changes how code is compiled rather than which thread runs it.

questions.text: After enabling R8 in release, an app crashes deserializing a model that works in debug. What is the most likely cause?

answers.text: R8 renamed or removed members the serializer resolves by name at runtime.
R8 reorders fields, so the serializer reads the values in the wrong sequence.
R8 strips the debug symbols the serializer needs to construct the class.
R8 disables reflection entirely, so no runtime type lookup can succeed.

questions.explanation: R8 shrinks and obfuscates based on what it can prove is reachable from code, and a member only referenced reflectively looks unused, so it is renamed or removed and the lookup fails at runtime. Keep rules, or a compiler-assisted serializer that does not depend on runtime names, are the fixes. R8 does not switch reflection off; the problem is that it cannot see through it.

questions.text: Which conditions typically cause visible jank during scrolling? Select all that apply.

answers.text: Loading data on Dispatchers.IO while the list is being scrolled.
Allocating heavily inside a frame, so collection pauses interrupt rendering.
Rendering more frames per second than the display can present.
Doing layout-heavy work per item so a frame exceeds its deadline.

questions.explanation: Jank appears when a frame misses its deadline, so anything that lengthens work on the frame-producing path matters: expensive per-item layout, and allocation churn whose collection pauses land mid-frame. Work moved to a background dispatcher is off that path and does not itself cause jank. Producing frames faster than the display can show them is bounded by the pipeline rather than being a source of stutter.

questions.text: What does enabling StrictMode's thread policy in a debug build accomplish?

answers.text: It blocks disk and network calls on the main thread before they execute.
It moves offending calls onto a background thread so the UI stays responsive.
It reports main-thread disk and network access so the calls can be found.
It fails the build when it detects a blocking call in application code.

questions.explanation: StrictMode watches for policy violations at runtime and reports them, typically by logging or flashing the screen, so accidental disk and network work on the main thread becomes visible during development. It is a detector, not a guard: the offending call still runs, nothing is relocated for you, and because it is enabled programmatically in debug it has no effect on the build or on release behaviour.

questions.text: Why should an app request a runtime permission close to the user action that needs it?

answers.text: Because a permission requested at startup is denied without a prompt.
Because a later request is granted without showing a dialog.
Because contextual requests explain the purpose and improve user trust.
Because the system revokes permissions not requested in context.

questions.explanation: A request made at the moment the feature needs it carries its own justification, so the user can see why access is required and is more likely to grant it. A request at launch is still shown and can still be granted, but without context it is more often denied, and a denial is harder to recover from than never having asked.

questions.text: Before requesting a dangerous permission, an app calls shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale() and gets false. What does that tell it?

answers.text: The permission has already been granted, so no request is needed.
The user denied it once, so the next request will show the dialog again.
Either it has never been asked for, or the user has denied it permanently.
The permission is missing from the manifest and the request will fail.

questions.explanation: The rationale check is not a permission check: it returns true only in the middle state, where the user has declined at least once but the system will still show the dialog. False covers both ends, the first ever request where the dialog will appear and the permanently denied state where calling the request API returns a denial with no dialog at all. Telling those apart means remembering whether the app has asked before, which is why the recommended flow checks the grant state first and tracks its own request history.

questions.text: Why should exported Android components be reviewed carefully?

answers.text: Because other apps on the device may be able to invoke them.
Because exported components run in a separate process by default.
Because exporting makes a component visible only to signed apps.
Because exported components bypass the app's own permission checks.

questions.explanation: Exporting makes a component part of the app's external attack surface: any app on the device can send it an Intent, so its inputs are untrusted and must be validated, and access should be limited with permissions or by not exporting it. Exporting changes visibility only; it does not change the process the component runs in or disable permission checks.

questions.text: A release build writes an access token to Logcat at debug level. Why is that a problem even though the message never reaches the screen?

answers.text: Logcat output is encrypted on device, so only a rooted device could recover the token from it.
Log entries are retained on the device indefinitely and can be read by any installed app.
The system redacts values that look like credentials from Logcat in release builds.
Log output is collected into bug reports and crash attachments, carrying the token outside the app.

questions.explanation: Logcat is a shared diagnostic channel rather than a private one. Its contents are captured into bug reports, vendor crash attachments, and support uploads, so anything written there travels beyond the boundary the data was collected under. Nothing removes it for you: the platform does not inspect log values, an ordinary app cannot read another app's log entries, and stripping log calls from a release build only happens if the app configures that itself. The rule is not to write the value at all.

questions.text: A notification supplies a PendingIntent to another app's process. Why does declaring FLAG_IMMUTABLE matter?

answers.text: It encrypts the wrapped intent so the receiving app cannot read its extras.
It restricts the PendingIntent to components declared inside the sending app.
It causes the PendingIntent to expire once it has been delivered a single time.
It stops the receiving app filling in fields the sender left unspecified.

questions.explanation: A PendingIntent runs with the sending app's identity, so a mutable one lets whoever holds it complete unspecified parts of the wrapped intent and redirect that authority. FLAG_IMMUTABLE fixes the intent as written, which is why recent platform versions require the mutability to be stated explicitly. It is not encryption: the extras remain readable, and controlling the target component is a separate matter of naming it explicitly.

questions.text: An app stores a symmetric key in the Android Keystore rather than in its own file. What is the primary protection gained?

answers.text: The key material can be backed up and restored on a new device securely.
The key is versioned, so rotating it invalidates previously encrypted data.
The key can be used for cryptographic operations but not read out of the system.
The key is shared with other apps signed by the same certificate.

questions.explanation: Keystore holds the key inside a system component, often hardware-backed, and exposes operations rather than bytes, so an attacker with access to app storage or a backup cannot extract it and use it elsewhere. That non-exportability is the point. Keys are deliberately not backed up for the same reason, sharing is not implied by signing, and rotation is a policy the app implements.

questions.text: A user denies a runtime permission twice, so the system stops showing the dialog. How should the app respond when the feature is next used?

answers.text: Request the permission again, since a repeated request re-enables the prompt.
Explain the impact and offer a route to system settings to grant it there.
Disable the whole screen until the permission has been granted.
Fall back to requesting a broader permission that covers the same capability.

questions.explanation: Once the system stops prompting, calling the request API again returns a denial without any user-visible dialog, so nothing changes and the feature silently fails. The app should explain what is unavailable and why, and let the user open settings if they want to grant it. Broadening the request does not bypass the state, and blocking unrelated functionality punishes a legitimate choice.

questions.text: An app needs to let the user attach one existing photo. Which approach best follows least-privilege on modern Android?

answers.text: Request broad media read permission so the gallery can be listed in-app.
Request legacy external storage access and read the file path directly.
Declare a permission for all files so future features need no further prompt.
Use a system picker, which returns the chosen item without a storage permission.

questions.explanation: A system picker runs outside the app and hands back only what the user selected, so the app gains access to one item and needs no broad permission at all. That is the least-privilege option and it avoids a prompt the user may refuse. Requesting media or all-files access grants standing visibility of content unrelated to the task, which is exactly what scoped storage was introduced to curtail.

questions.text: Why does Gradle distinguish dependency configurations such as implementation, api, and runtimeOnly?

answers.text: To decide which repository each dependency is downloaded from.
To model how dependencies are declared, resolved, and exposed.
To control the order in which the modules are compiled.
To pin the version that transitive dependencies resolve to.

questions.explanation: A configuration expresses the role a dependency plays: implementation keeps it off the consumer's compile classpath, api exposes it to consumers, and runtimeOnly excludes it from compilation entirely. Choosing implementation over api is what keeps module rebuilds narrow. Repository selection and version resolution are configured separately.

questions.text: Twenty modules repeat the same Android and Kotlin configuration. Why is a convention plugin in an included build usually preferred to shared logic in buildSrc?

answers.text: buildSrc cannot declare plugins, so shared configuration is impossible there.
Convention plugins apply automatically to every module without being requested.
A change in buildSrc invalidates the whole build; an included build behaves like a dependency.
buildSrc is evaluated after the modules it configures, so its settings arrive too late.

questions.explanation: Both approaches put shared configuration in one typed place; the difference is how Gradle reacts to a change. buildSrc is an implicit dependency of every project, so editing it invalidates far more than the modules that actually use it, whereas a build-logic project pulled in with includeBuild participates like any other dependency and affects only its consumers. A convention plugin still has to be applied explicitly by each module, which is what keeps the configuration visible in that module's own build file.

questions.text: What problem do Gradle version catalogs solve in a multi-module project?

answers.text: They resolve version conflicts between transitive dependencies.
They cache dependency artifacts so that builds work offline.
They centralize dependency coordinates and versions behind aliases.
They enforce that every module uses the same dependency set.

questions.explanation: A version catalog declares dependency and plugin coordinates once and exposes them as type-safe aliases, so modules stop repeating literal versions and an upgrade is a single edit. It is a declaration mechanism: conflict resolution between transitive versions and artifact caching remain Gradle's normal resolution behaviour.

questions.text: What is a key difference between an APK and an Android App Bundle?

answers.text: An APK is installable; an App Bundle is a publishing format for generating APKs.
An App Bundle is installed directly and an APK is generated from it later.
An APK is unsigned, while an App Bundle carries the signing key.
An App Bundle is an APK compressed with a different algorithm.

questions.explanation: An APK is what a device installs. An App Bundle is uploaded to the store, which uses it to generate and sign APKs tailored to each device's density, ABI, and language, so users download less. A device cannot install a bundle directly.

questions.text: A library module exposes a type from another library in its public function signatures. Which configuration must it use for that dependency?

answers.text: implementation, since consumers resolve transitive types at runtime anyway.
compileOnly, because the consumer supplies the dependency at build time.
runtimeOnly, because the type is needed only when the code executes.
api, so the type is on the compile classpath of modules that consume it.

questions.explanation: If a type appears in a module's public API, anything calling that API has to see the type at compile time, and only api puts it on the consumer's compile classpath. implementation deliberately hides the dependency, which is what keeps rebuilds narrow, so the consumer fails to compile against the exposed signature. compileOnly and runtimeOnly each omit one half of what is required here.

questions.text: A team needs free and paid editions, each buildable as debug or release. How does the Android Gradle Plugin model this?

answers.text: Two build types multiplied by two signing configurations, giving four variants.
Two product flavors combined with the debug and release build types.
Four separate modules, since a variant cannot vary code and configuration.
Two source sets selected at runtime by a flag read from the manifest.

questions.explanation: Product flavors express different editions of the product, while build types express how any edition is built, and the plugin produces a variant for each combination, so two flavors and two types give four. Build types are not the place for edition differences, nothing needs separate modules for this, and variant selection happens at build time rather than from a runtime flag.

questions.text: Two feature modules both need the same user model and repository interface. What is the appropriate structure?

answers.text: Have one feature module depend on the other and export the shared types.
Duplicate the model in each feature so neither depends on the other.
Place the shared types in a core module that both feature modules depend on.
Move both features into the app module so the types are visible to each.

questions.explanation: Shared contracts belong in a module lower in the graph that features depend on, which keeps features siblings that can be built and tested independently. Making one feature depend on another couples their release cycles and tends to grow into a cycle. Duplication drifts, and collapsing features into the app module gives up the modular boundaries that motivated the split.

questions.text: A project has the configuration cache enabled, yet one developer sees it discarded on almost every build. What is the most likely cause?

answers.text: The build has too many modules for the cache entry to be stored.
Build logic reads something at configuration time that varies between builds.
The configuration cache is discarded whenever any source file changes.
Kotlin build scripts cannot be cached, only Groovy ones.

questions.explanation: The configuration cache stores the task graph produced by configuring the build and reuses it while nothing that graph depended on has changed. Reading a system property, an environment variable, the current time, or a file during configuration makes the entry depend on that input, so it is invalidated whenever the value differs. Source changes are exactly what the cache is designed to survive, since they affect task execution rather than configuration, and neither module count nor the scripting language decides whether it works.

questions.text: Which outcomes does enabling code and resource shrinking for a release build produce? Select all that apply.

answers.text: Unreachable classes and methods are removed from the packaged output.
Unused resources can be stripped once resource shrinking is also enabled.
Reflective lookups continue to resolve, because names are preserved.
Resources referenced only from XML are removed, because shrinking analyses Kotlin and Java sources alone.
Remaining code is obfuscated unless that behaviour is explicitly turned off.

questions.explanation: Shrinking walks the reachability graph from declared entry points and drops what it cannot reach, resource shrinking does the equivalent for resources when enabled alongside it, and the surviving code is renamed by default. The one thing it cannot do is see through reflection: names change, so any member resolved by name at runtime must be protected with a keep rule or it will fail after the build succeeds.

questions.text: A news app must remain readable during poor connectivity. Which design choice best supports that requirement?

answers.text: Show a loading state until the newest articles have finished downloading.
Read from a local source of truth and sync remote updates in the background.
Keep responses in an in-memory cache for the current session.
Retry failed requests immediately until the network recovers.

questions.explanation: Rendering from a persistent local store means the article list is available immediately and stays readable with no connectivity, while background synchronisation refreshes it when possible. An in-memory cache disappears with the process, and blocking on the network or retrying tightly makes the poor-connectivity case worse rather than better.

questions.text: A client must reflect server-side changes that happen unpredictably, perhaps a few times a day. Which approach best balances freshness against battery?

answers.text: Poll on a short fixed interval so the delay never exceeds one period.
Hold an always-open socket so the server can deliver changes immediately.
Push the full changed payload so the client never needs a follow-up request.
Push a lightweight signal and let the client fetch the changed data.

questions.explanation: Polling spends battery and requests in proportion to the interval rather than to how often anything changes, and it still adds latency of up to a full period. A push carrying only a signal wakes the client when there is genuinely something to fetch, and having it fetch over the normal API keeps one code path, avoids the size and ordering limits of the push channel, and lets the client reconcile whatever it missed while offline. A persistent socket suits genuinely conversational features but is expensive to hold open for a handful of events a day.

questions.text: When designing background sync that the system may defer, which factors can the platform scheduler honour? Select all that apply.

answers.text: The exact wall-clock time at which each sync must run.
Network availability and whether the connection is metered.
Battery level and whether the device is charging.
The specific dispatcher on which the worker's coroutines should resume.
OS background execution limits and the retry policy.

questions.explanation: A deferrable scheduler decides when to run work, and it can act on connectivity and metering, battery and charging state, and the platform's background execution limits, applying a backoff policy between retries. It cannot promise a specific moment: deferrable work is batched and delayed, so a requirement for exact wall-clock execution has to be met by a different mechanism rather than by a sync constraint.

questions.text: A note-taking app allows edits offline on two devices, and both sync the same note afterwards. Which decision most determines whether a user loses work?

answers.text: Whether the client retries the failed upload with exponential backoff.
Whether the local database stores the note in a single table or several.
Whether sync runs under a network constraint or on an unconstrained schedule.
Whether the merge policy is last-write-wins or preserves both versions.

questions.explanation: Concurrent offline edits create two valid histories, and the merge rule decides what survives: last-write-wins is simple and silently discards one edit, while keeping both, merging by field, or surfacing a conflict preserves the work at the cost of more complexity in the client and API. Retries, scheduling, and local schema all affect when and how sync happens, but none of them changes which version wins once both arrive.

questions.text: Which signals most directly help diagnose why a sync feature fails only for some users in production? Select all that apply.

answers.text: Structured logs recording the outcome and reason for each sync attempt.
A count of daily active users on the screen that triggers sync.
Crash reports covering unhandled exceptions raised during sync.
A single aggregate sync success rate covering all users and app versions together.
Metrics broken down by app version and connectivity type.

questions.explanation: Diagnosing a partial failure needs signals that separate the affected population from everyone else, so per-attempt outcomes, crashes, and metrics dimensioned by version and network are all actionable. A raw engagement count says how many people opened the screen but nothing about which attempts failed or why, so it cannot narrow the cause. Diagnostic value comes from dimensions that partition the failure, not volume.

questions.text: A server team wants to rename a JSON field consumed by shipped mobile clients. What makes this safe?

answers.text: Renaming it and requiring clients to update through a forced upgrade.
Renaming it and having clients ignore unknown fields when parsing.
Renaming it behind a feature flag the server toggles per request.
Emitting both the old and new field until the old clients fall out of use.

questions.explanation: Installed clients cannot be changed, so the contract has to keep working for them: emitting both names makes the change additive and lets old and new clients coexist until usage of the old field drops. Ignoring unknown fields protects a client from additions but not from a field it needs disappearing. Forced upgrades are a blunt fallback, and a per-request flag still requires the client to have been built for the new shape.

questions.text: A screen must render instantly on launch and reflect server changes within a minute. Which arrangement satisfies both?

answers.text: Query the network on launch and cache the response for the next launch.
Render from local storage and refresh it from the network in the background.
Render from an in-memory cache populated by the previous session's response.
Query the network and local storage together, rendering whichever returns first.

questions.explanation: Reading from a persistent local source makes the first frame independent of the network, and a background refresh that writes into that same source keeps one observable path so the UI updates when new data lands. Fetching on launch ties the first render to connectivity, an in-memory cache is empty after process death, and racing two sources yields nondeterministic content and duplicated update paths.

questions.text: Why does a remotely controlled flag around a risky rewrite help more than relying on a staged store rollout alone?

answers.text: It removes the need to test the new path before shipping the release.
It lets the new path be disabled without waiting for users to update.
It guarantees the old and new paths produce identical results.
It allows the release to skip review because the code is inactive.

questions.explanation: A staged rollout limits how many users receive a build, but the code in an installed build cannot be changed, so recovering means halting the rollout and shipping again while affected users stay broken. A remote flag turns the new path off for everyone already on that version, which shortens recovery from days to minutes. It complements testing and staged release rather than replacing either.

questions.text: An endlessly scrolling list must survive rotation without refetching every page. Where should the loaded pages and the next-page key live?

answers.text: In the composable, remembered so the list restores itself on recomposition.
In the saved instance state, so the entire page contents are restored.
In a state holder that survives configuration change, backed by local storage.
In the network layer, which replays the previous responses after rotation.

questions.explanation: Rotation destroys and recreates the UI, so paging state has to sit somewhere that outlives it; a retained state holder keeps the loaded pages and the continuation key in memory, and persisting them locally extends that across process death. Composable state alone dies with the UI, saved instance state is size-limited and unsuited to page contents, and a network layer that replays responses is a cache by another name without a defined owner.

questions.text: What is a good rule of thumb when deciding what to put in Kotlin Multiplatform common code?

answers.text: Put all code in commonMain and add expect/actual wherever it fails to compile.
Share only data models and keep all behaviour in platform code.
Share platform-independent logic and use platform source sets for platform APIs.
Duplicate logic per platform so each target can diverge freely.

questions.explanation: Code belongs in common when the concept itself is platform-independent, such as domain rules, validation, and data transformation. Reaching for expect/actual whenever common code fails to compile inverts that test and produces a shared layer full of platform holes. Limited duplication is preferable to a shared abstraction that fits no platform well.

questions.text: A shared Kotlin Multiplatform module exposes a suspend function and a Flow. What does Swift code get by default?

answers.text: The suspend function becomes a completion-handler callback; the Flow needs a wrapper.
Both appear as Swift async functions, since Kotlin and Swift concurrency map directly.
Neither is exported, because Kotlin coroutines cannot cross the Objective-C boundary.
Both are exported as blocking calls that Swift must move off the main thread.

questions.explanation: Kotlin/Native exports to Swift through Objective-C, so a suspend function is bridged as a function taking a completion handler, which Swift can await with a small adapter. Flow has no Objective-C equivalent, so it arrives as an opaque type and is normally wrapped, by hand or with a library such as SKIE, into a callback, an AsyncSequence, or a Combine publisher. Planning that boundary is part of designing a shared module, because the Kotlin API shape decides how idiomatic the Swift side can be.

questions.text: What problem do expect and actual declarations solve in Kotlin Multiplatform?

answers.text: They let common code call a declaration that every platform implements itself.
They generate the platform implementations from the common declaration.
They let common code call platform APIs with no implementation needed.
They allow a common class to inherit from a platform-specific type.

questions.explanation: An expect declaration defines the contract common code compiles against, and every target must supply a matching actual, which the compiler checks. Nothing is generated automatically: the point is that the developer writes each platform implementation behind one shared signature. Where a plain interface plus constructor injection suffices, that is usually the simpler option.

questions.text: A KMP module targets Android, iOS, and JVM. Where should code that only the two iOS targets share be placed?

answers.text: In commonMain, guarded at runtime by a check of the current platform.
In an intermediate iosMain source set the iOS targets both depend on.
Duplicated in iosArm64Main and iosSimulatorArm64Main to keep targets independent.
In commonMain as an expect declaration with an actual for every target.

questions.explanation: The default hierarchy creates intermediate source sets for groups of related targets, so iosMain is compiled once for both iOS targets and can use iOS APIs directly. Putting the code in commonMain is impossible when it touches platform APIs, and adding expect/actual for every target would force JVM and Android to supply implementations they have no use for. Duplicating per target compiles but doubles the maintenance for no benefit.

questions.text: Shared code needs a platform-specific way to read a setting. When is a plain interface with injected implementations preferable to expect/actual?

answers.text: When the implementation must be selected at compile time for each target.
When the declaration is a top-level function rather than a class member.
When only one platform actually needs a distinct implementation.
When the shared code should be testable by substituting a fake at runtime.

questions.explanation: expect/actual binds an implementation at compile time for each target, so shared code has no seam a test can substitute and there is no way to supply a fake. An interface satisfied by constructor injection keeps the platform detail out of shared code while remaining replaceable, which is why it is usually preferred unless something genuinely must be resolved per target. The choice is about substitutability rather than the shape of the declaration.

questions.text: A shared data layer in commonMain needs JSON parsing and HTTP. Why can a typical Android-only library not be used there?

answers.text: Because commonMain compiles for every target, so it can only use multiplatform artifacts.
Because Gradle forbids Android dependencies in a module with several targets.
Because Android libraries are published without the metadata Kotlin needs to resolve them.
Because commonMain is compiled before any platform source set is configured.

questions.explanation: Code in commonMain has to compile for each declared target, so every dependency it uses must publish artifacts for all of them; an Android-only library has nothing for iOS or Native to link against. That is why multiplatform equivalents such as Ktor and kotlinx.serialization exist for this layer. The library can still be used from androidMain, where only the Android target compiles it.

questions.text: Which layers are usually the strongest candidates for sharing in a KMP app? Select all that apply.

answers.text: Platform navigation and system permission handling.
Domain rules and validation that depend on no platform API.
Platform theming and typography definitions for each target's UI.
Data models and their serialization logic.
Repository logic coordinating local and remote sources.

questions.explanation: The layers worth sharing are the ones whose behaviour is identical everywhere: domain rules, model definitions with their serialization, and the coordination a repository performs between sources.
