Navigation and permissions are defined by each platform's own model and lifecycle, so forcing them behind a common abstraction produces a layer that fits neither well. Sharing is judged by whether the concept is platform-independent, not by how much code it moves.

questions.text: A team shares UI with Compose Multiplatform across Android and iOS. What remains platform-specific?

answers.text: The declarative composable functions, which must be rewritten for each target.
The state management model, which differs between Android and iOS runtimes.
The application entry point that hosts the shared composables on each platform.
The layout system, which delegates to native views on each target.

questions.explanation: Compose Multiplatform renders the same composables and uses the same state model on both platforms, so the shared UI code is genuinely shared. What each platform still owns is the host: an Activity on Android and a view controller on iOS, plus the platform bootstrap around them. The framework draws its own widgets rather than delegating to native views, which is what makes the rendering consistent across targets.

questions.text: When is limited duplication across platforms preferable to introducing a shared abstraction?

answers.text: When platform behaviour differs enough that the abstraction fits neither.
When the shared module would need more than one target declared in its Gradle configuration.
When one platform has substantially more users than the other.
When the team wants each platform to keep its own release schedule.

questions.explanation: A shared abstraction pays off when the underlying concept really is the same; when the platforms differ, the common contract accumulates flags and escape hatches until it is harder to follow than two direct implementations. Maximising shared code is not the goal, so deliberate duplication is a legitimate outcome. Needing a multiplatform dependency is an ordinary constraint rather than a reason to duplicate, and release cadence is a delivery matter.

questions.text: An app declares an activity that should be launchable only from inside the same app. Which manifest configuration best expresses that boundary?

answers.text: Declare the activity with android:exported="false".
Omit the intent filters but set android:exported="true".
Protect the activity with a normal custom permission.
Set the application element's debuggable flag to false.

questions.explanation: android:exported controls whether components of other applications can launch the activity. Removing intent filters changes implicit resolution, but an explicitly exported component remains externally reachable; debuggable and normal permissions express different concerns.

questions.text: A bound service must expose typed calls across app processes. Which Android mechanism is designed to define that Binder IPC contract?

answers.text: AIDL, which generates Binder-compatible interfaces from a declared contract.
A BroadcastReceiver, which returns synchronous method results to its caller.
A ContentObserver, which serializes arbitrary method calls between processes.
A Handler, which moves Messages across application sandboxes.

questions.explanation: AIDL describes an interface that the build tools turn into Binder client and service code for cross-process calls. Broadcasts and observers communicate events or changes, while a Handler targets a Looper and does not itself cross a process boundary.

questions.text: Why can posting work to a Handler associated with the main Looper still cause an ANR?

answers.text: The Handler runs each callback on a dedicated Binder thread.
The callback shares the main thread's message queue and can block later UI work.
The Looper executes posted callbacks once the process enters the background.
The callback bypasses the message queue and runs synchronously on the posting thread.

questions.explanation: A Handler schedules callbacks on its Looper's thread. For the main Looper that is the UI thread, so a long callback prevents input, drawing, and lifecycle messages from being processed; posting is scheduling, not offloading.

questions.text: An implicit Intent is sent with an action and a URI. What does an activity's intent filter have to satisfy to be considered a match?

answers.text: Matching the action alone is sufficient; category and data declarations only affect the order of the results.
The filter declaring the highest android:priority wins even when its data declaration does not match.
The filter must declare the action, accept CATEGORY_DEFAULT, and match the URI's scheme and host.
A filter that declares no data element matches any URI the Intent happens to carry.

questions.explanation: Implicit resolution tests the Intent against each filter's action, category, and data declarations, and a filter has to pass all three tests to match. An activity filter must also accept CATEGORY_DEFAULT, because the system adds that category to implicit intents before resolving them. Priority orders competing matches rather than excusing a failed test, and a filter that declares no data element matches only intents that carry no URI.

questions.text: A reusable UI factory inflates a themed View. Which Context should it prefer when the View must inherit the current screen theme?

answers.text: The process-wide application Context.
A newly constructed base Context with no theme wrapper.
The ContentProvider's Context captured during startup.
The Activity or another appropriately themed Context.

questions.explanation: View inflation resolves theme attributes through the supplied Context, so a screen's themed Context is appropriate. Application Context is safer for long-lived non-UI work but does not necessarily carry the Activity theme.

questions.text: Two navigation destinations need independent screen state. What is the key reason to scope each ViewModel to its destination owner?

answers.text: The ViewModel lifetime follows that destination's retained back-stack entry.
The ViewModel is recreated after each recomposition of the destination.
The ViewModel persists its repository data to disk on its own.
The ViewModel becomes accessible to all destinations in the application.

questions.explanation: A ViewModel is retained by its ViewModelStoreOwner and cleared when that owner is permanently removed. Destination scoping aligns state lifetime with the back-stack entry; it neither causes recomposition recreation nor provides automatic durable persistence.

questions.text: A Fragment collects a Flow to update its View. Which pattern stops collection when the View lifecycle is below STARTED and restarts it later?

answers.text: Collect once in the Fragment constructor so it survives view recreation.
Use viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope with repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED).
Launch in GlobalScope and check isAdded before handling each value.
Collect in onCreate and cancel the job in the Fragment's onDestroy.

questions.explanation: repeatOnLifecycle launches the collection block while the chosen lifecycle is at least STARTED and cancels it below that state. Using the view lifecycle avoids updating a destroyed Fragment view; a process-wide or Fragment-lifetime scope outlives that UI.

sources.title: Use Kotlin coroutines with lifecycle-aware components

questions.text: An HTTPS link should open directly in the verified app without a chooser when ownership is established. Which setup provides that association?

answers.text: A custom URI scheme declared alongside a runtime permission request.
A generic VIEW intent that the app broadcasts when it starts up.
An App Link intent filter plus a Digital Asset Links file on the domain.
A PendingIntent whose creator package matches the website's host name.

questions.explanation: Verified Android App Links combine an HTTP(S) intent filter with a domain-hosted assetlinks.json statement that associates the site and app. A custom scheme has no equivalent domain ownership proof, and PendingIntent identity is unrelated.

questions.text: A team is adopting the Navigation 3 library for a Compose app. Where should the app keep the navigation state that drives displayed destinations?

answers.text: Inside each destination composable as private remember state.
In the NavDisplay implementation as an inaccessible framework stack.
In Activity intent extras rewritten on each navigation action.
In app-owned state containing stable navigation keys.

questions.explanation: Navigation 3 makes the back stack app-owned data, typically a state-backed list of navigation keys supplied to NavDisplay. Keeping it outside individual destinations makes navigation state explicit, saveable, and testable rather than hidden in UI instances.

questions.text: Which value is the best candidate for SavedStateHandle rather than a database?

answers.text: A search query needed to restore the screen after process death.
A complete offline catalog containing many thousands of records.
A long-lived audit log shared by several user accounts.
A binary media cache managed with eviction policies.

questions.explanation: Saved-state APIs are intended for small UI-element state needed to reconstruct the screen, such as a query or selected ID. Durable or large application data belongs in persistent storage and should be reloaded after recreation.

questions.text: Why should a Fragment observe View-bound UI state with viewLifecycleOwner rather than the Fragment lifecycle?

answers.text: The Fragment lifecycle stops short of STARTED while its View exists.
The View lifecycle ends at onDestroyView even when the Fragment instance remains.
The View lifecycle survives process death longer than the Fragment lifecycle.
The View lifecycle stores emitted values in saved state for you.

questions.explanation: A Fragment can remain on the back stack after its View hierarchy is destroyed. Binding observation to viewLifecycleOwner stops View updates at onDestroyView and prevents stale references; it does not add persistence.

questions.text: A button is visible only when a LazyList has scrolled past its first item. Why can derivedStateOf be appropriate for the visibility flag?

answers.text: It moves list-state reads to a background dispatcher.
It persists the flag after process death.
It updates the derived value only when the threshold changes.
It prevents the LazyList itself from reading snapshot state.

questions.explanation: The list position can change far more often than the Boolean threshold. derivedStateOf lets consumers update when the derived result changes, reducing unnecessary recompositions; it is not a threading or persistence API.

questions.text: A LaunchedEffect must apply Flow operators to changes in a Compose State value. Which API creates the appropriate cold Flow?

answers.text: rememberSaveable
produceState
CompositionLocal
snapshotFlow

questions.explanation: snapshotFlow observes snapshot-state reads in its block and emits changed results to a cold Flow, allowing normal Flow operators in a coroutine. The other APIs retain state, produce Compose State, or provide values through composition.

questions.text: A LaunchedEffect loads details for itemId. What should happen when itemId changes and is used as the effect key?

answers.text: Compose cancels the previous effect coroutine and launches one for the new key.
Both effect coroutines remain active until the composable leaves composition.
The existing coroutine continues and its captured itemId is updated in place.
The effect restarts once the hosting Activity has been recreated.

questions.explanation: LaunchedEffect is tied to its composition and keys. A key change cancels the running coroutine and launches the block again, which prevents old-key work from continuing as if it belonged to the new item.

questions.text: Why can swapping clickable() and padding() in a Compose Modifier chain change behavior?

answers.text: Modifier order affects source formatting rather than runtime nodes.
Each modifier wraps what follows, so order changes hit area and layout.
padding() executes after input modifiers regardless of chain order.
clickable() replaces the layout modifiers that precede it.

questions.explanation: A modifier chain is ordered: each element wraps what follows. Placing padding before or after clickable can therefore include or exclude that space from the clickable region and alter constraints; Compose does not reorder the chain by category.

questions.text: A design-system colour is needed by many nested composables. What is the main trade-off of passing it through a CompositionLocal instead of a parameter?

answers.text: It makes the dependency implicit, so a composable is harder to reason about.
It prevents the value from changing after the composition has been created.
It forces every reader of the value to recompose whenever any sibling changes.
It restricts the value to types that Compose can save and restore.

questions.explanation: A CompositionLocal provides a value implicitly down the tree, which removes parameter plumbing but hides the dependency from the function signature: callers cannot see what a composable needs, and testing or reusing it requires knowing which providers must be in scope. That is why the guidance reserves it for cross-cutting values with a sensible default. Reads are tracked individually, so only composables that actually read the value recompose.

questions.text: Items in a LazyColumn each hold state created with remember. The list is reordered and no key is supplied. What does the user observe?

answers.text: Every row loses its state, because reordering recreates the whole list.
State stays with the position, so a moved row shows another row's state.
State follows the item, because Compose matches items by their contents.
State is preserved and reapplied once the reorder animation completes.

questions.explanation: Without a key, Compose identifies an item by its position in the layout, so remembered state belongs to the slot rather than the data. Reordering leaves the state where it was and the values appear attached to the wrong rows. Supplying a stable key ties identity to the item so its state travels with it. Compose never compares item contents to infer identity, which is exactly why the key parameter exists.

questions.text: A Compose screen hosts a legacy View with AndroidView. Which statements about that interop boundary are correct? Select all that apply.

answers.text: The factory lambda runs once, while update runs on relevant recompositions.
State the View owns is not tracked by Compose and must be driven through update.
The View is recreated from the factory on every recomposition of the composable.
The hosted View participates in Compose's snapshot system automatically.

questions.explanation: AndroidView keeps a real View in the hierarchy: the factory constructs it once and update pushes new values into it when the composable recomposes with changed inputs. The View keeps its own imperative state, which Compose neither observes nor restores, so anything that must react to state has to be applied in update. Treating the View as if it participated in snapshots is the usual source of stale interop UI.

questions.text: In a unidirectional Compose screen, a child composable needs to change a value the parent owns. What should the child expose?

answers.text: A mutable state object it shares with the parent by reference.
A callback parameter the parent supplies to apply the change.
A CompositionLocal the parent reads after the child has written it.
A ViewModel reference so the child can update the state directly.

questions.explanation: Under unidirectional data flow the child receives the current value and reports intent upward through a lambda, leaving the owner to decide how state changes. That keeps the child stateless, previewable, and reusable, and it keeps mutation in one place. Handing the child a mutable object or its own ViewModel reference gives it a second path to write state, which is what makes conflicting updates hard to trace.

questions.text: How do Handler, Looper, and MessageQueue cooperate when code posts a Runnable to a thread?

answers.text: The Handler enqueues it, the Looper retrieves it, and that Looper's thread runs it.
The Looper enqueues it, the Handler retrieves it, and a Binder thread runs it.
The MessageQueue creates a worker thread, and the Handler blocks until it finishes.
The Handler runs it immediately, while the Looper records it only for cancellation.

questions.explanation: A Handler places work in the MessageQueue associated with its Looper. The Looper continuously takes due messages and dispatches them on the thread that owns it; posting therefore changes scheduling, not necessarily threads.

questions.text: What distinguishes a Binder call to a service in another process from an ordinary call to an object in the same process?

answers.text: Both calls share object references, but Binder serializes exceptions for local calls only.
Binder marshals supported data across a process boundary instead of sharing ordinary references.
Binder always runs the remote method on the caller's thread with the caller's heap objects.
Both calls use the same heap, but Binder adds lifecycle callbacks around each invocation.

questions.explanation: Processes have separate address spaces, so Binder transports a defined representation of arguments and results rather than sharing ordinary object references. A local method call needs no IPC marshalling boundary.

questions.text: Select all that apply. Which statements correctly relate Android component lifetime to app-process lifetime?

answers.text: Destroying one Activity necessarily terminates the process that hosted it.
A process can remain cached after its last component stops executing.
The system can terminate a process and later recreate a needed component.
A started Service guarantees that its process cannot be killed by the system.

questions.explanation: Components affect a process's importance, but their lifetimes are not identical. Android can keep an empty process cached, or reclaim a process and later recreate a component; no ordinary component makes a process immortal.

questions.text: A bound service receives a remote Binder call and must update its Activity UI. Why should it explicitly hand the update to the main thread?

answers.text: Remote Binder callbacks are queued on the Activity's main Looper before service code runs.
Remote Binder callbacks run in a Binder thread pool, while View updates require the UI thread.
Remote Binder callbacks run in the client process, so only the client can touch service state.
Remote Binder callbacks suspend the main thread, so posting avoids recursive service binding.

questions.explanation: Incoming calls to a remotely bound service are dispatched from Binder threads in the service process. Those threads may do concurrent work, but Android's View toolkit must be updated from the main thread, so UI work needs an explicit handoff.

questions.text: Why can the same ViewModel instance be returned after an Activity is recreated for a configuration change?

answers.text: The old Activity instance is retained and continues to own the same View hierarchy.
The ViewModel is serialized into the Activity saved-instance-state Bundle automatically.
The Activity's ViewModelStore is retained and associated with the recreated owner.
The ViewModel is promoted to an application singleton until the task is removed.

questions.explanation: A ViewModelStoreOwner retains its ViewModelStore across configuration recreation, allowing the new Activity instance to retrieve the existing ViewModel. The Activity and its Views are recreated, and the ViewModel is not serialized into a Bundle.

questions.text: An Activity finishes normally and is removed rather than recreated for configuration. What happens to ViewModels owned by that Activity?

answers.text: They move into the Application's ViewModelStore until the process exits.
They remain retained in case the same Activity class is launched again.
They are written to SavedStateHandle and reconstructed as the same instances.
They are cleared because the owner's ViewModelStore is permanently discarded.

questions.explanation: Configuration recreation preserves the owner's store, but a permanently destroyed owner clears it and invokes ViewModel cleanup. Launching the Activity later creates a new owner and new ViewModel instances.

questions.text: After system-initiated process death, how can a recreated ViewModel receive a small saved screen parameter through SavedStateHandle?

answers.text: The parameter is restored through the saved-state registry into a newly created ViewModel.
The Navigation back-stack entry replays its arguments, so values the ViewModel wrote to SavedStateHandle return with them.
The value is restored only because SavedStateHandle mirrors each write into DataStore as it happens.
The repository re-fetches the value in the ViewModel's init block, since saved state does not outlive the process.

questions.explanation: SavedStateHandle is wired into the same saved-state mechanism as onSaveInstanceState: eligible values are written into a Bundle the system holds outside the app process and handed to a newly constructed ViewModel after recreation. Surviving system-initiated process death is exactly what separates it from an ordinary ViewModel field. It is not a mirror of navigation arguments, and it writes nothing to durable storage of its own.

questions.text: A Compose screen has an expanded-row flag and business state loaded by a repository. Which ownership split is most appropriate?

answers.text: Keep both in remember, because recomposition is the only lifecycle either value must survive.
Keep the UI flag with rememberSaveable and repository-backed screen state in a ViewModel.
Keep both in rememberSaveable, because it replaces a ViewModel for all screen state.
Keep the UI flag in the repository and business state in an Activity field.

questions.explanation: Small UI-element state can live close to the composable and use rememberSaveable when recreation matters. Screen business state and data-loading coordination belong in a longer-lived state holder such as a ViewModel; saved-state APIs are not general durable storage.

questions.text: Two destinations in one checkout flow must share temporary state, but a later checkout must start clean. Which ViewModel owner best matches that lifetime?

answers.text: The Application, so checkout state remains available across every task and account.
Each destination separately, so both screens receive independent state instances.
The checkout navigation graph or its back-stack entry, shared by those destinations.
The first composable's composition, retained after its destination leaves the stack.

questions.explanation: A navigation graph back-stack entry can own one ViewModel shared by destinations inside that flow. Popping the graph permanently removes the owner and clears its state, which matches a checkout session better than application or per-destination scope.

sources.title: Navigate with a ViewModel Scoped to a Graph

questions.text: When a destination is popped permanently from a Navigation back stack, what happens to state scoped to that back-stack entry?

answers.text: It transfers to the previous entry because both entries use one ViewModelStore.
It remains until every destination using the same Activity has been removed.
It is serialized as durable app data and restored on the next navigation to that route.
Its owner is destroyed, so entry-scoped ViewModels are cleared and a later entry is new.

questions.explanation: Each back-stack entry is a lifecycle, saved-state, and ViewModelStore owner. Once the entry is popped and destroyed, its scoped ViewModels are cleared; navigating to the route later creates a distinct entry rather than reviving the old one.

questions.text: Select all that apply. Which statements distinguish configuration recreation from process recreation?

answers.text: Process recreation preserves application singletons but configuration changes clear them.
A configuration change can retain ViewModels while replacing Activity and View instances.
Process recreation constructs new in-memory objects and relies on persisted or saved state.
A configuration change restores the old Activity object from a serialized heap snapshot.

questions.explanation: During configuration recreation the process normally remains and the owner's ViewModelStore can be retained, even though the Activity and Views are new. Process death removes all in-memory objects, so reconstruction depends on saved state and durable data, not singleton retention.

questions.text: What is the fundamental difference between a retained View hierarchy and Compose's declarative UI model?

answers.text: Views are immutable descriptions, while composables retain mutable widget objects for direct updates.
Views and composables both require callers to mutate the previously returned UI node instances.
Views retain mutable widget objects; composables describe UI from state and may be invoked again.
Views derive state from composables, while Compose serializes a View hierarchy after each frame.

questions.explanation: The View system keeps object instances whose properties are changed imperatively. Compose treats a composable invocation as a description derived from state and can re-execute it to update the composition, rather than exposing emitted UI nodes for direct mutation.

questions.text: How does initial composition differ from recomposition in Jetpack Compose?

answers.text: Initial composition records emitted UI; recomposition updates affected parts after observed state changes.
Initial composition runs on the main thread; recomposition is dispatched to a background thread pool.
Initial composition runs every composable once; recomposition re-runs all of them and discards results that did not change.
Initial composition builds the layout tree; recomposition remeasures and redraws it on every state change.

questions.explanation: Initial composition executes the composable functions once to build the composition and record what UI to emit. Recomposition re-executes only the scopes whose observed state changed and applies the difference: a composable whose inputs are unchanged is skipped rather than run and thrown away. Composition is also separate from the layout and drawing phases that follow it, so state read only during layout or draw can change the screen without recomposing anything.

questions.text: A text field should keep its draft through rotation but does not need durable database storage. Why use rememberSaveable rather than remember?

answers.text: rememberSaveable moves the draft into a process-wide singleton shared by all destinations.
rememberSaveable prevents the composable from ever leaving composition during navigation.
rememberSaveable writes every change to durable app storage on the calling thread.
rememberSaveable participates in saved-state restoration; remember survives recomposition only.

questions.explanation: Both APIs retain a value across recomposition, but rememberSaveable also saves supported values through the saved-state mechanism for Activity or process recreation. It is intended for small UI state, not general durable persistence.

questions.text: Select all that apply. Which statements describe how Compose state reads affect recomposition?

answers.text: A composable that reads changing State can be scheduled for recomposition.
Every composable in the Activity recomposes whenever any State object changes.
Reading State converts it into an untracked value until the Activity restarts.
Moving a state read into a smaller child can narrow the recomposition scope.

questions.explanation: Compose records state reads by the currently executing recomposition scope. A changed value invalidates scopes that read it, so deferring the read to a smaller child can limit work; unrelated scopes are not automatically invalidated.

questions.text: A custom View's colour changes without changing its size, then its desired size changes. Which invalidation calls fit those updates?

answers.text: Call requestLayout() for colour only, then invalidate() for the desired-size change.
Call invalidate() for colour only, then requestLayout() when measurement may change.
Call forceLayout() for both updates because invalidate() applies only to Compose nodes.
Call neither method because property writes schedule measure and draw automatically.

questions.explanation: invalidate() schedules drawing when visual content changed within the existing bounds. requestLayout() asks the parent hierarchy for another measure/layout pass when size or position may change; it can be followed by drawing as needed.

questions.text: A Fragment creates a ComposeView in onCreateView(). Why should its composition use a disposal strategy tied to the Fragment view lifecycle?

answers.text: It keeps the composition alive after onDestroyView() so the old View can be reused later.
It transfers remembered state from the Fragment view into the Activity's View hierarchy.
It disposes composition when that View lifecycle ends, avoiding work tied to a dead View.
It serializes every remembered value when the Fragment is placed on the back stack.

questions.explanation: A Fragment can outlive its View, so a ComposeView composition should be disposed with the view-tree lifecycle. This releases effects and observation associated with the destroyed View instead of retaining that UI until the Fragment itself is destroyed.

questions.text: Why can passing a stable parameter let Compose skip a recomposition when that parameter compares unchanged?

answers.text: Stability means Compose can trust change tracking for the value and safely reuse the prior group.
Stability moves the composable to a background thread where recomposition is unnecessary.
Stability freezes every referenced object and prevents its properties from changing at runtime.
Stability stores the parameter in saved instance state and restores the prior rendered pixels.

questions.explanation: A stable type gives the runtime a dependable contract for deciding whether a value changed, so when the parameter compares equal Compose can reuse the previous result instead of re-running the function. Stable parameters are compared with equals(); under strong skipping, which is on by default from Kotlin 2.0.20, unstable ones are compared by instance identity instead. Stability is a promise about change notification, not immutability enforcement, persistence, or thread selection.

questions.text: With strong skipping enabled, a composable takes an unstable List parameter and the caller rebuilds an equal list on every recomposition. Is the composable skipped?

answers.text: Yes, because strong skipping compares unstable parameters with equals().
No, because unstable parameters are compared by instance and each list is a new object.
Yes, because strong skipping makes every restartable composable skip unchanged calls.
No, because strong skipping turns off skipping entirely for unstable parameter types.

questions.explanation: Strong skipping, on by default since the Compose compiler shipped with Kotlin 2.0.20, makes restartable composables skippable even when a parameter is unstable, but it compares unstable arguments by instance identity rather than with equals(). A freshly built list is a different instance, so the comparison fails and the composable re-runs even though the contents match. Remembering the list, or using a type Compose treats as stable, is what actually restores skipping.

questions.text: A data class contains a MutableList and is copied with copy(). What happens when the copied instance mutates that list?

answers.text: The compiler clones the list, so the original instance keeps independent elements.
The compiler wraps both lists as immutable before constructing the copied instance.
The mutation fails because every property of a data class becomes deeply read-only.
Both see it, because copy() reuses every reference the caller does not replace.

questions.explanation: A generated data-class copy is shallow: constructor property values are passed to a new instance. A mutable object such as a list is therefore shared unless the caller explicitly supplies a separate copy.

questions.text: Why choose a companion object member when behavior belongs to a class-level API, rather than declaring a separate object?

answers.text: A companion is scoped and addressable through its containing class, while a separate object has its own name.
A companion creates a new instance per class instance, while an object is allocated per method call.
A companion can inherit interfaces, while an object declaration cannot implement any interface.
A companion guarantees Java static methods, while a separate object always compiles as static fields.

questions.explanation: Both constructs create singleton objects, but a companion is declared inside and associated with its containing class, making it suitable for class-level factories or constants. It is still an object and does not automatically make all members Java static.

questions.text: Select all that apply. Which variance choices are type-safe for a generic API?

answers.text: Use out T to accept arbitrary T values into mutable storage owned by the API.
Use in T to expose stored T values from getters typed as T.
Use out T when the API produces T values but does not consume them.
Use in T when the API consumes T values but does not return them as T.

questions.explanation: Covariant out positions are safe for producers, while contravariant in positions are safe for consumers. Allowing a covariant API to consume T or a contravariant API to produce T would break the subtype relationship variance promises.

questions.text: An inline function has two lambda parameters: one must be stored for later, and one is invoked inline but must not return from the caller. Which modifiers fit?

answers.text: Mark the stored lambda crossinline and the non-returning inline lambda noinline.
Mark the stored lambda noinline and leave the other unmodified, since inlining already forbids a non-local return.
Mark the stored lambda noinline and the non-returning inline lambda crossinline.
Mark both lambdas noinline, since a lambda that escapes and a lambda that must not return both need a real function object.

questions.explanation: noinline stops a lambda parameter from being inlined so it becomes a real object that can be stored and invoked later. crossinline keeps the lambda inlined while forbidding a non-local return, which is required once it may be invoked from another execution context. The two solve different halves of the problem, and inlining is precisely what permits a non-local return in the first place, so leaving the second lambda unmodified would allow a return the enclosing frame can no longer honour.

questions.text: A small list is mapped once and immediately materialized. Why might a Sequence pipeline be slower than ordinary collection operations?

answers.text: asSequence() copies the list into a new backing structure before the first operator runs.
A sequence cannot be iterated twice, so the pipeline is executed once to count and again to build the list.
Each operator is applied to the whole collection before the next one starts, exactly as with eager operations.
Sequence iteration adds dispatch overhead that may outweigh avoided intermediates.

questions.explanation: A sequence pushes one element through the whole chain before moving to the next, so it avoids materialising an intermediate list at every step, but each element pays for an iterator hop and an operator call at every stage. Over a short chain on a small list those per-element costs exceed the allocation they save, which is why laziness is a trade rather than an optimisation. asSequence() wraps the existing collection rather than copying it, and the chain runs once, when a terminal operation pulls it.

questions.text: What trade-off does an exhaustive when expression over a sealed UI-state hierarchy introduce when a new subtype is added?

answers.text: Existing exhaustive branches silently map the new subtype to the first declared state.
Call sites without a covering else branch fail to compile until they handle the subtype.
The sealed hierarchy becomes open at runtime so plugins can add unhandled subclasses.
The compiler removes the new subtype from common code until every platform restarts.

questions.explanation: The closed set lets the compiler verify exhaustive handling. Adding a subtype deliberately creates compile errors at exhaustive when expressions that need a decision, trading some update work for explicit state handling instead of silent fallback.

questions.text: A coroutine calls a well-behaved suspending delay. What happens to the underlying thread while the coroutine waits?

answers.text: The thread is blocked inside delay until the coroutine's continuation is ready.
The coroutine suspends and the thread can execute other work before continuation resumes.
The thread is destroyed and a new operating-system thread is guaranteed for resumption.
The coroutine keeps polling on the thread but lowers that thread's scheduling priority.

questions.explanation: Suspension stores the coroutine's continuation and releases the thread to run other work. Later the continuation is scheduled in its context, potentially on a different thread; suspension is therefore distinct from blocking a thread.

questions.text: A developer calls runBlocking on the main thread to read a value from a suspend function synchronously. What is the consequence?

answers.text: The suspend function moves to Dispatchers.IO, so the main thread keeps rendering.
The call returns at once with a Deferred the caller can await later.
The main thread blocks until the coroutine completes, so frames and input stall.
The coroutine is cancelled as soon as the main thread handles its next message.

questions.explanation: runBlocking is a bridge for non-coroutine code: it starts a coroutine and blocks the calling thread until that coroutine finishes. On the main thread that is precisely what suspension exists to avoid, so rendering, input, and lifecycle callbacks stop until the work completes and a slow call becomes an ANR. Code that already has a scope should launch and publish the result as state; runBlocking belongs in main functions and tests.

sources.title: Improve App Performance with Kotlin Coroutines

questions.text: Why should a CoroutineScope used by a repository have an explicit owner and cancellation point?

answers.text: A scope selects only a dispatcher, so ownership determines which thread pool it creates.
A scope serializes coroutine state, so ownership determines where results are persisted.
Its Job defines the lifetime of launched work, which should end with the owning operation or object.
Its Job prevents child failure, so ownership determines which exceptions become successful results.

questions.explanation: A scope carries a CoroutineContext whose Job parents launched coroutines. Defining who owns and cancels that Job makes child lifetime explicit and prevents work from outliving the repository or operation that requested it.

questions.text: A parent Job is cancelled while several child coroutines are suspended. What is the normal structured-concurrency result?

answers.text: Cancellation propagates immediately and preempts the children, so no further child code runs.
Cancellation propagates, and cancel() suspends until every child has finished unwinding.
Cancellation propagates, but a suspending call inside a child's finally block still completes without NonCancellable.
Cancellation propagates to the children, which resume cancellation at cooperative points.

questions.explanation: Cancelling a Job cancels its children recursively. A child suspended in a cancellable call resumes with a CancellationException at that point, so cancellation is observed rather than forced, and code that never suspends keeps running until it checks. cancel() only requests cancellation and returns at once, which is why cancelAndJoin() exists, and a suspending call in a finally block needs withContext(NonCancellable) to complete once its scope is already cancelled.

questions.text: Two sibling child tasks are independent, and one failure must not cancel the other. Which structured approach fits that constraint?

answers.text: Use coroutineScope, because it converts each child failure into a successful parent completion.
Use supervisorScope, and handle each child failure because siblings are not cancelled automatically.
Use GlobalScope for both children, because structured ownership would necessarily couple results.
Use withContext for each child, because changing dispatchers suppresses exception propagation.

questions.explanation: supervisorScope uses supervisory child-failure semantics while still waiting for its children and respecting cancellation of the scope itself. An ordinary coroutineScope fails and cancels siblings when a child fails; GlobalScope would discard structured ownership.

questions.text: A scope launches a child with launch(SupervisorJob()), expecting sibling failures to stay isolated. Why does that not behave like supervisorScope?

answers.text: SupervisorJob supervises only when it is created inside a coroutineScope block.
The passed Job becomes that coroutine's parent, detaching it from the scope rather than supervising.
SupervisorJob suppresses cancellation but still lets the exception reach the scope's handler.
A Job passed to launch is ignored, so the coroutine keeps the scope's original Job.

questions.explanation: Passing a Job into launch does not change how the scope treats failures; it re-parents that one coroutine onto the Job supplied. The coroutine leaves the scope's hierarchy, so the scope no longer waits for it and cancelling the scope no longer cancels it, while the other children keep the original parent and the original propagation rules. Supervision is a property of the parent that owns the children, which is why supervisorScope, or a scope built with SupervisorJob, is what isolates siblings.

questions.text: A caller starts async { save() } but never awaits or otherwise consumes the Deferred result. Why is launch usually the clearer builder?

answers.text: launch communicates resultless work, while async creates a Deferred whose result or failure should be consumed.
launch guarantees save() runs on Dispatchers.IO, while async always executes on the main thread.
launch prevents save() from being cancelled with its parent, while async inherits parent cancellation.
launch blocks the caller until save() returns, while async is the only suspending coroutine builder.

questions.explanation: async represents a concurrent computation with a Deferred result and captures its exception for await. If no value is needed, launch communicates the intent directly and its failure follows launch exception rules rather than being hidden in an ignored Deferred.

questions.text: A broad catch (e: Exception) surrounds a long coroutine operation. Why should it rethrow CancellationException?

answers.text: CancellationException changes the dispatcher, and rethrowing restores the previous thread.
CancellationException indicates cooperative cancellation, and swallowing it can let work continue.
CancellationException is always a fatal JVM error that the process must report to Android.
CancellationException carries the successful result that the parent reads after completion.

questions.explanation: Cancellable suspending functions use CancellationException to unwind cancelled coroutines. A broad Exception handler can intercept it; treating it as an ordinary recoverable failure may continue unwanted work, so it should normally be rethrown.

questions.text: A coroutine performs a long CPU loop with no suspending calls. Its Job is cancelled, but the loop keeps running. What should the loop do?

answers.text: Switch to Dispatchers.IO, whose threads stop CPU loops immediately when a Job is cancelled.
Catch CancellationException around every iteration and continue with the remaining work.
Periodically check isActive, call ensureActive(), or yield() so cancellation is observed.
Replace the parent Job with SupervisorJob, which interrupts running threads on cancellation.

questions.explanation: Coroutine cancellation is cooperative and does not forcibly interrupt arbitrary CPU instructions. A busy loop must reach a cancellable suspension or explicitly inspect the Job through isActive, ensureActive(), or yield().

questions.text: A coroutine calls a blocking JVM method that stops only when its thread is interrupted. Cancelling the coroutine leaves the call running. What resolves this?

answers.text: Wrap the call in runInterruptible, which interrupts the thread when the coroutine is cancelled.
Move the call to Dispatchers.IO, whose threads are interrupted when a Job is cancelled.
Call ensureActive() before the blocking method so cancellation is observed at that point.
Wrap the call in withTimeout, which abandons the blocking method once its deadline passes.

questions.explanation: Cancellation is cooperative: it marks the Job and waits for the coroutine to reach a suspension point or an explicit check. A blocking JVM call reaches neither, so nothing stops it. runInterruptible runs the block and interrupts its thread on cancellation, turning cancellation into the InterruptedException the blocking API already understands. No dispatcher interrupts threads by itself, a check before the call helps only before it starts, and withTimeout resumes the coroutine while leaving the blocked thread occupied.

questions.text: Why is wrapping every suspending network-library call in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) not automatically necessary?

answers.text: Every suspend function is forced onto Dispatchers.Default by the Kotlin compiler before it executes.
A properly asynchronous API can suspend without blocking its caller thread and may manage I/O itself.
Dispatchers.IO is reserved for database calls, while network calls must remain on Dispatchers.Main.
withContext disables cancellation for network calls, so it should be used only for non-cancellable work.

questions.explanation: The suspend modifier does not itself select a dispatcher, but an asynchronous client can enqueue I/O and suspend without blocking the caller. Dispatchers.IO is appropriate when code actually performs blocking I/O, not as a ritual around every suspending API.

questions.text: Where is CoroutineExceptionHandler useful, and why does it not replace try/catch around await()?

answers.text: It handles every child exception before propagation, while await() returns only successful values.
It retries failed coroutines at a context boundary, while try/catch can retry only blocking code.
It converts cancellation into success for supervised children, while await() ignores cancellation.
It observes uncaught root-coroutine exceptions; async exposes failure when its Deferred is awaited.

questions.explanation: CoroutineExceptionHandler is a last-resort handler for uncaught exceptions on an eligible root coroutine. async captures its outcome in Deferred, so the caller handles failure at await() with ordinary control flow; the handler does not consume that result.

questions.text: A producer must deliver each queued command to one receiver, rather than rerun production separately for every collector. Which abstraction fits?

answers.text: A cold Flow builder, because every collector shares the same producer and consumes one queued item.
A Channel, because send/receive coordinates queued values between producers and receivers.
A StateFlow, because it retains every command and distributes each to exactly one collector.
A SharedFlow with replay zero, because it queues every command until one future collector appears.

questions.explanation: Channel models communication: sent elements are received through the channel, commonly by one receiver per element. A cold Flow reruns its producer for each collector, while StateFlow is conflated current state and SharedFlow does not inherently queue values for absent subscribers.

questions.text: Select all that apply. Which statements correctly compare StateFlow with SharedFlow?

answers.text: StateFlow always exposes a current value and replays that latest value to a new collector.
SharedFlow can configure replay without requiring a distinct current-value property.
StateFlow queues every intermediate value until every slow collector processes it.
SharedFlow is cold by default and starts a separate producer for each collector.

questions.explanation: StateFlow is a hot, conflated state holder with an accessible current value and latest-value replay. SharedFlow is also hot but has configurable replay and buffering without StateFlow's mandatory current-state contract; neither is a cold per-collector builder.

questions.text: A cold Flow producer and collector are both slow. What trade-off does buffer() introduce between them?

answers.text: It lets producer and collector run concurrently up to capacity, trading memory for decoupling.
It drops every intermediate value and retains only the latest value for each collector.
It cancels the collector's current block whenever the producer emits a newer value.
It turns the flow into a hot stream whose producer remains active without any collectors.

questions.explanation: buffer() separates upstream emission from downstream collection so they can make progress concurrently until the buffer fills. That can improve throughput at the cost of queued memory and latency; conflate and collectLatest have explicit dropping or cancellation semantics instead.

questions.text: A feature reads Room and a remote API. What responsibility belongs to the repository rather than either data source?

answers.text: Rendering loading and error composables according to the screen lifecycle.
Coordinating the sources and exposing an application-facing data contract.
Declaring the HTTP wire format and executing SQL statements in one class.
Owning Activity navigation and converting user gestures into destination routes.

questions.explanation: A data source encapsulates access to one source, while a repository exposes data to the rest of the app and coordinates source selection, refresh, caching, or conflict policy. UI rendering and navigation remain presentation responsibilities.

questions.text: A reusable date-picker component needs state that survives recomposition but has no tie to business logic or to the screen's lifetime. What should own it?

answers.text: A ViewModel, so the state survives configuration changes.
The repository, so every screen using the component shares one instance.
A CompositionLocal, so nested composables can update it without parameters.
A plain state holder class remembered alongside the component.

questions.explanation: State holders come in two kinds. A ViewModel is a screen-level holder: it survives configuration change, reaches the data layer, and outlives the composition. A plain class created with remember is a UI-element holder: it owns the logic of one component and lives and dies with it, needing no framework. A picker's internal state is the second kind, so a ViewModel would give it a lifetime and a dependency surface it never asked for, while a repository or a CompositionLocal moves it further from the component that owns it.

questions.text: A screen refreshes account data and maps it into UI state. Which split keeps ViewModel and repository responsibilities clear?

answers.text: The ViewModel holds a Context to resolve the strings and formats the screen shows; the repository returns raw rows.
The repository exposes Room entities straight to the screen; the ViewModel passes them through unchanged.
The repository coordinates data operations; the ViewModel derives and exposes screen UI state.
The ViewModel owns the cache policy and retry rules; the repository only issues the calls it is asked for.

questions.explanation: The repository owns the application-facing data contract: which source answers a read, how results are cached and refreshed, and how persistence and wire types are mapped out of sight. The ViewModel is a screen-scoped state holder that calls those operations and turns the results into the state the screen renders. Lifting caching or retry policy into the ViewModel duplicates it across screens, letting persistence types reach the UI couples every screen to the storage schema, and holding a Context in a ViewModel to format that state retains an object that outlives the UI it came from.

questions.text: A payment result must still be represented correctly after rotation, while a snackbar should not repeat on every new collector. Which model is appropriate?

answers.text: Model payment completion in durable UI state and treat snackbar display as consumable UI behavior.
Put both values in an unbuffered Channel because screen state should disappear after one receive.
Put both values in replaying SharedFlow because every collector should repeat prior UI effects.
Store payment completion only in the composable and make the snackbar repository state.

questions.explanation: Payment completion affects what the screen is and should be derivable after recreation. Snackbar display is transient behavior; replaying it as durable state can duplicate the effect, so the UI should derive or consume that behavior deliberately from durable facts.

questions.text: Why might a mature app use separate network DTO, database entity, and domain model types even when their fields initially overlap?

answers.text: Separate models make network, storage, and domain evolution independent at the cost of mapping code.
Separate models guarantee the backend and database can never introduce incompatible fields.
Separate models let the UI bypass repositories and mutate database rows through DTO references.
Separate models remove serialization and migration work because every layer infers conversions.

questions.explanation: Layer-specific models prevent a wire-format or schema concern from becoming the application's core contract. This isolation costs explicit mapping and may be unnecessary for very small features, but it lets each boundary evolve without leaking annotations and compatibility rules everywhere.

questions.text: Why should a ViewModel avoid retaining an Activity or Fragment reference?

answers.text: A ViewModel can outlive that UI instance, so the reference can retain a destroyed owner and its Views.
A ViewModel always runs in another process, where Activity references cannot be marshalled by Binder.
An Activity automatically clears all ViewModel fields before each configuration change completes.
A Fragment reference forces every repository call onto the main dispatcher until process death.

questions.explanation: A ViewModel commonly survives configuration recreation while the Activity, Fragment View, and Context do not. Retaining those shorter-lived objects prevents collection and risks operating on stale UI; events and state should cross the boundary without UI-instance ownership.

questions.text: A use case only forwards one repository method and has no reuse or business rule. What is the main reason not to add it yet?

answers.text: Use cases prevent repository interfaces from being tested with fake implementations.
Use cases require Android Context and therefore cannot be called from a ViewModel.
The layer adds indirection without currently centralizing meaningful logic or reuse.
The extra layer changes every suspending repository function into a blocking function.

questions.explanation: A domain layer is useful for reusable or complex business logic, but a pass-through class can add navigation overhead without a behavior to own. It can be introduced when rules, orchestration, or reuse justify the boundary rather than by default.

questions.text: Select all that apply. Which Dagger binding declarations fit the stated constraint?

answers.text: Use @Provides only for interfaces because Dagger can instantiate them without an implementation.
Use @Inject on a third-party constructor without modifying that third-party class.
Use @Inject on a constructor when Dagger can construct the concrete type directly.
Use @Binds on an abstract method to map an interface to an injectable implementation.

questions.explanation: Constructor injection is the simplest binding when the class is under your control. @Binds delegates an abstraction to an injectable implementation, while @Provides handles factory logic or types whose constructors cannot be annotated, including third-party classes.

questions.text: Which role belongs to a Dagger @Module rather than a @Component?

answers.text: It declares binding methods that contribute ways to obtain graph values.
It owns the generated graph instance and exposes provision entry points to callers.
It retains every scoped object independently from any component instance.
It starts Android components and injects fields without being installed in a graph.

questions.explanation: A module groups binding declarations such as @Provides, @Binds, or multibindings. A component includes modules, forms a graph boundary, owns scoped instances, and exposes entry points; a module alone is not a running container.

questions.text: A feature graph needs a few types from the app graph but must not see the rest of it. Which relationship expresses that?

answers.text: A subcomponent, because a child sees only the bindings it redeclares.
A subcomponent, because the parent chooses which of its bindings to install.
A component dependency, which exposes only the parent's declared provision methods.
A component dependency, because it merges both graphs into one binding set.

questions.explanation: A subcomponent inherits its parent's entire binding graph, which is convenient and deliberately wide. A component dependency instead treats the other component as an ordinary dependency and can use only the types that component publishes as provision methods on its interface, so the shared surface is exactly what the parent chose to expose. That narrower contract is the reason to prefer it when a feature should not reach arbitrarily into the app graph, at the cost of declaring each type to be shared.

questions.text: Which responsibility belongs to a Dagger @Component rather than a module?

answers.text: Defining one factory method body that constructs a third-party dependency.
Declaring only interface-to-implementation mappings with abstract @Binds methods.
Connecting bindings into a graph and exposing injection or provision entry points.
Choosing which coroutine dispatcher every injected suspend function executes on.

questions.explanation: A component is the graph API and boundary: Dagger generates its implementation from reachable bindings and declared entry points. Modules contribute bindings but do not themselves assemble or expose a usable component instance.

questions.text: Select all that apply. Which statements describe a Dagger subcomponent's relationship to its parent component?

answers.text: The parent can request child-only bindings before creating the subcomponent.
The subcomponent can use every binding available from its parent graph.
The subcomponent is generated as an unrelated graph that duplicates every parent binding.
The subcomponent can add bindings and a shorter-lived scope below the parent.

questions.explanation: A subcomponent extends a parent graph: it inherits parent bindings and may add bindings or scopes for a narrower lifetime. Dependency visibility flows downward, so child-only bindings do not become available to the parent.

questions.text: How does Dagger assemble a dependency graph into code an application can use?

answers.text: It scans all loaded classes at runtime and reflects over constructors on each resolution.
It combines component entry points and reachable bindings, then generates an implementation at compile time.
It asks Android's Application object to construct missing dependencies when the graph is first used.
It serializes module instances into resources and loads the selected binding graph from the APK.

questions.explanation: Dagger's compiler resolves the keys requested by component entry points through constructor and module bindings. It emits a generated component implementation containing the factories and wiring, rather than discovering the graph through runtime reflection.

questions.text: A ViewModel needs an injected repository and an item id known only at navigation time. What does assisted injection provide?

answers.text: It supplies the id from the graph, so the caller passes nothing.
It makes the id optional so the ViewModel can be built before navigation.
It stores the id in the graph so later injections reuse the same value.
It generates a factory taking the id, while the graph supplies the rest.

questions.explanation: Some constructor parameters belong to the graph and some are known only at the call site. Marking the runtime value @Assisted tells Dagger to generate a factory accepting exactly those parameters and to resolve everything else itself, so the ViewModel keeps one constructor and no partially built state. On Android such an id often arrives as a navigation argument, where SavedStateHandle is the other standard route; what neither does is put a per-instance runtime value into the graph.

questions.text: A component requests Foo, but no binding can provide Foo; elsewhere two unqualified bindings provide the same Bar key. When are these problems reported?

answers.text: At compile time, when Dagger resolves every binding key the component can reach.
Only when the first Activity requests Foo or Bar from the generated component.
When R8 analyzes release code, because debug component graphs accept missing keys.
When Android recreates the process, because component validation depends on saved state.

questions.explanation: Dagger resolves requested keys while compiling a component. A missing binding leaves no dependency path, while conflicting unique bindings make one key ambiguous; both produce compile diagnostics rather than deferred runtime lookup failures.

questions.text: A graph provides two OkHttpClient instances with different authentication policies. How should callers request the intended one?

answers.text: Give both providers the same scope so Dagger selects the most recently declared binding.
Place each provider in a separate module so module inclusion order selects one implicitly.
Apply distinct qualifiers to providers and matching injection sites so their keys differ.
Use two unqualified bindings and let the generated component inspect parameter names.

questions.explanation: Dagger keys include a type and an optional qualifier. Distinct qualifiers make the two OkHttpClient bindings unambiguous and require each consumer to state which policy it needs; scopes control reuse, not selection among same-key bindings.

questions.text: What actually determines the lifetime of an object provided by a scoped Dagger binding?

answers.text: The annotation keeps one instance in a global cache until the Android process exits.
The owning component instance caches it, so its lifetime follows that component instance.
The module instance caches it, so rebuilding a component with the module reuses the object.
The injected Activity caches it, even when the binding belongs to an application component.

questions.explanation: A scope tells a component to reuse a binding result within that component instance. Creating another component creates another scoped cache, and releasing the owning component makes those objects eligible for collection; the annotation is not a process-global store.

questions.text: An app stores a user theme and also a searchable collection of thousands of notes. Which storage split fits their data shapes?

answers.text: Use DataStore for the theme and Room for structured notes and queries.
Use Room for the theme and rememberSaveable for the notes across app restarts.
Use DataStore for both because it supports relational joins and partial indexed updates.
Use SharedPreferences for notes and Room only for values that fit in one database row.

questions.explanation: DataStore is suited to small preference or typed-object state and does not provide relational partial updates. Room is designed for structured datasets, queries, relationships, and transactional updates, making the two tools complementary rather than interchangeable.

questions.text: A Room DAO returns Flow<List<Item>>. Why can collectors receive a new list after another transaction changes the observed table?

answers.text: Room's invalidation tracking notices relevant table changes and reruns the observable query.
Room compares each row's contents after every write and emits only the rows that differ.
The Flow emits once per changed row, so a multi-row update produces several emissions.
The DAO method must be annotated @Transaction before Room will observe the table at all.

questions.explanation: Room keeps an invalidation tracker over the tables an observable query reads. When a write touches one of those tables, Room re-runs the query and emits its current result: a complete list, not a per-row delta and not one emission per changed row. Observation does not depend on @Transaction, which matters when a DAO method runs several statements that must see a consistent snapshot.

questions.text: Why is destructive migration usually inappropriate for user-authored offline data?

answers.text: It keeps every row but removes database indexes, making later reads permanently unindexed.
It recreates the database when no migration path exists, which can discard local user data.
It uploads the old database to the server before Room applies any schema statements.
It blocks only new installations because existing databases skip version validation.

questions.explanation: A destructive fallback lets Room drop and recreate tables when it cannot migrate from an installed version. That may be acceptable for disposable caches, but it loses authoritative offline or user-created data and therefore needs an explicit product decision.

questions.text: Select all that apply. An offline-first editor commits locally before syncing. Which design properties make that strategy reliable?

answers.text: The local transaction records both the edit and enough sync state to retry it.
The UI waits for network success before the local source of truth may show the edit.
The server operation has a stable identity or idempotency policy for repeated attempts.
A failed attempt deletes the local edit so the next retry starts from remote state.

questions.explanation: A local-first write can update the source of truth immediately while atomically marking pending synchronization. Stable operation identity and retry semantics prevent duplicate remote effects; deleting the edit or requiring immediate connectivity would undermine offline behavior.

questions.text: In a typical Retrofit stack backed by OkHttp, how are responsibilities divided?

answers.text: Retrofit defines the HTTP API mapping; OkHttp executes requests, connections, and interceptors.
Retrofit manages sockets and TLS; OkHttp generates Kotlin service implementations from annotations.
Retrofit owns the response cache and conditional requests; OkHttp only opens and closes sockets.
Retrofit maintains the connection pool and keep-alive behaviour; OkHttp converts response bodies into Kotlin types.

questions.explanation: Retrofit turns an annotated service interface into HTTP requests and adapts the results, delegating the transport to the OkHttp client it is built with. Connection pooling, TLS, timeouts, interceptors, and the response cache all belong to OkHttp. Body conversion is neither one's own work: it comes from the converter factory installed on Retrofit.

questions.text: Select all that apply. Which statements correctly compare OkHttp application and network interceptors?

answers.text: An application interceptor runs only for cached responses and never for network responses.
A network interceptor replaces DNS and opens sockets without continuing the interceptor chain.
An application interceptor is invoked once for the logical call, even when redirects occur.
A network interceptor can observe intermediate network responses such as redirects.

questions.explanation: Application interceptors observe the application's logical call and are not repeated for redirects or retries. Network interceptors operate around each network exchange and can inspect connection details and intermediate responses; both must continue or short-circuit the chain deliberately.

questions.text: An OkHttp call reaches the server and the response headers arrive, then the connection goes quiet for longer than the client allows, while the call as a whole is still well within its overall budget. Which configured timeout fires?

answers.text: The connect timeout, which covers everything after the TCP connection is established.
The write timeout, which bounds how long the client spends sending the request body.
The read timeout, which bounds how long the client waits between bytes of the response.
The call timeout, which bounds the total duration of the call from start to finish.

questions.explanation: OkHttp splits the budget by stage: the connect timeout bounds establishing the connection, the write timeout bounds sending the request, and the read timeout bounds inactivity while receiving the response, measuring the gap between bytes rather than the total transfer. A call timeout, when set, bounds the whole exchange independently of those stages, which is the setting a long but healthy download needs raised.

questions.text: A Retrofit suspend call backed by OkHttp is cancelled with its owning coroutine. What behavior should the integration provide?

answers.text: It should cancel the underlying HTTP call where supported and resume with cancellation.
It should detach the HTTP call so the result can update the destroyed screen later.
It should convert cancellation into HTTP 408 and retry the request without its parent.
It should block the caller thread until the server closes the connection normally.

questions.explanation: A cancellable suspend adapter connects coroutine cancellation to the in-flight call, avoiding network work whose owner no longer needs the result. Cancellation remains coroutine cancellation rather than a fabricated HTTP response or an automatic detached retry.

questions.text: A WorkRequest requires unmetered network and charging. Why can the app not promise an exact start time once those constraints become true?

answers.text: Constraints are persisted only after the Worker starts, so they never affect scheduling.
The system scheduler still accounts for quotas, battery policy, and other execution limits.
WorkManager converts constrained work into an exact alarm on every supported Android version.
Meeting constraints starts work synchronously on the thread that reported the state change.

questions.explanation: Constraints define conditions under which work may run, not a deadline or exact trigger. WorkManager cooperates with platform schedulers, quotas, and power policies, so eligible work can still be deferred.

questions.text: A Worker may be stopped after a server accepts its upload but before local success is recorded. Why should the upload operation be idempotent?

answers.text: Result.retry() re-runs only work that never reached the network, so a duplicate cannot arise any other way.
WorkManager deduplicates requests carrying the same tag, so a second attempt is dropped before doWork() runs.
A retry can repeat an already accepted effect, so stable operation identity prevents duplicates.
Enqueuing the upload as unique work guarantees at-most-once execution, so a retry never repeats an accepted effect.

questions.explanation: WorkManager guarantees that enqueued work runs, not that it runs exactly once. A process death or timeout between the server accepting an upload and the Worker recording success leaves the app unable to tell whether the remote side committed, so the retry sends the request again. An idempotency key or an equivalent server-side contract makes that repeat converge on a single logical effect. Neither tags nor unique work names bound the number of attempts: tags label work for querying and cancellation, and uniqueness governs what happens when the same named work is enqueued again.

questions.text: Select all that apply. Which workload characteristics favor a foreground service over ordinary WorkManager?

answers.text: The task is deferrable maintenance that may wait for charging and unmetered network.
The user starts a long operation and expects continuous, immediately visible progress.
The task must begin now and is valid only while its ongoing notification remains visible.
The task should run at an exact clock time even when the app is idle.

questions.explanation: A foreground service is for user-noticeable work that must run immediately and continuously under an ongoing notification. Deferrable constrained work belongs to WorkManager, while an exact-time requirement is a separate alarm-policy decision.

questions.text: On Android 13+, why are creating a notification channel and receiving POST_NOTIFICATIONS permission separate requirements?

answers.text: Permission allows posting; a channel categorizes notifications and exposes user controls.
The channel grants posting permission; POST_NOTIFICATIONS controls only channel sound selection.
The permission selects importance per category; the channel authorizes the app process globally.
The channel applies only before Android 8, while the runtime permission replaces it on Android 13+.

questions.explanation: POST_NOTIFICATIONS is the app-level runtime authorization introduced for most notifications on Android 13. Channels remain the required category and user-control mechanism on Android 8+, so obtaining permission does not create or configure a channel.

questions.text: Select all that apply. An app sends targeted FCM messages through its backend. What should it do when the registration token changes?

answers.text: Derive the replacement token locally from the old token so the backend needs no update.
Send the new token to the backend and associate it with the current app/user installation.
Treat send responses that mark old tokens invalid as a signal to remove stale mappings.
Store one token in the APK because all installations of an app share the same token.

questions.explanation: An FCM registration token identifies an app instance and can rotate, so the client must report updates and the server must maintain current mappings. Invalid-token send responses help clean stale entries; tokens are neither derivable nor shared by all installations.

questions.text: A ViewModel launches work on Dispatchers.Main during a local JVM test. Why replace Main with a TestDispatcher?

answers.text: It gives the test scheduler control of queued coroutine work and avoids relying on an Android main Looper.
It converts every production dispatcher into one real background thread shared across the test suite.
It prevents child coroutines from failing, so tests need no exception assertions.
It makes every Flow cold and guarantees collection completes after the first emission.

questions.explanation: Local tests do not have Android's production main Looper. Setting Main to a TestDispatcher routes main-bound work through a controllable scheduler, allowing deterministic advancement and cleanup; it does not change coroutine failure or Flow semantics.

questions.text: A stateIn flow uses SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed, but a test only reads value and never collects. Why might upstream not start?

answers.text: WhileSubscribed requires an active subscriber, so the test needs a collector in its test scope.
Reading value permanently closes StateFlow before its first upstream subscription begins.
stateIn starts upstream only on a real Android main thread and cannot be tested on the JVM.
WhileSubscribed ignores test collectors because it accepts only LifecycleOwner subscriptions.

questions.explanation: WhileSubscribed activates sharing according to subscription count. Reading StateFlow.value does not create a subscriber, so tests commonly launch a background collector and then advance the shared test scheduler before asserting values.

questions.text: A Compose test cannot find text inside a parent whose semantics merge descendants. What should the test inspect before changing production UI?

answers.text: The layout tree in Layout Inspector, because Compose test matchers query layout nodes rather than semantics.
The unmerged semantics tree, because descendant nodes may be hidden by merged semantics.
The recomposition count for the parent, because a node joins the tree only once it has recomposed.
The modifier order on the parent, because clearAndSetSemantics runs before any child semantics are attached.

questions.explanation: Compose test matchers traverse the semantics tree, and by default they see its merged form, where a parent that merges descendants collapses their semantics into itself. Asking for the unmerged tree exposes those descendant nodes and lets the test assert against the one that actually carries the text. The layout hierarchy and recomposition counts are not what matchers walk, so inspecting them explains nothing about a missing node.

questions.text: What should a Room migration test verify beyond merely opening the latest empty schema?

answers.text: That production tables are dropped before every version transition to avoid old rows.
That a real older schema with representative data migrates and preserves required values.
That the migration runs only in an in-memory database created at the newest version.
That Room ignores exported schemas and infers every historical column from current entities.

questions.explanation: A useful migration test starts from an older exported schema, inserts representative data, runs the migration path, and verifies both schema validity and data semantics. Opening only a fresh latest-version database cannot expose a broken upgrade path.

questions.text: Select all that apply. Which test choices make a suite more resilient to an internal refactor without weakening behavior coverage?

answers.text: Assert public outputs and externally visible side effects for representative inputs.
Assert the exact order of all private helper calls even when order has no observable effect.
Use fakes at real architectural boundaries instead of mocking every private collaboration.
Read private fields after each line so implementation structure becomes part of the contract.

questions.explanation: Tests survive refactoring when they specify observable contracts and substitute dependencies at meaningful boundaries. Assertions about incidental helper calls or private storage couple the suite to one implementation without increasing confidence in user-visible behavior.

questions.text: At a conceptual level, how does ART decide which managed objects can be reclaimed?

answers.text: It reclaims objects older than a fixed time even when active code still references them.
It reclaims every object that is no longer reachable through references from GC roots.
It reclaims every object whose class has no finalizer after each rendered frame.
It reclaims objects only when their reference count reaches zero on every app thread.
