questions.explanation: Tracing garbage collection starts from roots and follows references to determine the live object graph. Managed objects outside that reachable graph can be reclaimed; age can guide collection strategy but does not override reachability.

questions.text: Why can an Android app leak an Activity even though ART uses garbage collection?

answers.text: GC can reclaim only unreachable objects; an unintended strong path from a root keeps the Activity live.
GC excludes every Android framework class, so Activities are reclaimed only when the process exits.
GC manages primitive arrays only, while application objects require explicit free() calls.
GC reclaims Activities after a fixed delay, but leaked Views extend that delay by one frame.

questions.explanation: Garbage collection distinguishes reachable from unreachable objects, not useful from obsolete ones. A singleton, listener, thread, or other rooted object can keep a destroyed Activity strongly reachable, so the collector correctly retains an object the app no longer intends to use.

questions.text: Select all that apply. Why can generational collection improve ART garbage-collection throughput?

answers.text: Every object that survives one young collection becomes permanently exempt from future collection.
Generational collection makes allocation free and removes any need to inspect performance traces.
Many newly allocated objects become unreachable quickly, so young collections can reclaim them cheaply.
Collecting a young region can delay the need to scan and compact the complete heap.

questions.explanation: Generational collectors exploit the common pattern that many objects die young. ART can collect young objects with less effort and postpone a full-heap collection, while survivors remain collectible later and allocation or collection still has a cost.

questions.text: A destroyed Activity remains in a heap dump. Which evidence most directly identifies why it cannot be collected?

answers.text: Its method count, because larger classes are retained before smaller classes during GC.
Its allocation timestamp, because objects older than the Activity timeout become permanent.
Its path of strong references to a GC root and the objects dominating its retained memory.
Its source-file package, because framework packages are the only valid roots in an app heap.

questions.explanation: A path to a GC root shows the reference chain that keeps an instance reachable. Dominator and retained-size information then highlights which owner prevents a large subgraph from being reclaimed, providing actionable evidence beyond allocation age or class size.

questions.text: How does a missed rendering deadline differ from an ANR caused by a prolonged main-thread stall?

answers.text: A missed deadline can produce a janky frame; a sufficiently long unresponsive condition can trigger ANR handling.
A missed deadline is reported as an ANR once a frame exceeds 700 ms, so the two are one signal at different thresholds.
An ANR is raised only when the main thread is blocked; a missed deadline only when the RenderThread is blocked.
A missed deadline drops the frame silently, while an ANR is raised by the system watchdog whichever thread is blocked.

questions.explanation: Both come from work taking too long, but they are different failures at different scales. A frame that misses its deadline produces visible jank and the app carries on. An ANR is the system's response to the main thread failing to service a time-sensitive event, most often input dispatch, for a far longer fixed period, and it surfaces a dialog or ends the process. The same blocked main thread can cause both in sequence, first as dropped frames and then, if it persists, as an ANR; a frozen frame reported by Play vitals is still jank rather than an ANR.

questions.text: Why is calling System.gc() repeatedly not a sound fix for allocation pressure or a memory leak?

answers.text: It permanently disables ART's concurrent collector after the first explicit collection request.
It can request collection but cannot make reachable leaks collectible or remove future allocation cost.
It clears every static reference, which can corrupt framework state and force process recreation.
It compacts only native memory, so managed Java and Kotlin objects are never examined.

questions.explanation: An explicit GC request does not change object reachability and does not repair an allocation-heavy design. It may add collection work or pauses while leaked objects remain live, so profiling ownership and allocation sources is the appropriate response.

questions.text: Why can an API secret compiled into an APK not be treated as confidential?

answers.text: Packaged code and resources can be inspected; obfuscation adds effort but no secure boundary.
R8 renames the constant in release builds, so the value on the device no longer matches the original.
Placing the value in NDK C++ code moves it outside the Java heap, where the packaged binary no longer exposes it.
Splitting the value across several resources and reassembling it at runtime keeps it out of the packaged output.

questions.explanation: The client runs on a device the developer does not control, so anything shipped inside the package can be unpacked, disassembled, or observed while it executes. R8 renames identifiers rather than string values, a native library's contents are as readable as the DEX, and reassembling a value at runtime only changes where an attacker looks. Obfuscation raises the cost of extraction without creating a boundary: privileged credentials belong on the server, and any credential the client must hold has to be scoped so that disclosure is survivable.

questions.text: What should Android Keystore hold when an app encrypts a larger sensitive document?

answers.text: The document itself, because Keystore is a general encrypted database for arbitrary byte arrays.
Every plaintext field, because keys are reconstructed from document contents after authentication.
The cryptographic key, while encrypted document bytes remain in ordinary app storage.
The server password, because Keystore prevents the running app from ever using stored credentials.

questions.explanation: Android Keystore protects cryptographic key material and can restrict how a key is used. Application data is normally encrypted with that key and stored elsewhere; Keystore is not a general document database and cannot hide a credential from code authorized to use it.

questions.text: Select all that apply. An exported Activity accepts a deep-link URI that selects an account and redirect. Which defenses belong at that boundary?

answers.text: Validate the URI scheme, host, path, and parameters before using them.
Authorize the requested account/action instead of trusting the caller-supplied identifier.
Treat intent extras as trusted because Android parsed them into typed Bundle values.
Allow any redirect URI if the Activity was reached through a verified app link.

questions.explanation: Exported components receive attacker-controlled input even when Android successfully parses the Intent. The component must validate allowed destinations and authorize the requested operation; app-link verification proves domain association, not that every parameter or redirect is safe.

questions.text: What tends to become costly when a sufficiently large Android codebase remains in one app module?

answers.text: Build speed always improves once the code is split, so a single module is the only reason builds are slow.
Change boundaries blur, dependencies spread widely, and more code may be invalidated or rebuilt together.
Gradle can compile modules in parallel only when they are split by layer, so one module forfeits parallelism entirely.
Kotlin's internal visibility stops compiling in an application module, so every declaration has to be public.

questions.explanation: A single module keeps wiring simple, but as it grows the compiler has to consider more code for any change, ownership boundaries stop being enforced by anything the build checks, and internal covers the whole module so it no longer marks a real boundary. Splitting can shrink the surface a change invalidates, but it is not automatic: module count alone does not decide build speed, and Gradle parallelises work across whatever module graph it is given.

questions.text: What trade-off appears when an Android project is split into many tiny modules with little independent responsibility?

answers.text: Every module must republish its transitive dependencies as api, so implementation stops being usable.
Modules should mirror the package structure, so a fine-grained split is the only correct outcome as a codebase grows.
Configuration, graph complexity, and cross-module APIs can outweigh useful isolation and parallel work.
Each module runs in its own Gradle daemon, so memory use grows linearly with the number of modules.

questions.explanation: Each module adds build configuration, dependency edges, a public API to design, and coordination between the people who own it. Splitting where cohesion and ownership justify a boundary pays for that; fragmenting trivial responsibilities spends it for nothing, slowing configuration and making the code harder to navigate. Module boundaries are a design decision rather than a mechanical mapping from packages, and neither dependency configurations nor the Gradle daemon behave differently because a project has more of them.

questions.text: Two sibling feature modules need the same navigation contract and user identifier. Which dependency direction avoids coupling one feature to the other's implementation?

answers.text: Move the shared contract into a lower-level core module that both features depend on.
Make each feature depend on the other so either one can construct the other's internal screen.
Move both feature implementations into the Application class and expose mutable globals.
Duplicate the contract with unrelated types and cast between them in the app module.

questions.explanation: Sibling features should not form horizontal or cyclic implementation dependencies. A small lower-level contract or navigation module gives both a stable abstraction, while the application composition root can connect concrete feature implementations.

questions.text: Why can using implementation instead of api for a private library dependency improve build isolation?

answers.text: implementation removes the dependency from the runtime APK, so downstream code loads it over the network.
implementation hides the dependency from consumers' compile classpaths, reducing recompilation from its internal changes.
implementation prevents the current module from referencing the dependency in production source code.
implementation forces Gradle to compile the dependency once globally and reuse it across unrelated repositories.

questions.explanation: An implementation dependency is available inside the declaring module but is not exposed as part of its consumers' compile API. That smaller classpath improves encapsulation and can prevent internal dependency changes from invalidating downstream compilation.

sources.title: Java Library Plugin: API and Implementation Separation

questions.text: A large app has teams that own complete user journeys. Why can feature-oriented modules fit better than only ui/data/domain layer modules?

answers.text: Feature modules remove the need for layers, interfaces, or dependency rules inside each feature.
Feature modules guarantee every feature compiles in parallel regardless of shared core changes.
Feature modules make all code public so teams can reuse implementation details across journeys.
Feature boundaries align ownership and change locality; pure layer modules mix unrelated journeys.

questions.explanation: Feature modules can keep the UI, domain, and data pieces of one journey near its owning team and limit unrelated changes. Layer modules may centralize technical concerns but often become broad coupling points; real projects commonly combine feature and core/layer boundaries.

questions.text: Select all that apply. Why can modularization improve incremental builds without making every build faster?

answers.text: Unchanged modules can sometimes reuse outputs when dependency boundaries isolate a change.
More modules add configuration and task-graph overhead that can dominate small projects.
Gradle always recompiles every module after any source change, regardless of dependency edges.
Each module starts a dedicated Gradle daemon, guaranteeing linear memory growth and speedup.

questions.explanation: Well-chosen module boundaries can shrink the invalidated compilation graph and improve parallel or cached work. Modules also add configuration and coordination overhead, so graph shape, plugin cost, and change patterns determine the result rather than module count alone.

questions.text: An offline task app queues CreateTask followed by RenameTask for the same local ID while unrelated edits also wait. Which sync strategy fits?

answers.text: Preserve order per entity while allowing operations for independent entities to sync concurrently.
Send every rename first because newer operations always make earlier creates unnecessary.
Send all operations concurrently and rely on device timestamps to establish server ordering.
Pause local editing until the complete queue succeeds so no dependencies need tracking.

questions.explanation: Create and rename have a causal dependency for one entity, so reordering can target an object the server does not know. Independent entities need no shared ordering and may sync concurrently; a durable queue should encode dependencies rather than blocking offline edits.

questions.text: A paged feed caches pages in Room. Why should inserting a page and updating its next-page key happen in one transaction?

answers.text: It makes HTTP page requests execute inside SQLite and inherit the database lock timeout.
It prevents a crash from leaving cached rows and pagination metadata describing different progress.
It guarantees the server never inserts items before the page currently visible to the user.
It lets every account share one pagination key without partitioning cached rows by user.

questions.explanation: Rows and remote pagination keys form one consistency unit. Updating them atomically prevents a crash between writes from causing duplicates, skipped pages, or a cache that cannot determine where to resume; network I/O should remain outside the database transaction.

questions.text: A messaging app receives live messages over a socket and must show history after process death. Where should incoming messages be committed?

answers.text: To a MutableStateFlow held by an application-scoped repository that every screen collects.
To a local database keyed by a client-generated id assigned when the socket frame arrives.
To a local database keyed by stable server identity, with UI observing that database.
To an unbounded Channel drained by the visible screen, so no message is handled twice.

questions.explanation: A socket is a delivery mechanism, not durable state. Committing each message under the identity the server assigns lets a redelivered frame be recognised as the same message, gives the UI one observable source that survives process death, and keeps history readable offline. A process-scoped stream, whether StateFlow, SharedFlow, or Channel, holds nothing once the process is gone, and keying on an id the client invents defeats deduplication at the moment the socket redelivers.

questions.text: Select all that apply. A multi-account app caches private data locally. Which design choices prevent one account from seeing another's data?

answers.text: Partition cached rows and queries by a stable account identifier.
Clear or cryptographically make inaccessible account data according to logout policy.
Reuse one unscoped in-memory repository after account switches because the UI route changed.
Use the display name as the sole partition key because it is unique and immutable.

questions.explanation: Account identity belongs in local-data boundaries, cache keys, and repository scope, not only in navigation. Logout must dispose or protect prior-account state according to product requirements; mutable display names and reused unscoped caches are unsafe boundaries.

questions.text: What is the relationship between Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform?

answers.text: Kotlin Multiplatform shares code across targets; Compose Multiplatform can share declarative UI on top.
Kotlin Multiplatform is only a UI toolkit; Compose Multiplatform supplies networking and persistence targets.
They are alternate names for the same compiler plugin and always share every platform screen.
Compose Multiplatform replaces platform bootstrap, while Kotlin Multiplatform requires native hosts for UI.

questions.explanation: Kotlin Multiplatform is the broader code-sharing technology for common and platform source sets. Compose Multiplatform is a UI framework that can be used within that project; teams may share logic without UI, and platform applications still provide their host and bootstrap.

questions.text: When might a KMP product share domain/data logic but keep each platform's UI native?

answers.text: When all business rules differ by platform but screens and navigation are identical.
When platform interaction and design conventions outweigh shared UI maintenance savings.
When commonMain requires UIKit on Android and Jetpack Compose on iOS for domain compilation.
When native UI is the only way a KMP project can call shared suspend functions or observe Flow.

questions.explanation: Sharing logic and sharing UI are separate product choices. Native UIs can preserve platform-specific experience and team autonomy while still reusing stable business and data behavior, at the cost of implementing presentation twice.

sources.title: Kotlin Multiplatform: Share Code on Your Terms

questions.text: A developer returning to Kotlin/Native expects to call freeze() before sharing an object between threads. What is the current situation?

answers.text: freeze() is still required, but only for objects crossing into Swift.
The current memory manager removed that restriction; objects are shared without freezing.
Freezing is now automatic, so every shared object becomes immutable on first access.
Sharing between threads is no longer supported; each thread must own its objects.

questions.explanation: The original Kotlin/Native model required an object graph to be frozen, made deeply immutable, before more than one thread could see it, and InvalidMutabilityException was the usual result of getting that wrong. The current memory manager lifts the restriction and brings concurrency closer to the JVM: objects are shared across threads without ceremony and the freezing API is deprecated. Ordinary concurrency discipline still applies, so shared mutable state needs the same care it would need anywhere.

questions.text: Select all that apply. Where should tests live in a KMP library with shared validation rules and an Android-only ContentResolver adapter?

answers.text: All tests belong in commonTest because test source sets may reference every platform API.
Validation-rule tests belong in commonTest when they use only common APIs.
All tests belong in androidTest because common code cannot be tested for non-Android targets.
ContentResolver adapter tests belong in an Android test source set with Android dependencies.

questions.explanation: Tests follow the same boundary as production code. Platform-independent behavior can run from commonTest across targets, while an adapter that uses Android APIs needs the corresponding Android test source set and environment.

questions.text: A search screen maps every new query string to a Flow of repository results. When the user types another character, the request already running for the previous query should stop. Which operator expresses that?

answers.text: flatMapConcat, which waits for the previous inner flow to finish before starting the next one.
flatMapLatest, which cancels the previous inner flow when a new query arrives.
flatMapMerge, which runs the inner flows concurrently and interleaves their emissions.
conflate, which drops intermediate query values when the collector falls behind.

questions.explanation: flatMapLatest cancels the inner flow it started for the previous upstream value each time a new one arrives, which is exactly search-as-you-type behaviour. flatMapConcat and flatMapMerge both let the earlier request keep running, sequentially or concurrently. conflate is a backpressure operator: it discards upstream values a slow collector has not reached yet, but it never cancels work that has already been started.

questions.text: A Flow of query strings feeds a search repository. What is the difference between applying debounce(300) to it and applying distinctUntilChanged() to it?

answers.text: debounce drops a value equal to the one before it, while distinctUntilChanged waits for a quiet period.
Both suppress duplicates; debounce compares values by identity and distinctUntilChanged compares with equals().
debounce waits until emissions pause for the given time, while distinctUntilChanged drops a value equal to the previous one.
debounce emits at most one value per fixed window, while distinctUntilChanged removes every value the flow has emitted before.

questions.explanation: debounce is time-based: it emits the latest value only after the upstream has stayed quiet for the timeout, so a burst of keystrokes collapses into one query. distinctUntilChanged is value-based and compares each emission only with the one immediately before it, so a value that reappears later still passes through. Emitting at most one value per fixed window is what sample() does, and neither operator keeps a history of every earlier value.

questions.text: One Flow emits the signed-in user and another emits a settings snapshot, and a screen state is built from both. How do combine and zip differ in when they produce a value?

answers.text: After both flows emit once, combine uses their latest values when either emits; zip pairs their next unused values.
combine emits only once both flows supply a new value; zip emits when either one emits, reusing the newest value.
combine waits for both flows to complete and emits a single merged value; zip emits pairs as values arrive.
Both emit on every upstream emission, but zip cancels the slower flow once the faster one has completed.

questions.explanation: combine first waits until every source has emitted at least one value. It then caches each source's most recent value and re-emits whenever any source changes, so a settings change alone still produces a fresh screen state. zip is strictly pairwise: it holds a value until the other flow has an unused one, which means a rarely emitting source throttles the whole pair — usually the wrong shape for UI state. Neither operator waits for all sources to complete before it can emit.

questions.text: A ViewModel reacts to every value of a repository Flow without suspending its own initialization. What does flow.onEach { }.launchIn(viewModelScope) actually do?

answers.text: It collects the flow on the calling thread and returns once the flow has completed.
It registers the onEach block as a listener that runs without any coroutine collecting the flow.
It starts a coroutine in that scope which collects the flow, and returns its Job immediately.
It turns the cold flow into a hot one that keeps emitting after the scope has been cancelled.

questions.explanation: launchIn is shorthand for scope.launch { collect() }. The terminal operator is still collect, but it runs inside a new coroutine owned by the scope, so the call returns a Job straight away and cancelling the scope stops the collection. It does not make the flow hot — shareIn and stateIn do that — and a Flow produces nothing unless a collector is running.

questions.text: A cold Flow wraps a long paged database read, and the coroutine collecting it is cancelled part way through. What happens to the producer block?

answers.text: It stops at its next suspension point, because the producer runs inside the collector's coroutine.
It runs to completion, because a cold flow's producer block is given its own independent Job.
It stops at whatever statement it is executing, because cancellation interrupts the running thread.
It keeps producing values that are discarded until the flow reaches its natural end.

questions.explanation: A cold Flow has no coroutine of its own: collect runs the producer in the collecting coroutine, so cancelling that coroutine cancels production too. Like all coroutine cancellation this is cooperative — the block stops when it next reaches a cancellable suspension point such as emit(), not in the middle of a CPU-bound statement, and nothing carries on in the background afterwards.

questions.text: A ViewModel starts a large upload with viewModelScope.launch. The user leaves the screen for good and the ViewModel is cleared. What happens to that coroutine?

answers.text: It keeps running to the end, because viewModelScope outlives the ViewModel that owns it.
It is suspended while no UI observes it and resumes if that ViewModel is requested again.
It is cancelled, because viewModelScope is cancelled when the ViewModel is cleared.
It is cancelled only when it was launched on Dispatchers.Main rather than Dispatchers.IO.

questions.explanation: viewModelScope is bound to the ViewModel's lifetime and is cancelled when onCleared() runs, so every coroutine launched in it is cancelled with it. That is the point of the scope, and it is also why work the user expects to finish regardless of navigation — an upload, a purchase confirmation — belongs in WorkManager rather than a ViewModel. The dispatcher a coroutine runs on has no effect on whether its scope cancels it.

sources.title: Use Kotlin coroutines with lifecycle-aware components

questions.text: A listener-based location API is adapted into a Flow with callbackFlow. Why must the builder block end with awaitClose { }?

answers.text: It waits for the callback to deliver a first value before the flow is allowed to emit anything.
It keeps the flow open until the collector stops and gives the callback a place to unregister.
It converts the channel-based builder into a cold flow that can be collected more than once.
It buffers the callback's values so that a slow collector never causes an emission to be dropped.

questions.explanation: The callbackFlow block finishes as soon as it has registered the listener, and the builder treats a block that returns while its channel is still open as a bug — it throws IllegalStateException pointing at awaitClose, because the alternative is a silent leak with the flow ended and the listener still registered. awaitClose suspends until the collector cancels or the channel closes, which keeps the subscription alive and gives the code one reliable place to unregister. Buffering is configured separately through the builder's capacity, and callbackFlow already returns a cold, re-collectable Flow.

questions.text: A Flow backed by a network call should be retried at most three times, and only when the failure is an IOException. Which operator expresses that condition?

answers.text: retryWhen, whose predicate receives the cause and the attempt index and decides whether to resubscribe.
catch, whose block receives the cause and can emit a fallback value but cannot restart the upstream.
A try/catch wrapped around collect, which re-runs the terminal operator when it throws.
flowOn, which moves the upstream onto another dispatcher and repeats a failed emission there.

questions.explanation: retryWhen gives the predicate both the throwable and the zero-based attempt index, so it can require the cause to be an IOException and stop after three attempts; retry(3) { it is IOException } is the shorthand for the same thing. catch is a genuine operator but it terminates the upstream error rather than resubscribing, and flowOn only changes the context the upstream runs in. A try/catch around collect catches the failure but does not re-run the flow by itself.

questions.text: A MutableSharedFlow created with replay = 0 carries one-off UI events. A collector subscribes one second after an event was emitted. What does that collector receive?

answers.text: The missed event, because emissions are queued until at least one collector consumes them.
The missed event, because a SharedFlow always keeps its most recent value for a new subscriber.
Nothing emitted before it subscribed, because with replay 0 only active collectors receive values.
Nothing, and the flow also stops accepting emissions once its last collector goes away.

questions.explanation: A SharedFlow delivers a value to whichever collectors are subscribed at the moment it is emitted; the replay cache is the only thing a later subscriber can still see, and replay = 0 means there is none. Always retaining the latest value for new subscribers is StateFlow's behaviour, which is replay 1. A shared flow with no collectors neither queues values for a future one nor refuses further emissions.

questions.text: Select all that apply. A team replaces LiveData with StateFlow for exposing screen state from a ViewModel. Which statements about that change are correct?

answers.text: StateFlow requires an initial value, while LiveData can be observed before any value is set.
StateFlow can be collected only on the main thread, while LiveData may be observed from any thread.
StateFlow is not lifecycle-aware by itself, so UI collection needs a lifecycle-scoped collector.
StateFlow delivers every value assigned to it, while LiveData drops a value equal to the previous one.

questions.explanation: StateFlow is an ordinary hot flow that always holds a value, which is why an initial value is mandatory, and it knows nothing about Lifecycle — an Activity or Fragment has to collect it inside repeatOnLifecycle or flowWithLifecycle so a stopped UI is not updated, which LiveData handles itself. Collection is not restricted to the main thread; the dispatcher is chosen by the collecting coroutine. The last statement is backwards: StateFlow conflates and does not re-emit a value equal to the current one, whereas LiveData dispatches every setValue.

questions.text: Select all that apply. A sync client must decide which failed requests are worth retrying with backoff rather than reporting as a permanent failure. Which responses normally qualify?

answers.text: 503 Service Unavailable, which reports a temporary server-side condition.
400 Bad Request, which reports that the request itself was malformed.
429 Too Many Requests, which asks the caller to slow down and come back later.
403 Forbidden, which reports that the authenticated caller lacks permission.

questions.explanation: A response is worth retrying when the condition it describes is expected to change without the client changing the request. A 503 explicitly describes a temporary server condition, while 429 asks the client to slow down; either can include a Retry-After header telling the client how long to wait. That does not make every 5xx response retryable: 501 Not Implemented and 505 HTTP Version Not Supported normally require a capability or protocol change. A 400 or 403 should not be retried blindly either, and a 401 is retried only after the token has actually been refreshed.

questions.text: Select all that apply. Which statements about HTTP method semantics are correct?

answers.text: GET is both safe and idempotent, because it is not intended to change server state.
POST is idempotent, because the server assigns the identifier of the created resource.
DELETE is safe, because removing an already removed resource has no further effect.
PUT is idempotent but not safe, because repeating it leaves the resource in the same state.

questions.explanation: Safe means a request is not intended to change state; idempotent means repeating an identical request has the same effect as making it once. GET is both. PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe, because they do change state and merely converge on the same result when repeated — so DELETE being harmless to repeat is not the same as being safe. POST is neither, which is why a retried POST can create duplicates unless the server deduplicates on a client-supplied key.

questions.text: A screen issues six small requests to the same host at once. Why does HTTP/2 usually finish them sooner than HTTP/1.1 over a high-latency mobile link?

answers.text: It compresses response bodies, so less data crosses the radio for the same payload.
It caches responses on the client by itself, so most of the requests skip the network.
It multiplexes concurrent streams on one connection without HTTP/1.1 response ordering.
It opens one connection per request in parallel, which removes the per-connection queue.

questions.explanation: HTTP/1.1 can reuse persistent connections and pipeline multiple requests, so these calls do not necessarily serialize or each require a new TCP and TLS handshake. However, pipelined responses must be returned in request order, creating application-layer head-of-line blocking; clients commonly use multiple connections to gain concurrency. HTTP/2 instead interleaves largely independent streams on one connection, so a stalled response does not prevent progress on the others, and it also compresses headers. Body compression is available with either version, HTTP/2 adds no response cache of its own, and it does not open one connection per request.

questions.text: After a backend outage every client retries its failed sync on the same fixed schedule, and the service collapses again as it comes back up. Which change addresses that most directly?

answers.text: Add randomised jitter to an exponential backoff so retries from different clients spread out.
Increase the fixed retry interval so that each client waits longer before its next attempt.
Raise the request timeout so a slow response is no longer counted as a failure to retry.
Retry immediately but cap the number of attempts that any single client is allowed to make.

questions.explanation: The problem is correlation rather than attempt count: every client failed at the same instant, so any deterministic schedule brings them all back at the same instant. Exponential backoff spreads attempts over time and the random jitter breaks the synchronisation between clients. A longer fixed interval keeps them in lockstep and just moves the spike later, while timeouts and attempt caps limit one client without decorrelating the fleet.

questions.text: A repository builds a fresh client with OkHttpClient.Builder() for every request it makes. What is the main consequence?

answers.text: Each call pays a new connection setup, because the connection and thread pools belong to the client.
Calls start failing after a few requests, because OkHttp permits one client instance per process.
Interceptors stop running, because they are registered on a shared default client behind the scenes.
Responses are never cached, because OkHttp disables caching for clients built at call time.

questions.explanation: OkHttp is designed around one shared client: the connection pool, the dispatcher's thread pools and the response cache all live on the instance. Building a client per call throws that state away, so every request repeats the TCP and TLS handshake and no idle connection is ever reused, which is expensive on mobile. Nothing limits how many clients may exist; the supported way to vary configuration is newBuilder(), which produces a client sharing the same pools and cache.

questions.text: A chat client holds a WebSocket open but has received no messages for a while. What is the protocol-level purpose of sending a Ping and expecting a Pong?

answers.text: It can act as a keepalive and verify that the remote endpoint is still responsive.
The protocol closes a connection once it reaches the maximum session length the RFC defines.
Each frame has to be acknowledged by the receiver or the sender closes the connection itself.
A WebSocket is torn down by the framework on every pause, so it exists only while a screen is resumed.

questions.explanation: RFC 6455 allows an endpoint to send a Ping after the connection is established, and requires the peer to answer with a Pong unless the connection is already closing. The RFC explicitly describes Ping as a keepalive or a check that the remote endpoint is responsive. If an expected Pong does not arrive, the application can apply its own timeout and reconnection policy. The protocol defines no maximum session length and no acknowledgement for every data frame, and platform backgrounding is a separate concern.

questions.text: An API issues a short-lived access token together with a long-lived refresh token. What does that split gain over issuing one long-lived access token?

answers.text: The access token can be stored in plain text, because the refresh token protects it cryptographically.
A stolen access token expires quickly, and the refresh token travels rarely and can be revoked.
The user never sees a sign-in screen again, because a refresh token does not have to be renewed.
Requests get faster, because the server validates a short token by looking it up in a session store.

questions.explanation: What changes is the window of damage. A leaked access token is useful only until it expires, typically minutes. The client retains the refresh token and sends it less often, only to the authorization server rather than to resource servers; the authorization server validates it and can revoke it to end the session. The split does nothing to make either token safe in plain text, and refresh tokens themselves expire or rotate, so the user is eventually asked to authenticate again.

questions.text: An API returns several event shapes tagged by a "kind" field, modelled as a sealed interface whose subclasses are all @Serializable. Decoding fails because kotlinx.serialization looks for a field named "type". What is the appropriate fix?

answers.text: Annotate every subclass with @Transient so the extra field is skipped while decoding.
Enable ignoreUnknownKeys on the Json instance so the unrecognised field is dropped.
Rename the Kotlin property holding the value to kind so encoder and decoder agree.
Set classDiscriminator = "kind" on the Json instance so polymorphic decoding reads it.

questions.explanation: For a sealed hierarchy kotlinx.serialization generates a polymorphic serializer that writes and reads a class discriminator, whose key defaults to "type". When the API uses a different key the fix is configuration — classDiscriminator on the Json instance, or @JsonClassDiscriminator on the base type. ignoreUnknownKeys is the operator people reach for first, but it only stops unmapped keys from failing; it never tells the decoder which subclass to construct. The discriminator is not an ordinary property, so renaming one or marking it @Transient does not affect it.

questions.text: A shared data layer must issue HTTP calls from commonMain on both Android and iOS. Which difference between Retrofit and the Ktor client decides that choice?

answers.text: Retrofit targets the JVM and Android, while Ktor's client is multiplatform with a per-target engine.
Retrofit issues its calls synchronously, while the Ktor client is the one that supports suspension.
Retrofit cannot use kotlinx.serialization, while the Ktor client accepts no other serializer.
Retrofit needs an interface for each endpoint, while Ktor generates its client from an API schema.

questions.explanation: Retrofit is built on OkHttp and runs only where the JVM does, so commonMain in a Kotlin Multiplatform module cannot call it; Ktor exposes one common HttpClient API and plugs a platform engine in behind it, such as OkHttp on Android and Darwin on iOS. The remaining differences are not real: Retrofit supports suspend functions and a kotlinx.serialization converter, and Ktor's client is a hand-written request DSL rather than something generated from a schema.

questions.text: On Android 8.0 and higher, an app targeting API 26 or higher is idle in the background and outside any temporary allowlist window. It calls startService() to begin a sync. What happens?

answers.text: The service starts, but the system stops it after a few seconds unless it posts a notification.
The call succeeds and the service is queued to run when the app next reaches the foreground.
The call succeeds, because the background execution limits apply to implicit broadcasts instead.
The call fails with an IllegalStateException, because a background app may not start a service.

questions.explanation: For apps targeting API 26 or higher, Android 8.0 introduced background execution limits: once an app is idle and outside a temporary allowlist window, it may not create a background service, and startService() throws IllegalStateException (or a subclass on newer releases). WorkManager is appropriate when the work can be deferred, which covers most syncs. For user-visible work, startForegroundService() followed promptly by startForeground() is the relevant API when current foreground-service start rules allow it. Implicit broadcasts are restricted by the same release, but the service restriction is separate from them.

questions.text: A started Service performs a long HTTP download directly inside onStartCommand(), and the app's UI freezes while it runs. Why?

answers.text: onStartCommand() blocks its caller until it returns, so the Activity that started it stalls.
A Service has no thread of its own, and its callbacks run on the main thread of the process.
A Service is bound to the component that started it and inherits that component's lifecycle.
A Service runs at a lower scheduling priority, so the main thread waits for it to release the CPU.

questions.explanation: A Service is a component, not a thread. onCreate(), onStartCommand() and onDestroy() all run on the process's main thread, so blocking work inside them freezes the UI exactly as it would inside an Activity. Long work needs its own thread or a coroutine on a background dispatcher — the job IntentService used to do automatically. Starting a service is asynchronous and does not block the caller, and a started service is independent of whatever component started it.

questions.text: A component calls startForegroundService() and the service then does some setup before promoting itself. What does the platform require of it?

answers.text: It may post the notification whenever ready; until then the service simply runs in the background.
It must first obtain the FOREGROUND_SERVICE permission from the user through a runtime prompt.
It must call startForeground() within the platform's timeout, or the system stops it and reports an error.
It may skip startForeground() as long as a foregroundServiceType is declared for it in the manifest.

questions.explanation: startForegroundService() is a promise to the system that the service will promote itself, and the platform allows only a short window for startForeground() to post the ongoing notification. Missing it stops the service and surfaces as an ANR or a did-not-start-in-time error, so setup work has to happen after promotion rather than before it. Declaring a foregroundServiceType is an additional requirement on newer versions, not a substitute, and FOREGROUND_SERVICE is an install-time permission with no user prompt.

questions.text: An Activity binds to a Service with bindService(), and nothing has ever called startService() on it. What determines how long that service lives?

answers.text: It lives while at least one client stays bound, and is destroyed when the last one unbinds.
It lives until it calls stopSelf(), because binding does not influence a service's lifetime.
It lives as long as the process does, because a bound service is a process-scoped singleton.
It lives until the bound Activity is stopped, because binding follows that Activity's lifecycle.

questions.explanation: A purely bound service exists for its clients: the system creates it on the first bindService() and destroys it once the last client unbinds. That is why a component binding in onStart() must unbind in onStop() — the platform tracks bindings, not lifecycles, so a forgotten unbind keeps the service alive. stopSelf() ends a started service, and a service that is both started and bound survives until both conditions end.

questions.text: A device sits unplugged and motionless overnight. What does Doze do with an app's pending network work and standard alarms?

answers.text: It cancels them, so the app has to reschedule everything the next time the user unlocks the device.
It runs them at their normal times but throttles the app's network to a lower bandwidth ceiling.
It defers them and releases them in periodic maintenance windows while the device remains idle.
It leaves them alone, because Doze restricts only apps the user has not opened for several days.

questions.explanation: Doze batches work rather than discarding it. While the device is idle, network access is suspended and jobs, syncs and standard alarms are held back; the system then opens a maintenance window in which everything deferred runs, and those windows grow further apart the longer idle continues. Restricting a particular app according to how recently the user engaged with it is App Standby — a related mechanism that applies per app rather than per device.

sources.title: Optimize for Doze and App Standby

questions.text: One feature runs a nightly cleanup with no user-visible time, and another must show a reminder at a moment the user chose. Which mapping to AlarmManager and WorkManager fits?

answers.text: Both with WorkManager, because its periodic work can be pinned to an exact clock time.
Cleanup with WorkManager and reminder with AlarmManager, because only the reminder needs the clock.
Both with AlarmManager, because it is the API that survives the app's process being killed.
Cleanup with AlarmManager and reminder with WorkManager, because deferrable work needs a trigger.

questions.explanation: AlarmManager exists to fire something at a point on the user's clock or on elapsed time, which is what a chosen reminder needs; exact alarms sit behind a permission precisely because that costs battery. WorkManager exists for work that must eventually happen and can wait for constraints, and its periodic work has a flex interval rather than an exact instant. Durability does not separate them — both survive process death — so the deciding question is whether the user can perceive when the work runs.

questions.text: A CoroutineWorker uploading large videos regularly exceeds the execution limit and WorkManager stops it part way. What is the supported way to let it keep running?

answers.text: Extend the limit by setting a longer backoff delay on the WorkRequest before enqueuing it.
Return Result.retry() before the limit so WorkManager restarts the upload from the beginning.
Make it a long-running worker with setForeground(), which shows an ongoing notification.
Enqueue it as expedited work, which lifts the execution time limit for that request.

questions.explanation: WorkManager gives a worker about ten minutes before stopping and rescheduling it. Work that genuinely needs longer must run as a long-running worker: CoroutineWorker exposes a suspending setForeground(), and ListenableWorker the equivalent setForegroundAsync(), which promotes the work to a foreground service with an ongoing notification — the user-visible cost of taking the extra time. Expedited work is about starting promptly and has its own quota rather than a longer runtime, and backoff only controls the delay before a retry, not how long an attempt may take.

questions.text: A queued upload must still happen after the user restarts the phone. What explains why WorkManager satisfies that requirement and a coroutine does not?

answers.text: WorkManager keeps a process alive across the restart so the pending coroutine can resume there.
WorkManager writes the request into SharedPreferences that the app re-reads on its next launch.
WorkManager registers a BOOT_COMPLETED receiver that the app itself must declare and implement.
WorkManager records the request in its own database and reschedules it once the device reboots.

questions.explanation: WorkManager persists every enqueued request in an internal database, so the request outlives both process death and a reboot, and the library's own components re-schedule pending work when the device comes back up. A coroutine exists only in process memory and disappears when the process ends. No app keeps a process running across a restart, and the developer does not have to write the persistence or the boot receiver — that is the guarantee WorkManager is providing.

questions.text: A ContentProvider needs a dependency from Hilt's SingletonComponent, but @AndroidEntryPoint does not support providers. Which Hilt facility supplies it?

answers.text: An @AndroidEntryPoint annotation on the provider, which Hilt accepts for all framework classes.
An @EntryPoint interface obtained through EntryPointAccessors for the component that owns it.
A @Module installed into the provider's own generated component, built when it is first used.
A field marked @Inject, which Hilt populates while the system instantiates the provider.

questions.explanation: @AndroidEntryPoint covers a fixed set of framework classes, and ContentProvider is deliberately not among them — providers are created before the Application's onCreate() completes. @EntryPoint declares an interface listing the bindings needed, annotated @InstallIn for the component that holds them, and EntryPointAccessors retrieves an implementation from a Context. Hilt does not create a component per provider, and field injection there has nothing to inject from.

questions.text: A Hilt module is annotated @InstallIn(ActivityComponent::class). What does that annotation decide?

answers.text: How long each binding's instance lives, regardless of any scope annotation on the provider.
That Hilt generates a separate component for every module installed with that annotation.
That the bindings are constructed when the Activity starts and released when it is stopped.
Which generated component receives the bindings, and therefore where they can be injected.

questions.explanation: @InstallIn attaches a module to one of Hilt's generated components, which is what decides visibility: bindings in ActivityComponent are injectable into an Activity and the Fragments and Views under it, but not into an application-wide singleton. Lifetime is a separate decision expressed by a scope annotation such as @ActivityScoped — an unscoped binding installed there still produces a new instance per request. Hilt's component hierarchy is fixed, and modules join it rather than creating components.

questions.text: A dependency is shared by an Activity and its Fragments and must keep the same instance across a rotation. Which Hilt component should hold it?

answers.text: ActivityComponent, which is recreated with the Activity and so starts fresh after a rotation.
FragmentComponent, whose bindings are shared upward with the Activity hosting the Fragment.
ActivityRetainedComponent, which is created with the Activity and survives configuration changes.
SingletonComponent, which is the one component whose bindings a Fragment is able to receive.

questions.explanation: Hilt's components mirror Android lifetimes. ActivityComponent is destroyed and recreated with the Activity instance, so anything scoped to it is lost on rotation, while ActivityRetainedComponent uses the same retention mechanism as ViewModels and spans configuration changes; @ActivityRetainedScoped is its scope. SingletonComponent would also survive but makes the dependency application-wide for the rest of the process. Bindings flow down the hierarchy, never up from a Fragment to its Activity.

questions.text: A team migrates an Android app from hand-written Dagger components to Hilt. What do they gain, and what do they give up?

answers.text: They gain runtime resolution of the graph, and give up the compile-time errors Dagger reported.
They gain a standard component hierarchy tied to Android lifetimes, and give up defining their own.
They gain support for constructor injection, and give up the ability to declare modules at all.
They gain smaller generated code, and give up the ability to scope a binding to a lifetime.

questions.explanation: Hilt is Dagger with the Android graph decided in advance: a fixed hierarchy from SingletonComponent down to FragmentComponent and ViewComponent, with entry points and scopes already named. That removes most of the wiring boilerplate and makes multi-module setups consistent, and the price is fitting the app into that hierarchy instead of designing one. Underneath it is still compile-time Dagger, still uses modules, and still supports scoping and constructor injection.

questions.text: A team wires every dependency by hand in an application-level container. Which cost grows fastest as the object graph gets larger?

answers.text: Instances can no longer be scoped, because scoping needs a code-generating framework.
Constructor injection has to give way to field injection as the number of classes grows.
Every new dependency has to be threaded by hand through each construction site above it.
Manual wiring stops working once one dependency has to be shared between two screens.

questions.explanation: Manual DI is a sound starting point and its mechanics — constructor parameters plus a container holding shared instances — keep working at any size. What grows is the clerical cost: adding a parameter deep in the graph forces an edit at every construction site above it, and the container turns into a long, order-sensitive file that is easy to get subtly wrong. A generator such as Dagger removes that work; it does not enable sharing, scoping or constructor injection, all of which handwritten code already expresses.

questions.text: A Kotlin Multiplatform shared module needs a dependency container usable from commonMain on both Android and iOS. Why is Koin a candidate where Dagger and Hilt are not?

answers.text: Koin resolves dependencies by reflection, which Kotlin/Native supports better than code generation.
Koin generates one container per platform from a shared schema during the build.
Koin needs an Android Context, which the iOS target supplies through an expect declaration.
Koin declares its graph in ordinary Kotlin that compiles for every target, with no annotation processing.

questions.explanation: Dagger and Hilt are annotation processors that emit JVM code, and Hilt is additionally tied to Android framework classes, so neither can process commonMain for an iOS target. Koin's modules are a plain Kotlin DSL evaluated at runtime, so they compile wherever Kotlin does — the trade-off being that a missing binding surfaces as a runtime failure rather than a compile error. Koin does not require a Context, does not generate per-platform containers, and does not rely on reflection to build its definitions.

questions.text: A class declares @Inject on its constructor and is requested from a Dagger component. How is the instance actually produced?

answers.text: Dagger emits a factory class during the build, which the generated component calls to construct it.
Dagger reads the annotation at runtime and constructs the object reflectively on first request.
Dagger rewrites the class's bytecode so its constructor resolves its own parameters from a registry.
Dagger registers the constructor in a service locator the class queries when it is instantiated.

questions.explanation: Dagger is an annotation processor. For each @Inject constructor it generates a Factory, and for each @Component it generates an implementation that wires those factories together; all of it is ordinary source compiled alongside the app. That makes an unsatisfied dependency a compile error rather than a runtime graph failure. At runtime Dagger follows generated factory and provider calls instead of discovering the graph with reflection, giving it low, predictable overhead rather than zero overhead: dependency resolution, object creation, scopes and lazy providers can still require work. Dagger neither inspects annotations at runtime nor rewrites bytecode, and a service locator is the pattern it exists to replace.

questions.text: Select all that apply. Which statements about the Android application sandbox are correct?

answers.text: The sandbox is enforced by the Java runtime, so native code in an app runs outside of it.
Each installed app is normally given its own Linux user ID, which owns its files and its process.
An app can read another app's private data once the user grants it any dangerous permission.
Files written into an app's internal storage directory are unreadable by other apps by default.

questions.explanation: The sandbox is a kernel-level construct: the system assigns each app a distinct UID and runs its process under it, so ordinary Linux file permissions keep one app's internal storage out of another's reach. Because the kernel enforces it rather than the runtime, native code sits inside the same sandbox as Kotlin code. Runtime permissions widen access to specific system resources such as the camera or contacts, and none of them opens another app's private directory.

questions.text: An app declares both INTERNET and ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION in its manifest, and only one of them ever produces a user prompt. Why?

answers.text: INTERNET is a normal permission granted at install, while location is dangerous and asked at runtime.
INTERNET is granted because the app targets a modern SDK, while location prompts on every API level.
INTERNET is prompted once at first launch, while location is prompted before each individual use.
INTERNET does not belong in the manifest at all, so nothing about it is ever shown to the user.

questions.explanation: Every permission carries a protection level. Normal permissions such as INTERNET describe low-risk capabilities, and the system grants them at install without involving the user; dangerous permissions such as ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION guard private user data, so they must be requested at runtime and can be revoked afterwards. The behaviour follows from the protection level rather than the target SDK or how often a dialog appears, and INTERNET still has to be declared in the manifest to be granted.

questions.text: A WebView loads a page from a partner domain, and addJavascriptInterface() exposes an object with a getAuthToken() method to it. What is the risk?

answers.text: The exposed object is serialized into the page, so the token ends up visible in the HTML source.
The interface stays disabled unless the page is served over HTTPS, so the call silently returns null.
Any script the WebView ends up running, including injected or redirected content, can call the method.
The method is invoked on the main thread, so a slow implementation of it can produce an ANR.

questions.explanation: A JavaScript interface is a bridge from whatever the WebView happens to be executing into app code, and the WebView cannot distinguish first-party script from injected script, a redirect, or a compromised third-party resource already on the page. The documentation is explicit that the API should not be used unless you wrote all of the HTML and JavaScript in the WebView, so anything reachable through the exposed object has to be assumed reachable by an attacker — which rules out a token accessor. The danger is what the method can do, not where or when it runs.

sources.title: Build web apps in WebView: binding JavaScript code to Android code

questions.text: A debug build has to reach a development server over plain HTTP, while the release build should keep cleartext traffic blocked. Which configuration expresses that?

answers.text: A Network Security Config in the debug variant permitting cleartext for that one host.
Setting usesCleartextTraffic to true in the main manifest, which applies to debuggable builds.
Adding the host to a trust-anchor list, which is what allows plain HTTP for a named domain.
Disabling TLS verification inside an OkHttp interceptor added only to the debug source set.

questions.explanation: Cleartext HTTP is off by default for apps targeting Android 9 and later, and the Network Security Config is the mechanism for a scoped exception: a domain-config that sets cleartextTrafficPermitted for the development host, placed in the debug source set so release keeps the default. usesCleartextTraffic is a blunt manifest flag with no variant awareness, trust anchors decide which certificate authorities are trusted rather than whether HTTP is allowed at all, and turning off TLS verification addresses a different problem badly.

questions.text: An app decrypts a stored secret after BiometricPrompt reports success. Why is trusting that callback weaker than binding the key to authentication in the Keystore?

answers.text: The callback arrives on a background thread, so the result can land after the secret is read.
The callback is an in-app signal, while an auth-bound Keystore key stays unusable until authentication.
The callback reports success for any enrolled user, while a Keystore key is tied to a single finger.
The callback cannot be observed from Compose, so the result has to be cached inside a ViewModel.

questions.explanation: A success callback is a branch in the app's own code, and anyone able to modify the app or hook the process can take that branch without authenticating. Creating the key with setUserAuthenticationRequired(true) moves the check into the Keystore itself: the cryptographic operation fails unless the platform has recorded a recent authentication, so skipping the UI does not yield the plaintext. Biometric-only keys that require authentication for every use are also invalidated by biometric enrolment changes by default, but this is configurable with setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(false), not an inherent property of every authentication-bound key.

questions.text: An app must keep a refresh token on the device between launches. Which approach matches the realistic threat model for a mobile client?

answers.text: Ship it encrypted with a key compiled into the APK, so the token and its key travel together.
Keep it in shared external storage, where files sit outside the reach of other installed apps.
Keep it in app-private storage and rely on server-side revocation, which a compromised device cannot undo.
Obfuscate it inside SharedPreferences, since obfuscation prevents extraction from a device backup.

questions.explanation: App-private storage is the right location because the sandbox keeps other apps out, but it protects against other apps rather than against the device owner or malware with root. What actually bounds the damage is that the server can revoke the refresh token and that the access tokens it mints are short-lived. A key compiled into the APK is recoverable by anyone who unpacks it, shared external storage is readable by other apps, and obfuscation is not encryption and does not stop a backup being inspected.

questions.text: A team adds root detection so the app refuses to run on rooted devices. What should they realistically expect that control to achieve?

answers.text: It prevents the app's traffic from being inspected, because a proxy needs root to install its CA.
It guarantees the integrity of local data, because the sandbox holds while the device is unrooted.
It raises the effort for casual tampering, while the server still trusts nothing the client asserts.
It removes the need for server-side authorization checks, since only trusted devices reach the API.

questions.explanation: Root detection runs inside the very environment it is trying to assess, so an attacker who controls the device also controls the answer — it is a signal and a source of friction, not a trust boundary. Every authorization decision that matters therefore still belongs on the server, which is the one place the attacker does not control; platform attestation such as the Play Integrity API is designed to be verified there for the same reason. Traffic inspection does not always require root, and no client-side check can guarantee the integrity of local data.

questions.text: A BroadcastReceiver compresses a large file synchronously inside onReceive(), taking longer than the receiver timeout. Users see the app freeze whenever that broadcast arrives. What explains it?

answers.text: onReceive() runs on a binder thread, and the framework blocks the main thread until it returns.
The receiver is discarded after onReceive() returns, so the compression restarts on every broadcast.
onReceive() runs on the main thread with a short time budget, and exceeding it produces an ANR.
Broadcasts are delivered serially, so the app waits behind other apps' receivers before running its own.

questions.explanation: onReceive() is normally invoked on the main thread of the app's process, and the system gives a receiver only a short time to finish before treating the app as unresponsive. Long synchronous computation there therefore blocks the UI and produces an ANR when it exceeds the timeout. For brief asynchronous work, goAsync() lets onReceive() return while work scheduled on another dispatcher or thread finishes within the receiver's remaining budget; substantial durable work belongs in a WorkManager request. Receivers do not normally run on a binder thread, and another app's receiver does not stall yours in this way.

questions.text: Why does the Android View toolkit require a View hierarchy to be modified only from the main thread?

answers.text: The main thread holds a lock over the hierarchy, so another thread would block until it is released.
The toolkit is not thread-safe, and confining it to one thread replaces locking on every operation.
Only the main thread is permitted to allocate the native objects that back each View.
Rendering happens on the main thread, so an update from elsewhere would be applied a frame late.

questions.explanation: The View system is not designed for concurrent access: hierarchy state, measurement, layout and invalidation assume ordered access from the UI thread, avoiding synchronization around every operation. Some off-thread operations that reach an attached ViewRootImpl throw CalledFromWrongThreadException, but not every View method performs that check. Unchecked access can appear to work while racing state or causing a later failure, so the absence of an immediate exception does not make it safe. A separate render thread in the drawing pipeline does not make View mutation thread-safe.

questions.text: Select all that apply. Which of these keep a destroyed Activity reachable and therefore leak it?

answers.text: A companion-object field assigned the Activity in onCreate() and never cleared afterwards.
An Activity-scoped ViewModel holding that screen's UI state in a StateFlow it exposes.
A listener registered on an app-wide singleton by an anonymous class that calls into the Activity.
A View inside the Activity's own layout holding that Activity as the Context it was inflated with.

questions.explanation: A leak is simply a reference chain from something long-lived to an object that should be gone. A static or companion field outlives every Activity in the process, and a listener that calls back into its Activity necessarily holds a reference to it, so handing one to an application-scoped object keeps that Activity alive until it is unregistered. A ViewModel holds no Context and is cleared with its owner, and a View referencing the Activity that inflated it points down the tree — it dies together with the Activity, not after it.

questions.text: A Fragment registers a callback that updates one of its views on an application-scoped repository in onViewCreated(), and never removes it. What is the consequence?

answers.text: The callback is removed by the system as soon as the Fragment's view is destroyed.
The Fragment stops receiving callbacks after onStop() and resumes receiving them on restart.
The repository throws when it invokes a callback that belongs to an already destroyed Fragment.
The repository keeps the Fragment reachable, so each configuration change leaves a dead one behind.

questions.explanation: A callback that touches the Fragment's views holds a reference to the Fragment, so registering it creates a chain from the long-lived repository down to a screen. A configuration change destroys that Fragment instance and creates a new one that registers again, so the repository accumulates callbacks, each pinning a dead Fragment and its views. Returning from the back stack is a different bug rather than the same one: the instance survives and only its view is rebuilt, so onViewCreated() registers a second callback that fires twice. Nothing unregisters on the app's behalf and nothing throws. The fix is to unregister in the matching teardown callback, or to expose the data as a Flow collected in a lifecycle-scoped collector so the subscription ends with the scope.

questions.text: An app throws OutOfMemoryError while decoding large images even though the device reports several gigabytes of free RAM. Why?

answers.text: ART reserves memory for the system before an app starts, so free RAM is not offered to apps.
Each app process has a heap limit set by the device configuration, well below total system memory.
Bitmap memory is not garbage collected, so decoded images accumulate until the app is restarted.
The collector runs only while the device is idle, so a short burst of allocation overflows the heap.

questions.explanation: Android caps how much heap a single app process may use. The cap is a device property, readable through ActivityManager.getMemoryClass(), and it sits deliberately far below physical RAM so that many apps can coexist and the system can keep several in memory. Reaching it throws OutOfMemoryError no matter how much the rest of the device has spare, which is why large images are downsampled to the size actually displayed instead of decoded at full resolution. Bitmap memory is reclaimable, and ART collects continuously rather than waiting for an idle device.

questions.text: An adapter calls notifyDataSetChanged() after every refresh, and the list flickers and loses its item animations. What does moving to DiffUtil change?

answers.text: It caches the previous list in the adapter, so RecyclerView reuses the old ViewHolders as they are.
It computes the minimal set of item changes, so only affected rows are rebound and animated.
It moves item binding off the main thread, so a long list no longer blocks the current frame.
It replaces the LayoutManager's measurement pass with a cached one, so layout is skipped entirely.

questions.explanation: notifyDataSetChanged() tells RecyclerView that anything may have changed, so it rebinds every visible holder and can animate nothing, because it has no idea which item corresponds to which. DiffUtil compares the old and new lists and issues precise insert, remove, move and change notifications, so RecyclerView rebinds only what actually differs and its default item animations work again. ListAdapter and AsyncListDiffer additionally run the comparison off the main thread — the binding itself still happens there.

questions.text: A CPU profiler offers both sampled and instrumented call recording for a Java or Kotlin method trace. What is the trade-off between them?

answers.text: Sampling records every call but covers the main thread; tracing covers all threads at the same cost.
Sampling is exact but limited to native code; tracing is approximate and limited to managed code.
Sampling needs a debuggable build; tracing works on release builds without any extra configuration.
Sampling captures stacks at an interval with low overhead; tracing sees every call but distorts timing.

questions.explanation: A sampled recording captures the call stack at a fixed interval, so its cost stays roughly constant and a short or infrequently executed method can be missed altogether — which makes it the right tool for finding where wall-clock time concentrates. An instrumented trace hooks method entry and exit, so it sees every call and an exact call count, but the instrumentation is heavy enough to change the timings it is measuring. Neither technique is restricted to one thread or to one kind of code.
