questions.text: A ViewModel test asserts with verify(repository).save(item) and breaks every time the ViewModel changes how it persists. What does replacing that mock with a fake repository change?

answers.text: The test can assert the item ended up stored, rather than that one particular call was made.
The test no longer needs the repository interface, because a fake can extend the concrete class.
The test verifies more, because a fake records each interaction that the mock would have recorded.
The test becomes an integration test, because a fake exercises the real persistence layer beneath.

questions.explanation: verify() pins the interaction — which method, how often, with which arguments — so it fails when the implementation changes even though the observable behaviour did not. A fake is a working in-memory implementation of the same interface, which lets the test ask what the state is afterwards: the property the feature actually promises. That is the trade-off, not a free upgrade — a fake still needs the interface, records nothing on its own, and touches no real persistence.

questions.text: Inside runTest, a ViewModel receives StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler) and launches work on it. The assertion runs before that work has happened. Which call makes the pending work run first?

answers.text: runBlocking { }, which suspends the test until the other coroutine's Job has completed.
advanceUntilIdle(), which runs everything the test scheduler has queued until nothing is left.
Thread.sleep() for a short interval, which gives the dispatcher time to pick the work up.
setMain(UnconfinedTestDispatcher()), which is required before any assertion inside runTest.

questions.explanation: runTest exposes its virtual-time scheduler as testScheduler. Passing that scheduler to StandardTestDispatcher makes the injected dispatcher share the scheduler controlled by the TestScope, so advanceUntilIdle() drains its queued tasks and skips their delays before the assertion. advanceTimeBy() and runCurrent() give finer control over the same scheduler. A StandardTestDispatcher created with a separate scheduler would not be advanced by this call; real blocking or sleeping does not advance virtual time, and an UnconfinedTestDispatcher changes when coroutines start rather than being a prerequisite.

questions.text: A repository emits cached data first and then refreshes it from the network. Which setup exercises that policy most directly?

answers.text: A mock of the repository itself, verifying that its refresh method runs after each read.
A unit test of the ViewModel, asserting that its UI state eventually shows the refreshed data.
A fake remote source and an in-memory local source, asserting what the repository emits over time.
An instrumented test against the real API, asserting the final value matches what the server holds.

questions.explanation: The behaviour under test is the repository's own decision-making, so both collaborators must be controllable and neither may be the class under test. Fakes let the test hold the network response, observe the cached emission, then release it and assert the refreshed one — that sequence is the policy. Mocking the repository tests nothing about it, a real network makes the result non-deterministic, and routing the assertion through the ViewModel adds a layer that can mask where the failure came from.

questions.text: A Compose test must assert on a colour part-way through a 250 ms animation, but the default synchronization lets the animation finish before the assertion runs. What lets the test observe an intermediate frame?

answers.text: Call waitForIdle() before the assertion so the test re-reads the tree mid-animation.
Wrap the assertion in waitUntil() with a timeout shorter than the animation's duration.
Run the assertion inside runOnIdle() so that it executes while the animation is going.
Set mainClock.autoAdvance to false and step the clock forward with advanceTimeBy().

questions.explanation: The test rule advances the test clock and synchronizes before every action and assertion, which is what makes most Compose tests deterministic without explicit waiting — and it is also why a finite animation has already settled by the time an assertion runs. Taking the clock over with autoAdvance set to false freezes it, and advanceTimeBy() moves it a controlled amount so the assertion observes a chosen frame. waitForIdle() and runOnIdle() do the opposite and wait for the animation to finish first, while waitUntil() polls a condition without ever stopping the clock.

questions.text: A class decides whether a cached response is stale by calling System.currentTimeMillis() inside the method under test. Why is that hard to test, and what is the smallest fix?

answers.text: The call is slow; wrap it in a coroutine so the test can await the result deterministically.
The value is a Long; convert it to an Instant so the test can compare it with an expected date.
The call is unavailable in a JVM test; add a Robolectric shadow so that it returns a real value.
The test cannot control now; inject a time source the test sets to a fixed value.

questions.explanation: The class has no seam: the value that decides the outcome comes from a global the test cannot set, so the test can only assert whatever happens to be true while it runs, and a boundary case such as an entry expiring exactly now is untestable. Taking the current time from an injected abstraction — a Clock, or simply a () -> Long — hands that decision to the test. The call is neither slow nor unavailable on the JVM, and changing its type does nothing to make it controllable.

questions.text: A local JVM unit test exercises a class that calls android.text.TextUtils, and it fails with a "not mocked" error. What does that indicate?

answers.text: The android.jar on the unit-test classpath is stubbed, so its methods throw unless configured otherwise.
The test is missing the AndroidJUnit4 runner, which would supply real framework implementations.
The class under test has to be instrumented, because a local test loads no Android classes at all.
Code shrinking removed the method from the test classpath, so the call resolves to a stub instead.

questions.explanation: Local unit tests compile against a stubbed android.jar in which every method throws, so an accidental dependence on the framework is visible rather than silently returning a wrong default. The options are to keep the framework out of the class under test, which is usually the best outcome, to run the test with Robolectric, which provides working implementations on the JVM, or to move it to an instrumented test. returnDefaultValues silences the exception without addressing the dependency. Local tests do load Android classes — those classes simply have no behaviour.

questions.text: A team adopts DataStore for local settings. What distinguishes Preferences DataStore from Proto DataStore?

answers.text: Preferences writes synchronously on the calling thread, while Proto writes through a Flow.
Preferences stores untyped key-value pairs, while Proto stores a schema-defined object with typed fields.
Preferences is limited to primitives, while Proto persists arbitrary Kotlin classes with no schema.
Preferences persists into a database file, while Proto keeps its data for the current process only.

questions.explanation: Both variants are the same asynchronous, transactional store; what differs is the shape of the data. Preferences DataStore holds keys and values with no schema, so a mistyped key or a wrong type only shows up at run time. Proto DataStore serializes a single object whose fields are declared in a schema, which buys compile-time type safety at the cost of defining that schema and evolving it compatibly. Neither writes on the caller's thread, and both persist to a file.

questions.text: A SharedPreferences editor can be finished with apply() or with commit(). What is the practical difference?

answers.text: apply() queues the change until the next app launch; commit() makes it visible immediately.
apply() writes to disk at once; commit() batches several edits together into one atomic write.
apply() updates memory at once and writes to disk in the background; commit() writes before returning.
apply() is safe from any thread, while commit() may be called only from the main thread.

questions.explanation: Both change the in-memory map atomically and immediately, so a subsequent read sees the new value either way. apply() then persists asynchronously and returns nothing, while commit() performs the disk write synchronously and returns a boolean — which is exactly why calling it on the main thread is the classic StrictMode violation. Neither defers the change to a later launch, and commit() is not restricted to the main thread; it is the one to keep off it.

questions.text: A developer mistypes a column name inside a Room @Query annotation. When does that mistake surface?

answers.text: At run time on first execution, because the query string reaches SQLite unchanged.
At run time when the database opens, because Room validates queries during its migration check.
It does not, because Room quietly drops a projection column that it is unable to resolve.
At build time, because Room verifies each query against the schema derived from the entities.

questions.explanation: Room's annotation processor knows the schema from the @Entity classes, so it parses and checks every @Query while compiling: a wrong column, a return type that does not match the projection, or an unbound parameter becomes a build error rather than a crash on a user's device. That verification is the main practical argument for Room over hand-written SQLite strings. Room does compare the on-device schema at open time, but that is the migration identity check, not query validation.

questions.text: Select all that apply. A feed repository caches responses both in an in-memory map and in a Room table. Which statements about that two-level cache are correct?

answers.text: The in-memory level disappears when the process is killed, while the Room table survives it.
The Room table removes the need to decide how long a cached entry stays valid.
The in-memory level avoids a network call and a disk read on an immediately repeated request.
The in-memory level is shared with other apps that happen to request the same resource.

questions.explanation: The two levels answer different questions. Memory is the fastest and is scoped to the process, so it goes away with process death, while the database survives restarts and reboots and is what lets the screen render instantly on a cold start. Neither level answers the freshness question — a staleness policy, a timestamp or a validator still has to decide when an entry must be refetched. And a cache inside an app is private to that app's sandbox; nothing about it is shared with other applications.

questions.text: An app stores PDFs the user explicitly saved, and also thumbnails it can regenerate at any time. Which app-specific directories fit those two kinds of file?

answers.text: The PDFs in filesDir and the thumbnails in cacheDir, which the system may clear under pressure.
Both in cacheDir, because anything downloaded over the network is by definition a cached copy.
Both in filesDir, because cacheDir is readable by other apps and unsuitable for user content.
The PDFs in cacheDir and the thumbnails in filesDir, since generated data must survive a cleanup.

questions.explanation: filesDir and cacheDir both live inside the app's private sandbox, so neither is visible to other apps; what differs is the promise the system makes about them. Files in cacheDir are declared expendable and may be deleted when storage runs low, which is right for anything the app can produce again. Content the user chose to keep belongs in filesDir, where it remains until the app deletes it or the user clears the app's data.

questions.text: A shared Kotlin Multiplatform data layer must persist relational data on Android and iOS. What is the substantive difference between Room and SQLDelight for that job?

answers.text: Room supports observable queries as Flow, while SQLDelight can expose only one-shot reads.
Room generates its schema from annotated Kotlin classes; SQLDelight generates Kotlin from .sq files.
Room runs on any Kotlin target, while SQLDelight targets the JVM and requires a JDBC driver.
Room requires SQL to be written by hand, while SQLDelight derives statements from a Kotlin DSL.

questions.explanation: The direction of code generation is the real difference. Room starts from Kotlin — @Entity classes and @Dao interfaces — and derives the schema and the query verification from them, while SQLDelight starts from SQL in .sq files and generates typed Kotlin APIs out of it, which keeps the dialect explicit. Both support Kotlin Multiplatform targets today and both can expose results as Flow, so the decision is really about which artefact should be the source of truth for the schema.

questions.text: Select all that apply. You are asked to design the client for a photo feed. Which clarifying questions change the client architecture most?

answers.text: Whether the feed must render before the network responds on a cold start.
Which analytics events the product team wants recorded when a photo is opened.
Whether users can post while offline and expect the post to appear immediately.
Which image codec the backend uses when it stores the original uploaded files.

questions.explanation: The questions worth asking first are the ones whose answers change the shape of the client. Whether the feed must render before the network answers decides whether there is a local source of truth at all, and whether users can write offline decides whether there is a durable outbox, locally generated identifiers and conflict handling. Analytics requirements and the backend's storage format are real concerns, but the client's data flow looks the same whichever way they are answered.

questions.text: A background sync must keep data reasonably fresh on a metered connection without draining the battery. Which requirement should shape the design first?

answers.text: How large each payload is, because compression removes the need to think about frequency.
Which HTTP client is used, because its connection pooling decides the battery cost of a sync.
How stale the data may be, because that sets how often the app has to wake the radio at all.
How many requests run concurrently, because parallelism decides the total radio time used.

questions.explanation: On a mobile device the dominant cost is waking the cellular radio and holding it awake, not the number of bytes sent, so the acceptable staleness window is the requirement everything else follows from: it fixes the sync frequency, decides whether several pieces of work can be batched into one wake-up, and determines whether constraints such as unmetered or charging are acceptable. Payload size, client choice and concurrency all matter, but they optimise within a frequency the freshness requirement has already chosen.

questions.text: An offline app queues writes and replays them in order. One write is rejected by the server on every attempt, and the user's later edits stop syncing entirely. What does the design need?

answers.text: A longer backoff on that write, so the queue reaches it less often and progresses in between.
A larger queue, so later edits are not dropped while the failing write is still pending.
A retry that restarts from the head of the queue each time, so that no write is ever skipped.
An attempt cap that quarantines the failed write and dependents while unrelated writes continue.

questions.explanation: A permanently failing item at the head of an ordered queue is a poison message: retrying it forever turns one bad write into a complete sync outage for that user. The design needs a dependency-aware terminal state. After an attempt or age limit, it should quarantine the failed write together with operations that causally depend on it, surface that chain when the user must resolve it, and let unrelated entities continue syncing. Sending a dependent rename after its create failed would only create another invalid request. Backoff slows the loop, and a bigger queue just postpones the same failure.

questions.text: A pricing rule changes several times a quarter, and shipped app versions stay in use for months. Where should the rule be evaluated?

answers.text: On the client, so each release can be tested against the exact rule that it will apply.
On both, with the client recomputing the server's result so a mismatch can be detected.
On the server, so a change reaches every installed client without needing an app release.
On the client, with the server validating only the final total that it receives back.

questions.explanation: What decides the split is who can change the rule and how quickly the change propagates. Logic compiled into shipped binaries is frozen for as long as those versions remain installed, so a rule that moves quarterly would leave a long tail of clients computing the wrong price with no way to correct them. Evaluating on the server — with the client rendering what it is told, and caching the last answer for offline display — makes the change take effect at once. Recomputing on the client to cross-check only doubles the places that must be updated together.

sources.title: Guide to app architecture: common principles

questions.text: A feature is gated by a remotely fetched flag, and the app launches offline before any fetch has ever succeeded. What must the design provide?

answers.text: A blocking fetch during startup, so the flag is known before the first screen is composed.
An in-app default plus the cached last-known value, so the flag resolves without a network call.
A fallback that turns the feature on, since a new path is safer than an outdated one.
A retry loop around the fetch, so that the flag arrives before the user can interact.

questions.explanation: A remote flag introduces a network dependency into the launch path, and it must never be able to block or break a cold start. The pattern is an in-app default that makes the app behave sensibly with no configuration at all, plus persistence of the last fetched values so a returning user keeps the behaviour they had, while the fetch happens in the background and applies at the next opportunity. Blocking or retrying at startup trades a configuration problem for a launch failure, and defaulting a risky feature to on removes the kill switch the flag exists to provide.

sources.title: Get started with Firebase Remote Config

questions.text: A shared Kotlin Multiplatform module declares an iOS target and configures binaries.framework for it. What does the build produce for the Xcode project to consume?

answers.text: A JVM library that the iOS app loads through an embedded Kotlin runtime at launch.
Swift source files generated from the Kotlin declarations and then compiled by Xcode.
A native framework compiled by Kotlin/Native that Xcode links like any other framework.
A JavaScript bundle that the iOS app evaluates inside a WebView-backed runtime.

questions.explanation: Declaring the target registers a Kotlin/Native compilation; configuring a framework binary is what makes the build emit one. It is compiled ahead of time into a binary framework — static or dynamic, often packaged as an XCFramework or delivered through CocoaPods or Swift Package Manager — which Xcode links exactly as it would a framework written in Objective-C or Swift. The Kotlin declarations are exposed through a generated Objective-C header, so there is no JVM in the iOS app, no generated Swift sources to compile, and no JavaScript runtime involved.

questions.text: Select all that apply. Which of these can be referenced directly from commonMain in a module targeting Android and iOS?

answers.text: java.time.Instant, for the date arithmetic that both platforms need.
kotlin.collections and the rest of the common Kotlin standard library.
android.util.Log, for the diagnostics that both platforms want to emit.
java.io.File, for reading a configuration file bundled with the app.

questions.explanation: commonMain is compiled for every target, so it may reference only declarations that exist on all of them: the common Kotlin standard library and multiplatform libraries such as kotlinx.coroutines, kotlinx.serialization and kotlinx-datetime. Anything from the JDK, including java.time and java.io, and anything from the Android SDK exists on the JVM and Android targets alone, so naming it in commonMain fails to compile for iOS. Reaching such an API needs an expect/actual declaration or an interface implemented per platform.

sources.title: Kotlin Multiplatform project structure: source sets

questions.text: A team shares androidx ViewModel classes from commonMain across Android and iOS. What still has to be supplied by each platform?

answers.text: The owner that creates and clears the ViewModel, whose lifetime belongs to a platform host.
The ViewModel base class itself, because androidx.lifecycle ships no multiplatform artifact.
The coroutine scope, because viewModelScope is defined only for the Android target.
The state holder, because StateFlow is unavailable outside the JVM and Android targets.

questions.explanation: The lifecycle-viewmodel artifact is published for Kotlin Multiplatform, so the ViewModel class, viewModelScope and the clearing behaviour are all usable from commonMain. What stays inherently platform-specific is the owner that decides the lifetime: on Android a ViewModelStoreOwner supplied by an Activity, Fragment or navigation entry, and on iOS whatever the host controller does to create the instance and clear it when the screen goes away. StateFlow belongs to kotlinx.coroutines and works on every target.

questions.text: Shared code declares an expect class, and one platform already has a class whose members satisfy that declaration exactly. What is the simplest valid actual declaration there?

answers.text: An actual class that extends the existing platform class and overrides nothing of its own.
An actual object that delegates to a fresh instance of the platform class on every call.
An actual typealias naming the existing platform class, whose API matches the expectation.
An actual interface that the existing platform class implements through an extension.

questions.explanation: actual typealias exists for exactly this case: when a platform already offers a type whose members satisfy the expected declaration, the actual can name it instead of wrapping it, and the compiler still checks that every expected member is present. Wrapping through subclassing or delegation compiles in some cases but adds a layer for no benefit and can fail outright if the platform type is final. An expect class also cannot be actualised as an object or an interface — the kind of declaration has to match.

questions.text: A Compose Multiplatform module keeps images and strings under composeResources. How does shared code in commonMain refer to them on Android, iOS and desktop?

answers.text: Through a generated Res object whose accessors resolve to the right asset for each platform.
Through android.R, which the Compose Multiplatform plugin makes available on every target.
Through a platform-specific expect/actual accessor written by hand for each supported target.
Through file paths passed as plain strings, since resource identifiers exist only on Android.

questions.explanation: The Compose Multiplatform resources library generates a Res object from the composeResources directory at build time, and shared composables use entries such as Res.drawable.icon or Res.string.title straight from commonMain while the library loads the right asset for the running platform. That is the whole point of the mechanism: no android.R, no hand-written expect/actual per resource and no raw file paths — and qualifiers such as locale, density and theme are handled by the same generated accessors.

questions.text: A screen must reflect later local writes that other parts of the app make. Which repository API shape supports that, and why?

answers.text: A suspend function returning a snapshot, because the screen can call it again after each write.
A property holding the last value, because the screen can read it during every recomposition.
A Flow of the data, because the repository can emit again whenever its source of truth changes.
A suspend read plus a callback the repository invokes, because callbacks cost less than a Flow.

questions.explanation: The requirement is that the screen learns about changes it did not itself initiate, so the repository has to be able to push. Returning a Flow lets the local source of truth — a Room query, a DataStore file — drive re-emission while the screen simply collects. A one-shot suspend read is correct at the instant it returns and stale immediately after, leaving the caller to guess when to repeat it. A callback API can work but re-implements what Flow already gives, including cancellation, and a plain property offers recomposition nothing to observe.

questions.text: How does an MVP presenter's relationship with its view differ from an MVVM state holder's?

answers.text: A presenter observes state the view exposes, while a ViewModel holds a reference to the view.
A presenter runs on a background thread by definition, while a ViewModel runs on the main one.
A presenter holds a view interface and pushes updates in; a ViewModel exposes state the view observes.
A presenter owns the navigation stack, while a ViewModel is forbidden from triggering navigation.

questions.explanation: The direction of the dependency separates them. A presenter is handed a view interface and calls methods on it, so it must not retain or invoke a detached view. That creates attach and detach bookkeeping even when another owner keeps the presenter alive across a configuration change. A ViewModel publishes observable state and knows nothing about the view, so it survives configuration changes and the view simply rebuilds itself from whatever state is current. Neither pattern dictates threading, and neither forbids modelling navigation.

questions.text: Select all that apply. A team follows Clean Architecture's dependency rule and keeps the domain layer free of framework types. Which consequences follow?

answers.text: The number of layers determines how fast the app builds, whatever the module structure is.
The domain layer can be unit-tested with no Android dependency and no instrumentation.
Business rules can no longer be plain Kotlin classes and have to become external configuration.
A Room entity or framework-annotated transport DTO cannot double as the domain model, so mapping appears there.

questions.explanation: Pointing every dependency inward means the innermost layer names no framework type, so it compiles and runs in a plain JVM test — and in a multiplatform project it is exactly the layer that can be shared. The cost lands wherever a framework-annotated type would otherwise have been reused: a Room entity or framework-annotated transport DTO may not double as the domain model, so mapping code and extra types appear at that boundary. An unannotated, domain-owned type can still be deserialized by a suitable converter without requiring mapping. That is real work, worth paying when the domain has rules to protect and hard to justify when it does not. Build speed follows from module structure rather than layer count, and the rules stay ordinary Kotlin.

questions.text: A domain-layer use case accepts an android.net.Uri parameter and returns a Retrofit Response. Which problem does that most directly cause?

answers.text: The use case cannot be injected, because a DI framework has no binding for framework classes.
The use case stops being suspendable, because Retrofit types do not cross a coroutine boundary.
The domain layer gains a compile-time cycle with the data layer, so the module stops building.
The domain becomes coupled to Android and Retrofit, losing framework independence and portability.

questions.explanation: The dependency rule exists so the innermost layer names nothing from the outer ones. Accepting a Uri requires the Android SDK and returning a Response ties the use case to Retrofit, so the domain module loses framework independence, cannot be shared unchanged with a non-Android target, and has to change whenever the transport contract changes. The use case can still be tested with appropriate Android-aware JVM or device infrastructure, so coupling does not mean untestability. The fix is to accept and return domain types and let the data layer do the mapping. Nothing here inherently breaks injection, coroutines or compilation, which is precisely why the design problem is easy to leave in place.

questions.text: An Android module has a drawable in src/debug/res/drawable whose file name matches one in src/main/res/drawable. What does the build do with them?

answers.text: The two are merged, and the debug copy's contents are combined with those of the main one.
The build fails with a duplicate resource error until one of the two files is renamed.
For the debug variant the debug copy replaces the main one; release keeps the main copy.
The main copy wins everywhere, because src/main takes precedence over variant source sets.

questions.explanation: The Android Gradle Plugin assembles each variant from several source sets — main, the build type, the product flavour and their combinations — where the more specific set takes priority. A same-named drawable in src/debug therefore replaces the src/main one for debug builds and leaves release untouched, which is the mechanism behind debug-only launcher icons and stub implementations. Files under values/ are the instructive exception: two strings.xml files are merged, and the build type's entries override same-named entries from main rather than replacing the whole file. Either way the precedence is defined, so there is nothing for the build to report as a conflict.

questions.text: Two libraries on one configuration transitively require different versions of the same dependency. What does Gradle do by default?

answers.text: It selects the highest requested version and uses that one for the whole configuration.
It fails the build and asks the developer to state which of the versions should be used.
It keeps both versions on the classpath, isolated from one another by separate class loaders.
It selects the version requested by whichever dependency is declared first in the build file.

questions.explanation: Gradle resolves a configuration to a single version per module, and its default conflict resolution takes the highest version any participant requested. That is usually convenient and occasionally wrong, which is why strict versions, dependency constraints and resolution strategies exist to override it — and why a dependency report is worth inspecting. A JVM classpath can physically contain JARs with duplicate class definitions; class-loader visibility and ordering then determine which definition is loaded and can cause linkage failures. Gradle's module conflict resolution provides a coherent dependency graph before that point, and build-file declaration order does not choose the winning module version.

questions.text: Select all that apply. An app is distributed using Play App Signing. Which statements about its keys are correct?

answers.text: The developer signs the bundle with an upload key, and Google Play signs the generated delivery APKs with the app signing key.
The app signing key is stored in the project repository so that continuous integration can sign releases.
Losing the upload key is recoverable, because Google Play can register a replacement for the app.
Play App Signing removes the need to sign the bundle at all, since Google Play signs the uploaded file.

questions.explanation: With Play App Signing, Google holds the key that signs the APKs users install, while the developer holds a separate upload key that proves who is uploading. Play verifies the app bundle's upload signature, generates the delivery APKs, and signs those APKs with the app signing key. This separation is why a lost upload key can be replaced through Play support, something that would be impossible for the key devices already trust. Neither key belongs in version control, and the bundle still has to be signed with the upload key before it can be uploaded.

questions.text: A project migrates its Room and Dagger annotation processing from kapt to KSP. Why does that usually shorten build times?

answers.text: KSP runs its processors in parallel with compilation, while kapt runs them strictly afterwards.
KSP caches its generated output remotely, while kapt regenerates everything on each build.
KSP reads Kotlin directly, while kapt first generates Java stubs for every Kotlin source file.
KSP skips annotation processing on incremental builds, while kapt reprocesses every source file.

questions.explanation: kapt is a bridge to Java annotation processing: before any processor can run, it generates Java stubs for all Kotlin sources so that javac-based processors can see the declarations, and that stub generation is usually the dominant cost. KSP is a Kotlin-native API, so processors read Kotlin declarations directly and the stub step disappears. Both support incremental processing, and neither runs concurrently with compilation nor caches generated output remotely on its own.

questions.text: A messaging app relies on FCM data messages to carry the full text of each new message to the client. Why is that a fragile design?

answers.text: FCM strips any data payload beyond a few bytes, so only an identifier can be carried.
FCM delivery is best effort, so a message can be dropped, collapsed or arrive late.
FCM delivers a data message only while the app is in the foreground, losing background ones.
FCM requires an acknowledgement for each message and redelivers one that is not acknowledged.

questions.explanation: FCM offers no delivery guarantee. A message that cannot be delivered is stored only until its time to live expires and is then discarded, and a pending message sharing a collapse key with a newer one is replaced by it. Treating the push as a signal — something changed, come and sync — and fetching the authoritative content over the app's own API keeps the client correct whatever FCM does. Data payloads are limited to a few kilobytes rather than a few bytes, data messages do reach a backgrounded app, and there is no client acknowledgement protocol.

questions.text: onMessageReceived() in a FirebaseMessagingService starts a long download of the content the message refers to. What should it do instead?

answers.text: Move the download to a coroutine on GlobalScope, since that outlives the callback itself.
Nothing differently, because the callback already runs off the main thread with no time limit.
Block inside the callback but raise the service's thread priority so that it finishes sooner.
Enqueue a WorkManager request, because the callback has a short window before it may be stopped.

questions.explanation: The onMessageReceived() callback has a short execution window, and background execution limits can pause or terminate processing before it finishes, so work that depends on the network must not run inline — the documentation names fetching an image for a notification as exactly the case to avoid. Handing it to WorkManager makes the work durable: it survives the callback returning, the process dying and even a reboot, and it can wait for connectivity. A GlobalScope coroutine dies with the process, and thread priority does not lengthen the window.

questions.text: An app targeting a recent Android version posts a notification whose channel ID was never created. What does the user see?

answers.text: The notification at default importance, because the system creates the missing channel.
The notification in a system-generated "Other" channel that offers no user controls.
Nothing, because the system does not display a notification whose channel does not exist.
A system dialog asking them to let the app create the notification channel it needs.

questions.explanation: Since Android 8.0 every notification has to belong to a channel the app created beforehand, because the channel is what carries the user's settings for that category — importance, sound, vibration and whether it appears at all. Posting to an unknown channel is dropped without an error, which is why channel creation belongs in an early idempotent step such as Application.onCreate(). The system invents no channels, and creating one needs no permission; posting a notification does on Android 13 and later, which is a separate requirement.

questions.text: Select all that apply. A messaging notification offers an inline reply from the notification shade. Which statements about that action are correct?

answers.text: The reply text reaches the app through a RemoteInput attached to the action's PendingIntent.
The action has to launch an Activity, because a notification cannot deliver input to a receiver.
The app should update the same notification after handling the reply so the user sees it was sent.
The reply is stored by the system and handed to the app the next time the user launches it.

questions.explanation: An inline reply is an ordinary notification action with a RemoteInput attached: the system collects the text and puts it into the Intent behind the action's PendingIntent, which the app reads with RemoteInput.getResultsFromIntent(). The target is normally a broadcast receiver or a service rather than an Activity, which is exactly why the user never leaves the screen they were on. The app then has to update or cancel that notification itself so the shade reflects what happened; nothing is deferred until the next launch.

questions.text: Kotlin has no checked exceptions. What does that mean for a Kotlin function that is also called from Java or from Swift?

answers.text: The exception is converted into a Result value at the interoperability boundary for the caller.
The exception cannot cross that boundary at all and is swallowed by the Kotlin runtime.
The caller gets no compiler-enforced signal, so @Throws is needed to declare it in the signature.
The caller has to wrap every Kotlin call in try/catch, because the compiler treats them as checked.

questions.explanation: Kotlin removed checked exceptions, so a Kotlin signature says nothing about what may be thrown and a Kotlin caller is never forced to handle anything. That is workable inside Kotlin, but Java's catch-or-declare rule and Swift's throwing-function model both need the information: annotating the declaration with @Throws puts the exception into the generated signature, which is what makes a Kotlin/Native function usable as a throwing function from Swift. Exceptions do cross the boundary — an undeclared one simply arrives unannounced, and from Swift it terminates the app.

questions.text: A builder is declared as fun buildQuery(block: QueryBuilder.() -> Unit). What does the receiver in that function type give the caller?

answers.text: Inside the lambda the builder is the implicit this, so its members need no qualifier.
The lambda runs on the builder's own thread, so the calls inside it are serialised for safety.
The builder instance arrives as the lambda's single parameter, reachable there as it.
The lambda is inlined by the compiler, so no object is allocated for it at the call site.

questions.explanation: A function type with a receiver makes that receiver the implicit this inside the lambda, so its members can be called with no qualifier — which is what produces the nested, declarative shape of Kotlin DSLs such as buildString or the Gradle Kotlin DSL. A plain (QueryBuilder) -> Unit would instead pass the builder as a parameter reached through it. Whether the lambda allocates an object is decided by the inline modifier rather than by the receiver, and a receiver says nothing at all about threading.

questions.text: Select all that apply. Which statements about Kotlin's internal visibility modifier are correct?

answers.text: An internal declaration is visible only inside the file that declares it.
An internal declaration is visible to subclasses that live in another module.
An internal declaration is visible everywhere inside the same compilation module.
An internal declaration is hidden from Java code compiled in the same module.

questions.explanation: internal scopes a declaration to the compilation module — the set of files compiled together, such as one Gradle source set — so it is reachable from every package in that module but not from a module depending on it. Restricting visibility to a single file is what a top-level private does, and a subclass in another module can see protected members rather than internal ones. On the JVM internal compiles to public with a mangled name, so Java in the same module can technically reach it: the boundary is enforced by the Kotlin compiler, not by the bytecode.

questions.text: A team wants to verify that a screen restores correctly after system-initiated process death. Which procedure actually reproduces that case?

answers.text: Enable "Don't keep activities", which destroys the process as soon as the app is backgrounded.
Background the app, terminate its process from the tooling, then return to it from Recents.
Rotate the device several times, which makes the system recreate the process on each rotation.
Call finish() on the Activity and then relaunch the app from its icon in the launcher.

questions.explanation: Process death is the case where saved instance state is restored but everything the process held is gone. Reproducing it means genuinely killing the process while the task stays in Recents and then resuming that task — what the tooling's terminate action or adb shell am kill does. "Don't keep activities" destroys the Activity but leaves the process running, so application singletons, the dependency graph and any static cache are still populated when the screen is rebuilt — and depending on one of those is exactly the bug that survives this setting and then fails in the field. Rotation is a configuration change within the same process, and finishing the Activity ends the task instead of restoring it.

questions.text: A dialog-themed Activity is launched over an existing screen and covers only part of it. Which lifecycle callbacks does the Activity underneath receive?

answers.text: onPause() and onStop(), because another Activity is now in the foreground above it.
onStop() alone, because pausing applies when an Activity loses focus rather than visibility.
None of them, because a dialog-themed Activity draws inside the existing Activity's window.
onPause() alone, because it remains partly visible and is therefore not stopped.

questions.explanation: Visibility is what separates onPause() from onStop(). onPause() means the Activity has lost focus but may still be seen, which is exactly the situation under a partly transparent or dialog-themed Activity; onStop() follows only once it becomes completely hidden. That is why anything the user can still see should be released and reacquired around onStart() and onStop() rather than onResume() and onPause(), and why slow work in onPause() delays the new screen from appearing. A dialog-themed Activity is a separate Activity with its own window, not a view added to the old one.

questions.text: Select all that apply. A Fragment is replaced by another one and added to the back stack. Which statements about it are correct?

answers.text: The Fragment instance is destroyed too, so its non-view fields are reinitialised on return.
Its view hierarchy is destroyed, so a view binding kept in a field points at detached views.
onDestroy() runs on it, so the Fragment is built from scratch when the user navigates back.
Its ViewModel is cleared, because clearing follows the Fragment's view lifecycle.

questions.explanation: A Fragment placed on the back stack goes through onDestroyView() but not onDestroy(): the instance survives and its non-view fields keep their values, while the views are torn down and rebuilt when the user comes back. That asymmetry is the source of the classic leak — a binding or view reference held in a Fragment field outlives the views it points at, which is why it has to be cleared in onDestroyView() and why View-bound observation should use viewLifecycleOwner. A Fragment's ViewModel is cleared with the Fragment, not with its view.

questions.text: Select all that apply. The system is low on memory and must reclaim some. Which statements about which app process it removes first are correct?

answers.text: A purely cached process with no active components and no dependent clients is among the first candidates.
Processes are reclaimed in the order they were started, with the oldest process killed first.
A process running a foreground service is ranked well above a purely cached process.
A process is spared as long as it still holds objects referenced from a static field.

questions.explanation: Android ranks every process by the most important active component or dependency associated with it — foreground, visible, service, then cached — and reclaims from the least important end. A process currently executing a BroadcastReceiver is foreground, even if it has no visible Activity or running service. A purely cached process with no active components or dependent clients sits at the bottom and can be removed at any moment, which is why in-memory state is no place for anything the user must not lose. A foreground service raises its process well above that level. Start order plays no part, and the app's own references have none either: the entire process goes, static fields included.

questions.text: A custom ViewGroup must take over a drag gesture that its children would otherwise consume. Which override expresses that?

answers.text: onTouchEvent(), returning false so the event travels past the children up to the parent.
dispatchTouchEvent() on each child, returning false to decline the event for that child.
setOnTouchListener() on the ViewGroup, which receives events before any child can see them.
onInterceptTouchEvent(), returning true once the gesture is recognised so later events come to it.

questions.explanation: A touch event travels down the hierarchy through dispatchTouchEvent(), and every ViewGroup on the way is offered onInterceptTouchEvent(). Returning true there takes the gesture away from the children — they receive ACTION_CANCEL — and the rest of the stream goes to the parent's own onTouchEvent(). That is how a scrolling container claims a drag once the finger has moved far enough. Returning false from onTouchEvent() passes the event back up rather than forward to children, and a touch listener on the ViewGroup runs as part of that view's own handling, after interception has already been decided.

sources.title: Intercept touch events in a ViewGroup
